ethereum-description: How Ethereum uses a blockchain: what it keeps track of, the programs anyone can add, ETH's jobs and who keeps it all running.
ethereum-anything-summary: Ethereum's blockchain keeps track of much more than money.
ethereum-anything-intro-p1: Bitcoin's blockchain was made to keep track of one main thing: who has how much of its money. Ethereum's blockchain was built to keep track of much more.
ethereum-anything-intro-p2: Concert tickets, digital art, items in a game, votes in a club: each can be written down on Ethereum, saying who owns what. Many of them are tokens: things on Ethereum that can be owned and sent, just as ETH can.
ethereum-anything-sort-prompt: Ethereum's blockchain is public: anyone can read it. Sort each thing: is it a good fit for Ethereum, or better kept off?
ethereum-anything-sort-explain: Who owns a ticket, a drawing or a game item, and how a club voted, all fit on Ethereum. Secrets don't: anyone can read what's written there, and it stays for good.
ethereum-anything-game-prompt: You win a rare sword in a game that keeps its items on Ethereum. Later, the company that made the game closes. What happens to the record that the sword is yours?
ethereum-anything-game-fb-gone: The record isn't on the company's computers. Think about who keeps Ethereum's copies.
ethereum-anything-game-opt-stays: It stays on Ethereum, still showing it's yours
ethereum-anything-game-fb-stays: Right. The record lives on Ethereum, not with the company, so it stays. The sword may not be much use without the game, though.
ethereum-anything-game-opt-moves: It moves into another game by itself
ethereum-anything-game-fb-moves: Nothing on Ethereum moves by itself. Think about where the record is kept.
ethereum-anything-takeaway-p1: Ethereum's blockchain can keep track of much more than money, like tickets, art, game items and votes. Everything on it is public, so secrets stay off.
ethereum-rules-summary: Programs with their own rules, run the same way by everyone.
ethereum-rules-intro-p1: Give the same recipe to cooks all over the world. If every cook follows it exactly, every kitchen makes the same cake.
ethereum-rules-intro-p2: Ethereum works like that for programs. Anyone can add a program with their own rules, and every node runs it exactly the same way, so every copy gets the same result. These programs are called smart contracts.
ethereum-rules-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: a program on Ethereum sends a prize to whoever scores highest in a quiz. Thousands of nodes run it. Do they all get the same answer?
ethereum-rules-predict-opt-same: Yes, every node gets the same answer
ethereum-rules-predict-fb-same: Good instinct. Each node follows the same rules exactly, like cooks with one recipe.
ethereum-rules-predict-opt-differ: No, each node can decide for itself
ethereum-rules-predict-fb-differ: Nodes don't get to choose. Think about cooks who follow one recipe exactly.
ethereum-rules-predict-opt-fastest: Only the fastest node's answer counts
ethereum-rules-predict-fb-fastest: Speed doesn't decide anything here. Think about what happens when every cook follows the same recipe.
ethereum-rules-life-prompt: Put the life of a program on Ethereum in order.
ethereum-rules-life-item-write: Someone writes a program with their rules
ethereum-rules-life-item-add: They add it to Ethereum and pay a fee
ethereum-rules-life-item-use: Someone sends a transaction to use it
ethereum-rules-life-item-run: Every node runs its rules the same way
ethereum-rules-life-item-record: Every copy records the same result
ethereum-rules-life-explain: Once a program is added, anyone can use it. Every node runs the same rules, so every copy ends up with the same result.
ethereum-rules-who-prompt: Who is allowed to add a program to Ethereum?
ethereum-rules-who-fb-anyone: Right. There's no one to ask. Anyone can add a program, as long as they pay the fee.
ethereum-rules-who-opt-approved: Only developers that Ethereum's company approves
ethereum-rules-who-fb-approved: There's no Ethereum company handing out permission. Think about who runs Ethereum's copies.
ethereum-rules-who-opt-nodes: Only people who run a node
ethereum-rules-who-fb-nodes: Running a node and adding a program are separate things. You don't need one to do the other.
ethereum-rules-takeaway-p1: Anyone can add a program with their own rules to Ethereum, and every node runs it the same way, so everyone gets the same result.
ethereum-jobs-summary: The three things Ethereum's own money does.
ethereum-jobs-intro-p1: When you rent skates, you leave a deposit. Bring them back in good shape and you get it all back. Break the rules and you lose some of it.
ethereum-jobs-intro-p2: ETH, Ethereum's own money, has three jobs. It pays the fee for every transaction. It can be sent to anyone, like money. And validators, the people who add Ethereum's pages, lock some up like that skate deposit, as a promise to play fair.
ethereum-jobs-match-prompt: Match each job of ETH to what it looks like in real life.
ethereum-jobs-match-match-fee: Every transaction needs some to go through
ethereum-jobs-match-match-send: Paying back a cousin who lives far away
ethereum-jobs-match-match-lock: A promise to add pages honestly
ethereum-jobs-match-explain: ETH pays for every transaction, travels like money and backs the promise validators make to play fair.
ethereum-jobs-miss-prompt: Ana thinks ETH is only for sending to friends. What is she missing?
ethereum-jobs-miss-opt-jobs: ETH also pays every fee and is locked up to help keep Ethereum safe
ethereum-jobs-miss-fb-jobs: Right. Sending is only one job. ETH also pays for every transaction, and validators lock it up as their promise to play fair.
ethereum-jobs-miss-opt-nothing: Nothing: sending is all ETH does
ethereum-jobs-miss-fb-nothing: Think about how a transaction gets paid for, and what validators put on the line.
ethereum-jobs-miss-opt-share: ETH is also a share in the company that runs Ethereum
ethereum-jobs-miss-fb-share: No company runs Ethereum, and ETH isn't a share in anything. Think about what every transaction needs.
ethereum-jobs-takeaway-p1: ETH has three jobs: it pays fees, it can be sent like money, and validators lock it up as a promise that helps keep Ethereum safe.
ethereum-running-intro-p1: Ethereum isn't run by a company. People all over the world run its nodes: at home, at work and in big computer centers.
ethereum-running-intro-p2: Nobody owns Ethereum, so it has no off switch. To stop it, someone would have to switch off every node, everywhere, all at once.
ethereum-running-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: who could switch Ethereum off?
ethereum-running-predict-opt-founders: The people who first built it
ethereum-running-predict-fb-founders: Building something first doesn't mean you control it now. Test it in the next step.
ethereum-running-predict-fb-company: Ethereum isn't owned by a company. Test it in the next step.
ethereum-running-predict-fb-nobody: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
ethereum-running-world-prompt: Try to switch Ethereum off. Turn off every computer here, add a block, then switch one back on.
ethereum-running-world-explain: Switching these computers off didn't stop Ethereum. Thousands of others around the world kept adding blocks, and the computer that came back caught up from them.
ethereum-running-matters-prompt: Why does it matter that nobody owns Ethereum?
ethereum-running-matters-opt-free: It means using Ethereum costs nothing
ethereum-running-matters-fb-free: You still pay a fee in ETH for each transaction. Ownership is about who's in control, not price.
ethereum-running-matters-opt-open: No one can shut it down or choose who's allowed to use it
ethereum-running-matters-fb-open: Right. With no owner, there's nobody who can switch it off or turn people away.
ethereum-running-matters-opt-frozen: It means nobody is allowed to improve it
ethereum-running-matters-fb-frozen: People around the world still work on improving Ethereum together. It just doesn't belong to any one of them.
ethereum-running-takeaway-p1: People all over the world run Ethereum's nodes. Nobody owns it, so no one can switch it off.
ethereum-uses-summary: Everyday needs that Ethereum helps with.
ethereum-uses-intro-p1: Think of the ways you use money and the things you own: paying people, keeping savings, collecting, playing. Ethereum lets people do many of them without a bank in the middle.
ethereum-uses-intro-p2: People send money to family in other countries, hold stablecoins (tokens built to keep a steady value, like a regular currency), collect digital art and play games where they truly own their items.
ethereum-uses-needs-prompt: Match each use of Ethereum to the everyday need it helps with.
ethereum-uses-needs-match-games: Truly owning the items you win
ethereum-uses-needs-explain: Each use meets an everyday need, with Ethereum keeping the record instead of a bank or a single company.
ethereum-uses-steady-prompt: Leo sends money to his grandma in another country. She wants it to buy just as much food when she spends it later. Which token fits best?
ethereum-uses-steady-fb-stable: Right. A stablecoin is built to keep a steady value, so what Leo sends still buys about the same later.
ethereum-uses-steady-fb-art: Art can be fun to collect, but it's hard to spend at a shop, and its value can swing a lot. Think about which token is built to hold its value.
ethereum-uses-steady-fb-eth: ETH is easy to send, but its price goes up and down, so what she can buy with it may change. Think about which token is built to hold its value.
ethereum-uses-takeaway-p1: People use Ethereum for everyday needs, like sending money abroad, steady-value coins, digital art and games, without a bank in the middle.
ethereum-exam-track-prompt: What can Ethereum's blockchain keep track of?
ethereum-exam-track-opt-eth: Only who has how much ETH
ethereum-exam-track-opt-many: Who owns things like tokens, tickets, art and game items
ethereum-exam-track-opt-files: A copy of every website in the world
ethereum-exam-track-explain: Ethereum was built to keep track of much more than money: tokens, tickets, art, game items, votes and more.
ethereum-exam-password-prompt: Why is Ethereum a bad place to keep your password?
ethereum-exam-password-opt-public: Anyone can read what's written on it
ethereum-exam-password-opt-forgets: It forgets things after a while
ethereum-exam-password-opt-long: Passwords are too long to fit
ethereum-exam-password-explain: A blockchain is public: anyone can read everything on it, and it stays there for good. That's great for who owns what, and terrible for secrets.
ethereum-exam-who-adds-prompt: Who can add a program with their own rules to Ethereum?
ethereum-exam-who-adds-opt-approved: Only developers approved by Ethereum's owners
ethereum-exam-who-adds-opt-nodes: Only people who run a node
ethereum-exam-who-adds-explain: Anyone can add a program, called a smart contract, by paying the fee. There's no owner handing out permission.
ethereum-exam-same-result-prompt: Thousands of nodes run the same program for the same transaction. What do they get?
ethereum-exam-same-result-opt-average: Slightly different answers that get averaged
ethereum-exam-same-result-opt-same: The same result, on every copy
ethereum-exam-same-result-explain: Every node follows the program's rules exactly, like cooks with one recipe, so every copy gets the same result.
ethereum-exam-fee-prompt: You use an app on Ethereum. What do you pay its transaction fee with?
ethereum-exam-fee-opt-free: Nothing: apps on Ethereum are free
ethereum-exam-fee-explain: Every transaction on Ethereum pays its fee in ETH. That's one of ETH's three jobs.
ethereum-exam-lock-prompt: Why do validators lock up some of their ETH?
ethereum-exam-lock-opt-promise: As a promise to add pages fairly, which they lose some of if they cheat
ethereum-exam-lock-opt-interest: To keep it safe in a bank
ethereum-exam-lock-explain: Locked-up ETH is a promise to play fair, like a deposit on rented skates. Validators who cheat lose some of it.
ethereum-exam-owner-opt-founders: The people who first built it
ethereum-exam-owner-opt-company: A company with a head office
ethereum-exam-owner-opt-nobody: Nobody: people all over the world run it together
ethereum-exam-owner-explain: Ethereum has no owner, no boss and no shareholders. It's kept running by computers that people all over the world run.
ethereum-exam-off-prompt: One country switches off every Ethereum node inside its borders. What happens to Ethereum?
ethereum-exam-off-opt-keeps: It keeps running on nodes everywhere else
ethereum-exam-off-opt-lost: Every copy of the blockchain is lost
ethereum-exam-off-explain: Thousands of nodes around the world each keep a copy. If some switch off, the rest keep Ethereum running.
ethereum-exam-stablecoin-prompt: What is a stablecoin built to do?
ethereum-exam-stablecoin-opt-steady: Keep a steady value, like a regular currency
ethereum-exam-stablecoin-opt-vanish: Disappear after you spend it once
ethereum-exam-stablecoin-explain: A stablecoin is a token built to keep a steady value, usually matching a regular currency.
ethereum-exam-drawing-prompt: Mia buys a one-of-a-kind digital drawing on Ethereum. What does Ethereum keep track of?
ethereum-exam-drawing-opt-owner: That Mia's address now owns it
ethereum-exam-drawing-opt-file: A private copy that only Mia can see
ethereum-exam-drawing-opt-nothing: Nothing, since art can't go on a blockchain
ethereum-exam-drawing-explain: Ethereum records who owns the drawing, for anyone to check. Like everything on Ethereum, that record is public.
upgrades-description: Nobody owns Ethereum, so who decides how it changes? Follow a proposal from first draft to live upgrade, and see why many software teams and node runners keep it in check.
upgrades-who-summary: No company runs Ethereum. Find out who has a say in changing it, and who has the last word.
upgrades-who-intro-p1: When an app on your phone changes, the company behind it ships an update and everyone gets it. Ethereum has no company like that. No person, foundation or team can change its rules alone.
upgrades-who-intro-p2: The rules live in the software that thousands of nodes, the computers that each keep a copy of the blockchain and check every block, choose to run. Deciding on changes and getting them adopted is called governance, and on Ethereum it happens in the open, not through any vote on the blockchain.
upgrades-who-predict-prompt: A famous Ethereum developer wants to change how fees work. What does it take?
upgrades-who-predict-opt-fame: An announcement: their reputation makes it happen
upgrades-who-predict-fb-fame: Reputation helps an idea get heard, but nobody's word changes the software nodes run. Every node runner decides what to install.
upgrades-who-predict-opt-agree: Convincing many groups, then node runners installing it
upgrades-who-predict-fb-agree: Right. Developers, software teams and node runners all have to go along, and a change only takes effect once nodes actually run it.
upgrades-who-predict-opt-vote: Winning a vote among ETH holders
upgrades-who-predict-fb-vote: Ethereum has no official vote that sets its rules. Holding ETH doesn't come with a ballot; decisions come from public debate and from what node runners choose to run.
upgrades-who-roles-p1: Several groups take part. Proposal authors write up an idea for everyone to pick apart. Client teams build the software a node runs, called a client, and there are several clients, each made by a separate team.
upgrades-who-roles-p2: Node runners pick which client and which version to install; validators, who stake ETH to add blocks, are node runners too. And the people and apps using Ethereum decide whether it's still worth using. No group can force the others.
upgrades-who-refuse-prompt: The client teams all ship a change that most node runners dislike. What can the node runners do?
upgrades-who-refuse-fb-automatic: Node software doesn't update itself behind the runner's back. Each runner chooses when, and whether, to install a new version.
upgrades-who-refuse-opt-refuse: Keep running the old version and refuse the change
upgrades-who-refuse-fb-refuse: Right. Nobody can make a node install new software. That's why client teams avoid changes a large part of the community opposes.
upgrades-who-refuse-opt-founders: Ask Ethereum's founders to overrule the teams
upgrades-who-refuse-fb-founders: Ethereum's founders have no special power over its rules today. There's nobody above the teams to appeal to.
upgrades-who-match-prompt: Match each group to its part in changing Ethereum.
upgrades-who-match-match-authors: Write up a change for review
upgrades-who-match-match-runners: Decide what their computers actually run
upgrades-who-match-match-users: Stay on the chain, or walk away
upgrades-who-match-explain: Authors propose, client teams build, node runners decide what actually runs, and users and apps decide whether to stay. A change needs all of them on board.
upgrades-who-takeaway-p1: Nobody owns Ethereum. A change needs wide agreement, and it only takes effect when node runners choose to install it.
upgrades-eips-summary: How anyone can propose a change, the stages a proposal moves through, and which proposals need the whole network.
upgrades-eips-intro-p1: Every change starts as an Ethereum Improvement Proposal, or EIP: a public document that describes the change precisely and explains why it's worth making. Each gets a number. EIP-1559, for example, changed how fees work and started burning the base fee.
upgrades-eips-intro-p2: A proposal moves through stages in the open: Draft while the author shapes it, Review when it's ready for feedback, Last Call as a final window for objections, and Final once it's settled. Many never get that far: they stall or are withdrawn.
upgrades-eips-author-prompt: You have an idea that could make Ethereum better. Who's allowed to write an EIP for it?
upgrades-eips-author-fb-devs: Most authors are developers, because a proposal needs a precise technical write-up. But no title or membership is required.
upgrades-eips-author-fb-anyone: Right. Anyone can write an EIP. Getting it accepted is the hard part: it has to win over the groups who'd build and run it.
upgrades-eips-author-fb-holders: Writing a proposal costs nothing and needs no ETH. It's a public document, open to anyone.
upgrades-eips-kinds-p1: Not every EIP changes the network. A core EIP changes the rules every node checks, so all nodes have to switch together in a network upgrade, or they'd disagree about which blocks are valid.
upgrades-eips-kinds-p2: An ERC is a standard for apps, like the common format most tokens follow. Apps can choose to adopt it, and nodes don't need to change at all. That's why core EIPs need much broader agreement.
upgrades-eips-sort-prompt: Sort each proposal: does it need every node to upgrade, or can apps choose to adopt it?
upgrades-eips-sort-explain: Core EIPs change what nodes check, so the whole network has to switch at the same moment. ERCs are app standards: a token or wallet can skip one and still work on Ethereum.
upgrades-eips-bundle-prompt: Core EIPs usually ship several at a time, bundled into one upgrade. Why not one at a time?
upgrades-eips-bundle-opt-fees: Bundling lowers gas fees for everyone
upgrades-eips-bundle-fb-fees: How changes are grouped has nothing to do with fees. Think about who has to do something for every upgrade.
upgrades-eips-bundle-opt-coordinate: Every upgrade means every client and every node switching at once
upgrades-eips-bundle-fb-coordinate: Right. Each upgrade needs every client team to release and every node runner to install, so it makes sense to bundle changes.
upgrades-eips-bundle-opt-rule: A rule says each upgrade must include several EIPs
upgrades-eips-bundle-fb-rule: There's no such rule: a few upgrades have contained a single change. Think about who has to act each time.
upgrades-eips-takeaway-p1: Changes start as public EIPs that anyone can write. Core EIPs change what every node checks, so they ship together in network upgrades.
upgrades-path-summary: Put a network upgrade in order, from the first draft to the moment it switches on.
upgrades-path-intro-p1: Getting a core EIP onto Ethereum takes months, often years. Its author brings it to All Core Devs, regular public calls where client teams discuss what goes into the next upgrade. Anyone can watch, and the notes are published.
upgrades-path-intro-p2: Once an upgrade's EIPs are chosen, every client team builds them. Then they run on testnets: practice copies of Ethereum where ETH has no value. Finally, the teams release new versions with the exact moment the upgrade switches on built in. Pectra, for example, switched on at 10:05 UTC on May 7, 2025.
upgrades-path-steps-prompt: Put the steps of a network upgrade in order.
upgrades-path-steps-item-calls: Client teams debate it on public calls
upgrades-path-steps-item-build: Every client team builds the change
upgrades-path-steps-item-install: Node runners install the new versions
upgrades-path-steps-item-activate: The upgrade switches on at a set moment
upgrades-path-steps-explain: Ideas are debated before anyone builds them, and every client is tested before release. Node runners install the new version ahead of time, so when the set moment comes, the new rules take over everywhere at once.
upgrades-path-testnet-prompt: Why does an upgrade run on testnets before the real network?
upgrades-path-testnet-opt-vote: So ETH holders can vote on it
upgrades-path-testnet-fb-vote: Testnets aren't voting booths. They're practice networks for the software itself.
upgrades-path-testnet-opt-bugs: To find bugs where mistakes cost nothing
upgrades-path-testnet-fb-bugs: Right. Testnet ETH has no value, so a bug there costs nothing, and the different clients get to prove they agree with each other.
upgrades-path-testnet-opt-fund: To earn the testnet ETH that pays for the upgrade
upgrades-path-testnet-fb-fund: Testnet ETH has no value, so it can't pay for anything. Think about what could go wrong on the real network.
upgrades-path-scam-prompt: An upgrade switches on next week. A message says you must "upgrade your ETH" through a link before then. What should you do?
upgrades-path-scam-opt-link: Follow the link before the deadline
upgrades-path-scam-fb-link: A deadline and a link are classic scam signs. An upgrade changes node software; your ETH needs nothing from you.
upgrades-path-scam-opt-exchange: Move your ETH to an exchange until it's over
upgrades-path-scam-fb-exchange: Your balance stays exactly where it is through an upgrade. Moving it costs fees, and on an exchange someone else holds your keys.
upgrades-path-scam-opt-ignore: Ignore it: an upgrade asks nothing of your ETH
upgrades-path-scam-fb-ignore: Right. Only node runners have to act, by updating their software. Anyone telling you to convert or upgrade your ETH is trying to scam you.
upgrades-path-takeaway-p1: An upgrade goes from EIP to public debate, to code in every client, to testnets, to a release node runners install, then switches on everywhere at one planned moment.
upgrades-clients-summary: Why Ethereum runs on several independent clients, and what happens when one of them has a bug.
upgrades-clients-intro-p1: Ethereum's clients are built by separate teams, in different programming languages, all following the same written rules. They can all talk to each other and check the same blocks.
upgrades-clients-intro-p2: That spread is called client diversity. If every node ran the same client, one bug could break the whole network at once. With several, a bug hurts only the nodes running that client, as long as it isn't too popular. Finality, the point after which a block can't be undone, needs two-thirds of staked ETH to agree, so the share of validators each client runs matters most.
upgrades-clients-drill-prompt: Pick a network, then give one client a bug that makes it accept a broken block. Try the biggest client in at least two networks.
upgrades-clients-drill-explain: A bug in a client with under a third of validators leaves the rest to carry on and finalize. Between a third and two-thirds, nobody has the two-thirds needed, so finality stalls. At two-thirds or more, the buggy client could finalize the broken chain.
upgrades-clients-share-prompt: A new client is the fastest, and more and more validators switch to it. From what point does its popularity put the network at risk?
upgrades-clients-share-opt-half: Once it runs more than half of validators
upgrades-clients-share-fb-half: Trouble starts earlier. Finality needs two-thirds agreeing, so a smaller group stuck on a bug is enough to block it.
upgrades-clients-share-opt-third: Once it runs a third of validators or more
upgrades-clients-share-fb-third: Right. From a third up, one bug in that client could stop the network from finalizing. That's why validators are encouraged to pick less-used clients.
upgrades-clients-share-opt-never: Never, as long as it's well tested
upgrades-clients-share-fb-never: Well-tested software still has bugs. The danger is how many validators one bug can hit at once.
upgrades-clients-pick-prompt: You're setting up a node. Two clients both work well: one runs on 60% of nodes, the other on 8%. Which choice helps the network most?
upgrades-clients-pick-opt-big: The 60% one, because it's the most tested
upgrades-clients-pick-fb-big: Popularity brings testing, but it also piles up risk: a bug there hits most of the network at once.
upgrades-clients-pick-opt-same: It makes no difference to anyone else
upgrades-clients-pick-fb-same: Each node's choice adds up. The share each client has decides how much damage a single bug can do.
upgrades-clients-pick-fb-small: Right. A less-used client spreads the risk, so no single bug can drag most of the network with it.
upgrades-clients-takeaway-p1: Several independent clients mean one bug can't take down Ethereum, as long as no single client runs a third or more of validators.
upgrades-forks-summary: What happens to nodes that don't upgrade, and how a deep disagreement can split one chain into two.
upgrades-forks-intro-p1: Changing the rules is called a fork: from the switch-on moment, new blocks follow the new rules. A node that didn't upgrade still checks blocks against the old rules, rejects the new ones and gets stuck, out of sync with everyone else.
upgrades-forks-intro-p2: Almost everyone upgrades in time, so the old rules simply die out. A stuck validator misses its duties and loses rewards until its runner installs the new version.
upgrades-forks-stuck-prompt: Your node missed an upgrade and has been stuck since. What fixes it?
upgrades-forks-stuck-opt-wait: Waiting: the network will go back to meet it
upgrades-forks-stuck-fb-wait: The network doesn't go back for anyone. New blocks keep piling up under the new rules.
upgrades-forks-stuck-opt-update: Installing the new version, so it can catch up
upgrades-forks-stuck-fb-update: Right. Once updated, it follows the same rules as everyone else and syncs the blocks it missed.
upgrades-forks-stuck-opt-restart: Restarting it with the same version
upgrades-forks-stuck-fb-restart: A restart changes nothing: the old version still rejects blocks made under the new rules.
upgrades-forks-split-p1: A fork splits Ethereum for good only if a large group refuses the new rules and keeps the old chain going on purpose. That's a contentious fork: two chains with a shared past and separate futures.
upgrades-forks-split-p2: It happened in 2016. An attacker drained over 3.6 million ETH from The DAO, a contract with a bug, and Ethereum upgraded to move those funds where their owners could withdraw them. A group who believed the chain should never be changed to undo a hack kept the old rules, and that chain continues today as Ethereum Classic.
upgrades-forks-balance-prompt: You held 10 ETH just before a contentious fork split the chain. What do you have afterwards?
upgrades-forks-balance-fb-half: A split copies the shared history, it doesn't divide it. Think about what each chain remembers from before.
upgrades-forks-balance-opt-winner: 10 on whichever chain wins, and nothing on the other
upgrades-forks-balance-fb-winner: Neither chain erases the other. Each keeps the whole history up to the split.
upgrades-forks-balance-fb-both: Right. Both chains keep every balance from before the split, and the same key controls both. After that, they're separate networks.
upgrades-forks-recap-prompt: Fill in what happens when the rules change.
upgrades-forks-recap-text: Nodes that don't {b1} get stuck on the old rules. If a large group keeps the old rules on purpose, the chain {b2} into two, each with the same {b3} up to that point.
upgrades-forks-recap-explain: An upgrade only binds nodes that install it. A node left behind is simply stuck, but a large group staying behind on purpose keeps a second chain alive, sharing everything before the split.
upgrades-forks-takeaway-p1: An upgrade only binds the nodes that install it. Usually everyone does; when a large group refuses, the chain splits in two.
upgrades-exam-alone-prompt: Who can change Ethereum's rules on their own?
upgrades-exam-alone-opt-developers: The core developers, by releasing a new version
upgrades-exam-alone-opt-nobody: Nobody: a change needs wide agreement and node runners installing it
upgrades-exam-alone-opt-holders: The biggest ETH holders, by voting
upgrades-exam-alone-explain: No person or group can change Ethereum alone. Developers can write and release new software, but a change only takes effect when node runners choose to run it, and there's no official ETH vote.
upgrades-exam-oppose-prompt: Client teams want a change that most node runners strongly oppose. What's most likely?
upgrades-exam-oppose-opt-forced: It goes live anyway, since nodes update automatically
upgrades-exam-oppose-opt-vote: ETH holders vote on the blockchain to settle it
upgrades-exam-oppose-opt-dropped: The teams drop or rework it, since they can't make anyone install it
upgrades-exam-oppose-explain: Nobody can force a node to install new software, so client teams avoid changes where the opposition outweighs the benefit. Ethereum's rules aren't settled by a vote on the blockchain.
upgrades-exam-write-prompt: A student has an idea for improving Ethereum and wants to propose it formally. What does that take?
upgrades-exam-write-opt-eip: Writing it up as an EIP, which anyone can do
upgrades-exam-write-opt-permission: Permission from a core developer first
upgrades-exam-write-opt-stake: Staking ETH to earn the right to propose
upgrades-exam-write-explain: Anyone can write an EIP, at no cost. Winning enough support for it is the hard part.
upgrades-exam-core-prompt: Which of these would need a core EIP and a network upgrade?
upgrades-exam-core-opt-gas: Changing how much gas an action costs
upgrades-exam-core-opt-token: A new standard format for tokens
upgrades-exam-core-opt-block: Changing how much data fits in a block
upgrades-exam-core-opt-wallet: A standard way for apps to talk to wallets
upgrades-exam-core-explain: Gas costs and what fits in a block are rules every node checks, so changing them needs every node to upgrade. Token and wallet formats are ERCs: apps can choose to adopt them.
upgrades-exam-before-prompt: A core EIP has been picked for the next upgrade. What happens before it goes live on Ethereum?
upgrades-exam-before-opt-vote: ETH holders approve it in a vote on the blockchain
upgrades-exam-before-opt-live: Nothing: picked EIPs go live right away
upgrades-exam-before-opt-testnet: Client teams build it and it runs on testnets
upgrades-exam-before-explain: Every client team builds the change, and it switches on for testnets before the real network, so bugs show up where mistakes cost nothing.
upgrades-exam-holder-prompt: A network upgrade switches on tomorrow. You keep ETH in your own wallet and don't run a node. What do you need to do?
upgrades-exam-holder-opt-convert: Convert your ETH to the new version
upgrades-exam-holder-opt-move: Move it to an exchange until the upgrade is done
upgrades-exam-holder-explain: Upgrades change node software, not your balance. Anyone telling you to upgrade or convert your ETH is running a scam.
upgrades-exam-minority-prompt: A client with a serious bug runs 20% of validators. What happens to the network?
upgrades-exam-minority-opt-carries: It keeps finalizing; only that client's nodes have trouble
upgrades-exam-minority-opt-stalls: Finality stops until the bug is fixed
upgrades-exam-minority-opt-wrong: The whole network follows the bug
upgrades-exam-minority-explain: Finality needs two-thirds of staked ETH to agree. With the bug on fewer than a third of validators, the rest carry on, and only the buggy client's validators miss out until it's fixed.
upgrades-exam-why-prompt: Why does Ethereum have several independent clients instead of one official one?
upgrades-exam-why-opt-resilience: So one bug or attack can't take down every node at once
upgrades-exam-why-opt-rules: So each client can follow its own rules
upgrades-exam-why-explain: Separate teams build clients to the same rules. A flaw in one usually isn't in the others, so the network keeps running while it's fixed.
upgrades-exam-skipped-prompt: A node runner skips an upgrade. What happens to their node once it switches on?
upgrades-exam-skipped-opt-fine: Nothing: old and new nodes still agree
upgrades-exam-skipped-opt-stuck: It rejects the new blocks and falls out of sync
upgrades-exam-skipped-explain: A node only follows the rules of the software it runs. To stay in sync after an upgrade, its runner has to install a version that includes it.
upgrades-exam-classic-opt-bug: A client bug split the chain by accident
upgrades-exam-classic-opt-kept: A group kept the old rules after the 2016 upgrade that returned The DAO's funds
upgrades-exam-classic-opt-rename: Ethereum changed its name, and the old name stayed with the old chain
upgrades-exam-classic-explain: After an attacker drained The DAO, Ethereum upgraded to return the funds. A group who believed the chain shouldn't be changed to undo a hack kept running the old rules, and that chain lives on as Ethereum Classic.
smart-accounts-description: Accounts that follow rules you choose: spending limits, extra approvers, recovery through friends, someone else paying the fee, and the one signature never to give a stranger.
smart-accounts-kinds-summary: A regular account does whatever its key signs. A smart account follows rules written in code.
smart-accounts-kinds-intro-p1: Most Ethereum accounts are controlled by a single private key: whoever has the key can do anything with the account, and whoever loses it loses everything. Here it's called a regular account; developers call it an externally owned account.
smart-accounts-kinds-intro-p2: A smart account is a smart contract that holds your funds instead. It has no private key of its own: its code checks each request, such as which of your keys signed it and how much it moves, against rules you choose.
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-prompt: Someone steals the private key to a regular account. What can stop them from emptying it?
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-opt-freeze: Asking validators to freeze the account
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-fb-freeze: Validators check that transactions follow the rules; they can't freeze an account or judge who really owns it.
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-opt-nothing: Nothing: the key alone can do anything
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-fb-nothing: Right. A regular account has no rules beyond its key, so a thief with the key can move everything at once.
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-opt-limit: The account's built-in daily spending limit
smart-accounts-kinds-stolen-fb-limit: Regular accounts have no limits of any kind. Whatever the key signs goes through.
smart-accounts-kinds-sort-prompt: Sort each statement: is it true of a regular account, or something only a smart account can do?
smart-accounts-kinds-sort-explain: A regular account is just a key: free to create, all-powerful in a thief's hands, and gone if the key is lost. A smart account is code, so it can wait, ask friends or bundle steps, but creating one costs gas.
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-prompt: A smart account has no private key of its own. So how does it ever do anything?
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-opt-itself: It sends transactions on its own whenever it likes
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-fb-itself: Contracts never act on their own. Their code sits still until something calls it.
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-fb-validators: Validators never sign for anyone's account. They only check and include transactions.
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-opt-called: A transaction calls it, and its code checks the request
smart-accounts-kinds-wake-fb-called: Right. A contract only runs when a transaction calls it. Its code then checks the signatures on your request against its rules.
smart-accounts-kinds-takeaway-p1: A regular account does whatever its one key signs. A smart account is a contract, so its code can add rules on top of your keys.
smart-accounts-rules-summary: Spending limits, extra approvers and recovery contacts: set up an account that's safe and still easy to use.
smart-accounts-rules-intro-p1: Because a smart account is code, it can enforce rules like these: a spending limit that caps how much can leave each day; multiple approvers, so a payment needs a second key, maybe on another device; and social recovery, where contacts you picked in advance can together approve a new key if you lose yours.
smart-accounts-rules-intro-p2: Every check also slows you down. The trick is to pick rules that stop a thief, or a lost key, without getting in your own way.
smart-accounts-rules-setup-prompt: Choose rules so the café payment goes through, a thief can't take everything, and losing your phone doesn't lock you out.
smart-accounts-rules-setup-explain: A daily limit caps what a stolen key can take, and recovery contacts let you replace a lost one. A second approval on every payment, or saved addresses only, also stop a thief, but they block everyday payments too.
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-prompt: You picked three recovery contacts, and any two together can approve a new key. One of them turns out to be dishonest. Can they take over your account alone?
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-opt-alone: Yes: any one contact can reset the key
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-fb-alone: Check the rule you set: how many contacts have to agree before a new key is approved?
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-opt-needs: No: they'd need a second contact to agree
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-fb-needs: Right. Needing several contacts means no single one can act alone, so one bad pick isn't a disaster.
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-opt-never: No: recovery contacts can never change keys
smart-accounts-rules-contacts-fb-never: Approving a new key is exactly what recovery contacts are for, when enough of them agree.
smart-accounts-rules-phone-prompt: Your account needs two of your three keys for every payment: one on your phone, one on your laptop, one on a hardware wallet. Your phone is stolen. What can the thief send?
smart-accounts-rules-phone-opt-everythin: Everything, since they have one of your keys
smart-accounts-rules-phone-fb-everything: One key isn't enough under this rule. Think about how many keys every payment needs.
smart-accounts-rules-phone-fb-small: The rule covers every payment, whatever its size. Check how many keys each one needs.
smart-accounts-rules-phone-fb-nothing: Right. Every payment needs a second key. And with your laptop and hardware wallet, you still have two keys to remove the stolen one.
smart-accounts-rules-takeaway-p1: A smart account can cap spending, require extra approvals and let trusted contacts help you recover, so one lost or stolen key isn't the end.
smart-accounts-fees-summary: How an app or helper can cover your gas, and how you might pay them back in a token instead of ETH.
smart-accounts-fees-intro-p1: Every transaction needs gas, paid in ETH. That's a hurdle for someone who holds only tokens, or for an app that wants its first steps to feel free. Smart accounts can use sponsored transactions: you sign a request, and a sponsor sends the transaction and pays the gas.
smart-accounts-fees-intro-p2: The network is still paid in ETH, by the sponsor. Some sponsors are apps covering their users' fees. Others let you pay them back in a token you already hold, so you never need ETH at all.
smart-accounts-fees-who-prompt: An app sponsors your first transaction. Who pays the gas?
smart-accounts-fees-who-fb-sponsor: Right. The network always gets its fee in ETH. Sponsoring only changes who hands it over.
smart-accounts-fees-who-opt-nobody: Nobody: sponsored transactions use no gas
smart-accounts-fees-who-fb-nobody: The transaction does the same work either way, so the gas still has to be paid. It just isn't paid by you.
smart-accounts-fees-who-opt-you: You do, out of your ETH
smart-accounts-fees-who-fb-you: With a sponsor, the fee doesn't come out of your ETH at all. You might not even own any.
smart-accounts-fees-flow-prompt: Put a sponsored transaction in order, from your tap to the result.
smart-accounts-fees-flow-item-choose: You pick an action in an app
smart-accounts-fees-flow-item-sign: You sign the request in your wallet
smart-accounts-fees-flow-item-send: The sponsor sends it, paying gas in ETH
smart-accounts-fees-flow-item-check: Your smart account checks your signature
smart-accounts-fees-flow-item-run: The action runs, such as a payment
smart-accounts-fees-flow-explain: You only pick and sign; the sponsor sends the transaction and pays the gas in ETH. When it arrives, your smart account's code checks your signature and its rules, and only then does the action run.
smart-accounts-fees-free-prompt: A sponsor offers to cover the fee for a request you didn't expect. What should you still check before signing?
smart-accounts-fees-free-opt-free: Nothing: if it's free, there's no risk
smart-accounts-fees-free-fb-free: The fee was never the risky part. What you sign is what happens, whoever pays the gas.
smart-accounts-fees-free-opt-key: That the sponsor has your private key
smart-accounts-fees-free-fb-key: A sponsor never needs your key, and you should never share it. You sign; the sponsor only pays to send it.
smart-accounts-fees-free-fb-action: Right. A free fee doesn't make a request safe. Read what you're approving, just as you would if you paid.
smart-accounts-fees-takeaway-p1: A sponsor can send your transaction and pay its gas in ETH, so you can start with no ETH, or settle up in a token you hold.
smart-accounts-delegation-title: Smart features for a regular account
smart-accounts-delegation-summary: How a regular account can run a smart contract's code at the same address, and why that's so powerful.
smart-accounts-delegation-intro-p1: Switching to a new smart account means a new address. Since the Pectra upgrade in May 2025, there's another way, from EIP-7702: your regular account signs a delegation, a message that points your address at a smart contract already on Ethereum.
smart-accounts-delegation-intro-p2: From then on, when your address is called, it runs that contract's code with your own balance, so it can bundle steps, use a sponsor or follow rules. Your private key still works as before, and the delegation stays until you sign a new one or clear it.
smart-accounts-delegation-key-prompt: You delegate your regular account to a contract that requires two approvals. Can your original private key still move funds on its own?
smart-accounts-delegation-key-opt-rules: No: the contract's rules now apply to everything
smart-accounts-delegation-key-fb-rules: The contract's rules only apply to calls that go through its code. Think about what the key could always do by itself.
smart-accounts-delegation-key-opt-yes: Yes: the key keeps full control
smart-accounts-delegation-key-fb-yes: Right. Delegation adds code; it doesn't take power from the key. Whoever holds the key can still send transactions directly, around the contract's rules.
smart-accounts-delegation-key-opt-limit: Only up to the contract's spending limit
smart-accounts-delegation-key-fb-limit: The contract's limits only apply to calls that go through its code. Think about what the key could always do by itself.
smart-accounts-delegation-recap-prompt: Fill in what a delegation does.
smart-accounts-delegation-recap-text: Signing a {b1} points your address at a contract's {b2}. Your address then runs that code when it's called, while your {b3} keeps full control.
smart-accounts-delegation-recap-explain: A delegation points your address at a contract's code, which then runs at your address. It adds abilities without removing your private key, which can still do everything it always could.
smart-accounts-delegation-power-prompt: Why is signing a delegation such a big deal?
smart-accounts-delegation-power-opt-toke: It's not: it covers only the one token an app asked about
smart-accounts-delegation-power-fb-token: That's how a token approval works. A delegation isn't limited to one token.
smart-accounts-delegation-power-opt-once: It's not: it expires after one transaction
smart-accounts-delegation-power-fb-once: A delegation stays until you replace or clear it, so the code keeps running for every call to your address.
smart-accounts-delegation-power-opt-ever: The contract's code can move anything at your address
smart-accounts-delegation-power-fb-every: Right. The code runs as your address, so it can move all your ETH and tokens, if that's what it was written to do.
smart-accounts-delegation-takeaway-p1: A delegation lets a regular account run a smart contract's code at the same address. That code can move everything you hold, and your key still works too.
smart-accounts-risks-summary: One signature can hand a stranger your whole account. Learn what a dangerous delegation request looks like.
smart-accounts-risks-intro-p1: If the contract you delegate to is malicious, its code runs as your address and can send away every coin and token you hold, including anything that arrives later. Scammers know this, so fake prizes, games and "account upgrades" may ask you to sign a delegation to their contract.
smart-accounts-risks-intro-p2: Careful wallets only offer delegations to contracts they've checked, through their own settings, and apps aren't meant to ask for them directly. A delegation request started by a website is a red flag, especially one that covers every network.
smart-accounts-risks-inspect-prompt: Your wallet shows four requests. Pick the one that could hand over everything at your address.
smart-accounts-risks-inspect-explain: The upgrade a website started points your whole address at an unknown contract, on every network. Your wallet's own upgrade uses a contract the wallet has checked, and the payment and the approval are each limited to what they show.
smart-accounts-risks-prize-prompt: A game's website says you must "upgrade your account" to claim a prize, and your wallet shows a delegation request. What should you do?
smart-accounts-risks-prize-opt-familiar: Sign it if the contract address looks familiar
smart-accounts-risks-prize-fb-familiar: Look-alike addresses are easy to make, and even a familiar address tells you nothing about what the code does.
smart-accounts-risks-prize-opt-reject: Reject it, and only upgrade through your wallet's own settings
smart-accounts-risks-prize-fb-reject: Right. A prize that needs a delegation is a trap. If you want smart features, start them from your wallet, never from a website's request.
smart-accounts-risks-prize-opt-small: Sign it, but keep only a little ETH in that account
smart-accounts-risks-prize-fb-small: A delegation covers everything at the address, including whatever arrives later. A little can still be lost, and so can the next deposit.
smart-accounts-risks-signed-prompt: You realize you signed a delegation to a scam contract an hour ago. What helps most right now?
smart-accounts-risks-signed-opt-wait: Wait and see whether anything goes missing
smart-accounts-risks-signed-fb-wait: The contract can act at any moment, without you signing anything else. Waiting only gives it time.
smart-accounts-risks-signed-fb-revoke: Approvals let other contracts move your tokens. Delegated code runs as your address itself, so it needs no approval at all.
smart-accounts-risks-signed-opt-move: Move what's left to a new account, then clear the delegation
smart-accounts-risks-signed-fb-move: Right. Get anything still there out of reach first, then clear the delegation through your wallet so the code stops running for your address.
smart-accounts-risks-takeaway-p1: Only delegate through your wallet's own upgrade settings. A delegation request from a website or a stranger can hand over everything at your address.
smart-accounts-exam-control-prompt: What controls a regular account, the kind developers call an externally owned account?
smart-accounts-exam-control-opt-code: Code that checks every request against rules
smart-accounts-exam-control-opt-app: The wallet app that created it
smart-accounts-exam-control-explain: A regular account has no rules beyond its key: whoever has the key can do anything, and losing it means losing access. Smart accounts are the ones controlled by code.
smart-accounts-exam-trigger-prompt: Your funds sit in a smart account. What makes its code run?
smart-accounts-exam-trigger-opt-timer: It runs by itself in every block
smart-accounts-exam-trigger-opt-validato: A validator deciding to run it
smart-accounts-exam-trigger-explain: Contracts only act when a transaction calls them. The code then checks the request's signatures against its rules.
smart-accounts-exam-thief-prompt: A thief copies one of your keys. Which smart account rules limit the damage?
smart-accounts-exam-thief-opt-name: A memorable name for the account
smart-accounts-exam-thief-opt-approvers: Needing a second key to approve payments
smart-accounts-exam-thief-opt-tip: Paying a higher tip on every transaction
smart-accounts-exam-thief-explain: A spending limit caps what one key can take, and a second approver means one key alone can't send. A name or a tip changes nothing about who can move your funds.
smart-accounts-exam-recover-prompt: Your smart account uses social recovery, and you've lost your only key. How do you get back in?
smart-accounts-exam-recover-opt-support: The wallet company resets it for you
smart-accounts-exam-recover-opt-contacts: Enough of the contacts you picked approve a new key
smart-accounts-exam-recover-opt-validato: Validators restore it once you prove who you are
smart-accounts-exam-recover-explain: With social recovery, contacts you chose in advance can together approve a new key. Nobody else, not a company and not the network, can reset it.
smart-accounts-exam-sponsored-prompt: An app sponsors your transaction. Which is true?
smart-accounts-exam-sponsored-opt-free: The transaction uses no gas, so nobody pays
smart-accounts-exam-sponsored-opt-token: Validators accept the app's own token as the fee
smart-accounts-exam-sponsored-opt-eth: The gas is still paid in ETH, by the sponsor
smart-accounts-exam-sponsored-explain: Gas is always paid in ETH. A sponsor pays it for you, and may let you pay them back in another token.
smart-accounts-exam-unexpected-prompt: A sponsor will cover the fee for a request you didn't expect. What matters most before you sign?
smart-accounts-exam-unexpected-opt-fast: How quickly it will go through
smart-accounts-exam-unexpected-explain: Who pays the gas doesn't change what a request does. Read what you're signing before you approve it, free or not.
smart-accounts-exam-same-prompt: What does EIP-7702 let a regular account do?
smart-accounts-exam-same-opt-new: Move its funds to a new smart account address
smart-accounts-exam-same-opt-run: Run a smart contract's code at the same address
smart-accounts-exam-same-opt-drop: Give up its private key for good
smart-accounts-exam-same-explain: Since the Pectra upgrade, a regular account can sign a delegation that points its address at a contract's code. The address stays the same, and so does the key's control.
smart-accounts-exam-bypass-prompt: You delegated to a contract with strict rules. Then someone steals your original private key. Can they get around the rules?
smart-accounts-exam-bypass-opt-no: No: the rules now cover every transaction
smart-accounts-exam-bypass-opt-limit: Only up to the contract's spending limit
smart-accounts-exam-bypass-opt-yes: Yes: the key can still send transactions directly
smart-accounts-exam-bypass-explain: A delegation adds code but leaves the key in full control. Transactions signed directly with the key don't need the contract's permission.
smart-accounts-exam-claim-prompt: A website asks you to sign an "account upgrade" to claim free tokens. What is it most likely to be?
smart-accounts-exam-claim-opt-gift: A genuine gift for early users
smart-accounts-exam-claim-opt-trap: A delegation that could hand over your whole account
smart-accounts-exam-claim-opt-required: A network upgrade every account must sign
smart-accounts-exam-claim-explain: Network upgrades never ask anything of your account. A delegation to a scammer's contract lets its code move everything at your address.
smart-accounts-exam-safe-prompt: What's the safe way to give your account smart features with a delegation?
smart-accounts-exam-safe-opt-app: Through any app that offers it
smart-accounts-exam-safe-opt-familiar: To any contract whose address looks familiar
smart-accounts-exam-safe-opt-wallet: Through your wallet's own upgrade settings
smart-accounts-exam-safe-explain: Careful wallets only delegate to contracts they've checked, and apps aren't meant to request delegations directly. Start any upgrade from your wallet.
tokens-description: Tell a real token from a copy, see what keeps a stablecoin steady, and send tokens without slipping up.
tokens-name-summary: Why anyone can copy a token's name, and what tells the real one apart.
tokens-name-intro-p1: Anyone with a printer can make a card that says "Gift card" and copy a famous store's logo onto it. But the store's checkout only accepts cards the store issued itself, so the copy is worth nothing.
tokens-name-intro-p2: Tokens work the same way. A token is a smart contract that keeps a list of balances, and whoever creates one picks its name and picture, so copying a popular token's look is easy. What a copy can't share is the contract address: the address of the token's own smart contract. Every contract has a different one.
tokens-name-predict-prompt: Two tokens in your wallet have the same name and the same picture. What does that tell you?
tokens-name-predict-fb-same: A name and a picture are easy to copy, so matching ones prove nothing. Test it in the next step.
tokens-name-predict-opt-unknown: Not much: they could come from two different contracts
tokens-name-predict-fb-unknown: Right. Only the contract address tells two tokens apart. Try it in the next step.
tokens-name-predict-opt-wallet: Both are real, since wallets only show real tokens
tokens-name-predict-fb-wallet: A wallet shows whatever tokens an address holds, real or fake. Test it in the next step.
tokens-name-check-prompt: You want the real Pebble Dollar. The official website of the team that made it lists the contract address shown at the top. Which token in your wallet is the real one?
tokens-name-check-explain: All four tokens had the same name and picture, and one even called itself official. Only the contract address, checked character by character against the official one, picked out the real token.
tokens-name-source-prompt: A friend wants to send you a token you've never used before. Where should you get its real contract address to check it?
tokens-name-source-opt-chat: From a link someone posted in a group chat
tokens-name-source-fb-chat: Anyone can post a link, including someone pushing a fake. Think about who knows the real address for certain.
tokens-name-source-opt-project: From the official website of the team that made it
tokens-name-source-fb-project: Right. The team that created a token publishes its real contract address. Bookmark their site, so you always go back to the same one.
tokens-name-source-opt-search: From the first token that turns up when you search its name
tokens-name-source-fb-search: Fakes use the very same name, so a name search turns them up too. Think about who knows the real address for certain.
tokens-name-takeaway-p1: Anyone can give a token any name or picture. Only its contract address, checked against the one its creators publish, tells you it's the real one.
tokens-stable-summary: What a stablecoin is, and what stands behind it.
tokens-stable-intro-p1: A store voucher for a sandwich still gets you a sandwich long after you got it. Its value doesn't jump around, because the store stands behind it.
tokens-stable-intro-p2: The price of ETH, and of most tokens, goes up and down. A stablecoin is a token built to stay steady instead, usually matching a regular currency like the US dollar. That makes it handy for paying, saving and sending money anywhere in the world.
tokens-stable-why-prompt: Mia is saving up for a bike with a fixed price. Why might she save in a stablecoin instead of ETH?
tokens-stable-why-opt-steady: Its price stays steady, so her savings still cover the bike later
tokens-stable-why-fb-steady: Right. A stablecoin aims to keep the same value, so what she saves keeps buying the same bike.
tokens-stable-why-opt-grows: It always grows in value over time
tokens-stable-why-fb-grows: A stablecoin aims to stay level, not to grow. Think about what Mia needs from her savings.
tokens-stable-why-fb-free: A stablecoin is a token, so moving it still needs a fee like any transaction. Think about what Mia needs from her savings.
tokens-stable-backing-p1: A voucher is only worth something if something real stands behind it. A stablecoin needs that too: its backing. Some are backed by money or gold that a company keeps, some by crypto locked in a smart contract, and a few by nothing at all, only rules that try to hold the price.
tokens-stable-sort-prompt: Sort each stablecoin by what stands behind it.
tokens-stable-sort-explain: Look behind each coin. A company's coins rest on what it keeps in a bank or a vault. Crypto-backed coins rest on tokens locked in a smart contract. The rest have only their rules.
tokens-stable-takeaway-p1: A stablecoin is a token built to stay steady, usually matching a currency like the US dollar. Its backing is what keeps it there: money a company holds, crypto locked away, or only rules.
tokens-steady-summary: What can go wrong with each kind of stablecoin.
tokens-steady-intro-p1: A company that keeps money behind its stablecoin stays in charge of it. You have to trust that the money really is there, and many such companies can freeze the coins at an address, so nobody can move them.
tokens-steady-intro-p2: Crypto-backed stablecoins have no company in charge, but crypto prices rise and fall. So they lock up extra crypto, worth more than the coins it backs, as a cushion for when prices drop.
tokens-steady-predict-prompt: A smart contract holds exactly enough ETH to back its stablecoins, with nothing extra. Then the price of ETH falls. What happens?
tokens-steady-predict-opt-short: There's no longer enough behind the coins
tokens-steady-predict-fb-short: Right. The locked ETH is now worth less than the coins it backs. Watch it happen in the next step.
tokens-steady-predict-opt-fine: Nothing, since each coin is still meant to stay steady
tokens-steady-predict-fb-fine: The coins aim to stay steady, but the ETH behind them just lost value. Test it in the next step.
tokens-steady-predict-opt-more: The contract makes more ETH to fill the gap
tokens-steady-predict-fb-more: A smart contract can't create ETH out of nothing. Test it in the next step.
tokens-steady-vaults-prompt: Two vaults back the same stablecoins. One locked just enough ETH, the other locked extra. Lower the price of ETH and watch both.
tokens-steady-vaults-explain: The vault with just enough fell short at the first drop. The extra ETH gave the other one a cushion, but a big enough fall used that up too. That's why these systems watch prices closely and sell a vault's crypto before its cushion runs out.
tokens-steady-freeze-prompt: Your stablecoins come from a company that keeps money in a bank behind them. Which of these can that company usually do?
tokens-steady-freeze-opt-freeze: Freeze the coins at an address so they can't be moved
tokens-steady-freeze-fb-freeze: Right. Many of these companies can freeze coins at an address, for example when a law requires it. Holding their coins means trusting the company.
tokens-steady-freeze-opt-undo: Undo a payment you sent by mistake
tokens-steady-freeze-fb-undo: A company like this can stop coins from moving, but it isn't there to reverse your payments. Think about what the company controls.
tokens-steady-freeze-opt-eth: Freeze the ETH at your address too
tokens-steady-freeze-fb-eth: ETH isn't a company's token, so no company can freeze it. Think about the coins this company controls.
tokens-steady-nothing-prompt: A stablecoin has no backing at all, only rules that add or remove coins to steer its price. What's the big risk?
tokens-steady-nothing-opt-trust: If people stop trusting it, there's nothing behind it to fall back on
tokens-steady-nothing-fb-trust: Right. With nothing set aside, its price rests on trust alone. Some stablecoins like this have collapsed and lost almost all their value.
tokens-steady-nothing-opt-company: A company can freeze it at any address
tokens-steady-nothing-fb-company: No company holds anything behind this kind. Think about what's missing behind the coins.
tokens-steady-nothing-opt-rises: Its price keeps climbing higher and higher
tokens-steady-nothing-fb-rises: The rules try to hold its price steady, not push it up. Think about what's missing behind the coins.
tokens-steady-takeaway-p1: Every kind of backing has a weak spot. A company can freeze its coins, crypto backing needs extra to survive price drops, and coins with no backing rest on trust alone.
tokens-send-summary: Why sending a token needs a little ETH, and the right network.
tokens-send-intro-p1: Sending a token is a transaction: you ask the token's contract to update its list. Every transaction pays a fee in ETH, so you need a little ETH, even when all you want to send is a stablecoin.
tokens-send-intro-p2: Many tokens also exist on other networks connected to Ethereum, with a separate version on each. Your friend has to be using the same network you send on. We'll learn more about these networks in a future lesson.
tokens-send-no-eth-prompt: Zoe has stablecoins in her wallet but no ETH at all. She tries to send some stablecoins to a friend. What happens?
tokens-send-no-eth-opt-token: The fee comes out of the stablecoins she sends
tokens-send-no-eth-fb-token: The fee is normally paid in ETH, not in the token being sent. Think about what Zoe is missing.
tokens-send-no-eth-opt-stuck: Usually, her wallet can't send them until she has a little ETH
tokens-send-no-eth-fb-stuck: Right. The fee for a token transfer is paid in ETH, so she needs some first. A few wallets can cover the fee another way, but don't count on it.
tokens-send-no-eth-opt-free: It goes through for free, since tokens don't pay fees
tokens-send-no-eth-fb-free: Sending a token is a transaction, and every transaction pays a fee. Think about what Zoe is missing.
tokens-send-network-prompt: You send tokens to a friend on a different network from the one their wallet uses. What's most likely?
tokens-send-network-opt-moves: The tokens move over to their network on their own
tokens-send-network-fb-moves: Networks don't pass tokens to each other on their own. Think about where the tokens actually landed.
tokens-send-network-opt-bounce: The tokens bounce back to you
tokens-send-network-fb-bounce: Transactions don't bounce. Think about where the tokens actually landed.
tokens-send-network-opt-missing: Your friend doesn't see them, and getting them back can be hard or impossible
tokens-send-network-fb-missing: Right. The tokens land on the network you used, not theirs. Sometimes your friend can switch networks to reach them, but not always, so ask before you send.
tokens-send-steps-prompt: Put these steps for sending tokens to a friend in a safe order.
tokens-send-steps-item-ask: Ask your friend for their address and network
tokens-send-steps-item-switch: Switch your wallet to that network
tokens-send-steps-item-eth: Check you have a little ETH there for the fee
tokens-send-steps-item-approve: Paste their address, check all of it, then approve
tokens-send-steps-explain: First find out where the tokens should go: which address, and on which network. Your wallet needs to be on that network, with a little ETH there for the fee. Then check the whole address before you approve, because sending is final.
tokens-send-takeaway-p1: Sending a token is a transaction, so you need a little ETH for the fee. Send on the same network your friend uses, and check the whole address before you approve.
tokens-free-summary: Why surprise tokens are usually bait, and what to do with them.
tokens-free-intro-p1: A flyer lands in your mailbox: "You've won a prize! Visit our website to claim it." You never entered any contest. The flyer is only there to get you to that website.
tokens-free-intro-p2: Your address is public, so anyone can send tokens to it. Tokens you never asked for often have a website or a reward in their name. They're usually bait: the trap waits on that website, where you're asked to approve something.
tokens-free-spot-prompt: These tokens are in your wallet. Which one is most likely bait?
tokens-free-spot-explain: It came from a stranger, and its name sends you to a website. Surprise tokens like that are lures: the trap waits at the site, not in your wallet.
tokens-free-move-prompt: A token you never asked for shows up in your wallet. Its name says you can claim more on a website. What's the safest move?
tokens-free-move-opt-visit: Visit the website to see what it's about
tokens-free-move-fb-visit: That's where the trap is. The site may ask you to approve something that lets it take what you own.
tokens-free-move-opt-ignore: Leave it alone, and hide it if your wallet lets you
tokens-free-move-fb-ignore: Right. A token just sitting at your address can't take anything. Trouble starts when you visit the site or try to trade the token.
tokens-free-move-opt-swap: Trade it for ETH quickly, before it loses value
tokens-free-move-fb-swap: Trying to trade a bait token can mean approving its contract, which may be built to trick you. A token like this is rarely worth anything anyway.
tokens-free-takeaway-p1: Anyone can send tokens to your address. Ones you didn't ask for are usually bait: leave them alone, and never visit the websites they name.
tokens-exam-copy-prompt: A new token in your wallet has the same name and picture as a well-known one. What tells you whether it's the real thing?
tokens-exam-copy-opt-picture: Its picture looking sharp and official
tokens-exam-copy-explain: Names, pictures and even the word "Official" can be copied by anyone. A token's contract address can't, so compare it with the address its creators publish.
tokens-exam-source-prompt: You want to check a token's contract address. Which source can you trust most?
tokens-exam-source-opt-ad: An ad offering the token at a discount
tokens-exam-source-opt-chat: A link a stranger shares in a chat
tokens-exam-source-opt-project: The official website of the team that made it
tokens-exam-source-explain: The team that created a token publishes its real contract address. Ads and chat links can point to fakes with the very same name.
tokens-exam-stable-prompt: What is a stablecoin built to do?
tokens-exam-stable-opt-steady: Stay at a steady price, usually matching a currency like the US dollar
tokens-exam-stable-opt-grow: Grow in value faster than ETH
tokens-exam-stable-explain: A stablecoin is a token designed to hold a steady value, usually matching a currency like the US dollar, even when the price of ETH changes. Sending one still needs a fee.
tokens-exam-bank-prompt: A company keeps money in the bank to match every coin it issues. What kind of stablecoin is that?
tokens-exam-bank-opt-crypto: Backed by crypto locked in a smart contract
tokens-exam-bank-opt-company: Backed by money a company holds
tokens-exam-bank-explain: Money kept in a bank by the company that issues the coins is backing held by a company. You have to trust that the money is really there.
tokens-exam-extra-prompt: Why do crypto-backed stablecoins lock up more crypto than their coins are worth?
tokens-exam-extra-opt-cushion: To leave a cushion in case crypto prices fall
tokens-exam-extra-opt-grow: So the coins grow in value
tokens-exam-extra-explain: Crypto prices rise and fall. Locking up extra leaves a cushion, so the coins stay fully backed through smaller drops.
tokens-exam-freeze-prompt: Who can usually freeze a stablecoin at an address?
tokens-exam-freeze-opt-wallet: Your wallet app, if it spots a problem
tokens-exam-freeze-explain: Companies that issue stablecoins can often freeze the coins at an address, for example when a law requires it. ETH has no company behind it, so nobody can freeze it.
tokens-exam-fee-prompt: You hold only stablecoins and want to send some to a friend. What else do you usually need?
tokens-exam-fee-opt-eth: A little ETH for the fee
tokens-exam-fee-opt-nothing: Nothing else, since stablecoins pay their own way
tokens-exam-fee-opt-token: A second token to pay the fee
tokens-exam-fee-explain: Sending a token is a transaction, and transactions pay their fee in ETH. Make sure your wallet has a little ETH before you send.
tokens-exam-network-prompt: Before you send tokens to a friend, which network should you use?
tokens-exam-network-opt-cheapest: Whichever one has the lowest fee
tokens-exam-network-opt-same: The same network your friend's wallet uses
tokens-exam-network-opt-any: Any of them, since tokens always find their way
tokens-exam-network-explain: Many tokens exist on several networks, and the versions aren't interchangeable. Send on the network your friend uses, or the tokens can be hard or impossible to get back.
tokens-exam-public-prompt: A token you never asked for shows up in your wallet. How could a stranger send it to you?
tokens-exam-public-opt-leaked: Your private key must have leaked
tokens-exam-public-opt-approved: You must have approved it earlier
tokens-exam-public-opt-public: Your address is public, and anyone can send to it
tokens-exam-public-explain: Anyone can send tokens to any address, just as anyone can put a flyer in a mailbox. A surprise token doesn't mean your key is at risk. Trouble starts only if you act on it.
tokens-exam-claim-prompt: A surprise token's name tells you to visit a website to claim a reward. What should you do?
tokens-exam-claim-opt-connect: Connect your wallet there to check it's real
tokens-exam-claim-opt-ignore: Leave the token alone and skip the website
tokens-exam-claim-opt-visit: Visit the site, but only to look
tokens-exam-claim-explain: The token is the bait and the website is the trap, where you'd be asked to approve something. Leave the token alone and never visit the site it names.
nfts-description: Own one-of-a-kind tokens, tell an original from a copy, and give your address a name people can read.
nfts-unique-summary: How an NFT is different from a coin.
nfts-unique-intro-p1: Swap a coin with a friend and nothing changes: any coin is as good as another. Swap concert tickets and you might lose your front-row seat, because every ticket is for a different seat.
nfts-unique-intro-p2: An NFT (non-fungible token, meaning not interchangeable) is a token like that ticket. Its smart contract keeps a list of items, each with its own number, called its token ID, and exactly one owner. Coins are interchangeable. Every NFT is one of a kind.
nfts-unique-half-prompt: You own an NFT concert ticket. Can you send half of it to a friend?
nfts-unique-half-fb-split: Coins split because any part of one is as good as another. Test your idea in the next step.
nfts-unique-half-opt-whole: No: it has one owner, so it moves whole or not at all
nfts-unique-half-fb-whole: Right. The list holds one owner for each NFT, with no room for halves. Try moving one in the next step.
nfts-unique-half-opt-copy: Yes: the contract makes a copy for your friend
nfts-unique-half-fb-copy: A copy would give one NFT two owners. Test your idea in the next step.
nfts-unique-ledger-prompt: Alice sells ticket #2 to Bob. Update the NFT contract's list to match.
nfts-unique-ledger-explain: Only ticket #2 changed owner. Each ticket on the list has exactly one owner, and selling it hands the whole ticket over, never part of it.
nfts-unique-like-prompt: Which of these is most like an NFT?
nfts-unique-like-fb-coins: Any coin can stand in for another. Think about something where it matters which one you hold.
nfts-unique-like-opt-seat: A concert ticket for one particular seat
nfts-unique-like-fb-seat: Right. That seat's ticket is one of a kind, and only one person holds it.
nfts-unique-like-opt-card: The money on a gift card
nfts-unique-like-fb-card: Any dollar on the card is as good as another. Think about something where it matters which one you hold.
nfts-unique-takeaway-p1: An NFT is a one-of-a-kind token: an item on a contract's list with its own token ID and exactly one owner. Coins are interchangeable. NFTs aren't.
nfts-own-summary: The NFT lives on Ethereum. Its picture usually doesn't.
nfts-own-intro-p1: A theater ticket says which seat is yours, but the seat isn't inside the ticket. It's in the theater.
nfts-own-intro-p2: An NFT works like that. Its contract's list on Ethereum records who owns each token ID, plus a link to its details, like its name and picture. A picture is usually too big to keep on the blockchain, so it's stored on another computer, called a host, and the link points there.
nfts-own-predict-prompt: The computer hosting your NFT's picture shuts down for good. What happens to your NFT?
nfts-own-predict-fb-gone: Nothing on the blockchain changed. Test your idea in the next step.
nfts-own-predict-opt-still: You still own it, but its picture may stop showing
nfts-own-predict-fb-still: Right. Ownership lives on Ethereum. Only the picture lived somewhere else. Try it in the next step.
nfts-own-predict-opt-host: Whoever runs the host now owns it
nfts-own-predict-fb-host: Keeping a copy of the picture doesn't change the list on Ethereum. Test your idea in the next step.
nfts-own-host-prompt: Here's your NFT. Take the picture's host offline and see what changes.
nfts-own-host-explain: The picture vanished, but the list on Ethereum still says the NFT is yours. You own the token. Whether its picture keeps showing depends on where the picture is stored.
nfts-own-last-prompt: Which NFT's picture is most likely to keep showing for a long time?
nfts-own-last-opt-price: The one that cost the most
nfts-own-last-fb-price: Price says nothing about where a picture is stored. Think about what happens when one computer shuts down.
nfts-own-last-opt-many: One whose picture is stored on many computers, not just one
nfts-own-last-fb-many: Right. With many copies, no single shutdown can take the picture away. A few NFTs even keep small pictures on the blockchain itself.
nfts-own-last-opt-famous: The one with the most famous picture
nfts-own-last-fb-famous: Fame doesn't keep a computer running. Think about what happens when one computer shuts down.
nfts-own-takeaway-p1: Owning an NFT means owning a token ID on its contract's list. Its picture usually lives on a host somewhere else, so it can vanish while the NFT stays yours.
nfts-copy-summary: Why copying a picture doesn't copy the NFT.
nfts-copy-intro-p1: Anyone can buy a poster of a famous painting. It might look just like the real thing, but the museum's records show which one is the original.
nfts-copy-intro-p2: Pictures online are even easier to copy. Anyone can save one and make a new NFT of it, with the same name and even the same token ID. What a copy can't have is the original collection address: the address of the smart contract that made the real ones.
nfts-copy-allowed-prompt: Someone saves a picture from a famous NFT collection. Can they make their own NFT of it?
nfts-copy-allowed-opt-blocked: No, Ethereum checks who drew a picture
nfts-copy-allowed-fb-blocked: Ethereum has no way to know who drew a picture. Think about what stops someone, if anything.
nfts-copy-allowed-opt-anyone: Yes, nothing on Ethereum stops them
nfts-copy-allowed-fb-anyone: Right. Anyone can make an NFT of any picture. That's why the next step matters.
nfts-copy-allowed-opt-pay: Only if they pay the artist first
nfts-copy-allowed-fb-pay: Nothing on Ethereum checks for that. Think about what stops someone, if anything.
nfts-copy-proof-prompt: This NFT is for sale, and the seller says it's from the famous Sunset Fox collection. Which detail could prove that?
nfts-copy-proof-explain: A name, a picture, a creator's name and a number can all be copied. Only the collection address belongs to the original contract alone, so check it against the address the creators publish.
nfts-copy-twins-prompt: Two NFTs look identical: same picture, same name, same token ID. One is from the original collection. How do you tell which?
nfts-copy-twins-opt-price: Pick the one with the higher price
nfts-copy-twins-fb-price: Anyone can set any price, copiers included. Think about what a copy can't share.
nfts-copy-twins-opt-likes: Pick the one with more likes
nfts-copy-twins-fb-likes: Likes are easy to fake and say nothing about where an NFT came from. Think about what a copy can't share.
nfts-copy-twins-opt-address: Compare each collection address with the one the creators publish
nfts-copy-twins-fb-address: Right. A copy can share everything but the original contract's address, so that's the one detail worth checking.
nfts-copy-takeaway-p1: Anyone can copy a picture and make an NFT of it. Only the collection address, checked against the one its creators publish, proves an NFT is from the original.
nfts-names-summary: Readable names that point to addresses, and what to watch for.
nfts-names-intro-p1: Your phone's contacts let you tap "Grandma" instead of typing her number. The name is just a nickname that points to the number.
nfts-names-intro-p2: An Ethereum name, like alice.eth, does the same for an address: friends can send to the name instead of a long string of characters. The best-known system for these names is the Ethereum Name Service (ENS), and each .eth name is itself an NFT, so it has one owner.
nfts-names-why-prompt: Why can sending to a name like sam.eth be safer than pasting a long address?
nfts-names-why-fb-private: A name points to a public address, and anyone can look up both. Think about what's easier for you to check.
nfts-names-why-opt-spot: A misspelled name is easier to spot than a changed character in an address
nfts-names-why-fb-spot: Right. People notice a typo in a word far more easily than a change in the middle of a long address. You still need to read the name carefully.
nfts-names-why-opt-undo: Payments sent to names can be undone
nfts-names-why-fb-undo: Payments are final, whichever way you address them. Think about what's easier for you to check.
nfts-names-spot-prompt: Your friend Alice says her Ethereum name is alice.eth. Which of these is hers?
nfts-names-spot-explain: Each look-alike changed or added a character or two. Reading the whole name, letter by letter, catches it, just like checking a whole address.
