nfts-names-know-prompt: You've set up an Ethereum name for your address. Which two things should you know?
nfts-names-know-opt-public: Anyone can look up your address and its activity from your name
nfts-names-know-fb-public: Right. A name points to a public address, so it links you to everything that address does.
nfts-names-know-opt-hides: It hides your address from everyone
nfts-names-know-fb-hides: A name points to your address. It doesn't hide it, and anyone can look up where it points.
nfts-names-know-opt-renew: You have to renew it from time to time, or you can lose it
nfts-names-know-fb-renew: Right. Names are registered for a set time. If you let yours run out, someone else can register it.
nfts-names-know-opt-forever: It's yours forever once you have it
nfts-names-know-fb-forever: Names don't last forever on their own. Think about what happens when the time you registered it for is up.
nfts-names-know-explain: An Ethereum name is public: it points to your address, so anyone can see that address's activity. Names are registered for a set time, so renew yours before it runs out.
nfts-names-takeaway-p1: An Ethereum name is a readable nickname that points to an address. It's easier to check than a long address, but it's public, and you have to renew it.
nfts-approve-summary: The permission that covers every NFT in a collection at once.
nfts-approve-intro-p1: To sell an NFT, you can list it on a marketplace: an app where people buy and sell NFTs. Its contract needs your permission to move the NFT when someone buys it, much like a token approval lets a contract move your tokens.
nfts-approve-intro-p2: Many marketplaces ask you to approve all: permission to move every NFT you own in that collection, not just the one you're selling. It saves approving each one, but if that contract has a bug, or a fake site tricks you into approving one, every one of them is exposed. It lasts until you revoke it, a small transaction that cancels it.
nfts-approve-scope-prompt: You're selling one cat NFT. Pick the permission that lets the sale happen without putting anything else at risk.
nfts-approve-scope-explain: Approving one NFT covers just the sale. Approve all covers the whole collection until you revoke it, and nothing honest ever needs your recovery phrase. When an app gives you a choice, pick the narrowest one.
nfts-approve-later-prompt: You approved all for a collection to sell one NFT. Later you buy another NFT from the same collection. Is the new one covered by that permission?
nfts-approve-later-opt-covered: Yes: approve all covers new ones too
nfts-approve-later-fb-covered: Right. The permission covers every NFT you hold in that collection, including ones you get later, until you revoke it.
nfts-approve-later-opt-old: No: only the NFTs you had when you approved
nfts-approve-later-fb-old: The permission isn't a list of the NFTs you had then. It covers the whole collection. Think about how long it lasts.
nfts-approve-later-opt-ended: No: the permission ended when the sale finished
nfts-approve-later-fb-ended: Approvals don't end on their own. Think about how long it lasts.
nfts-approve-done-text: Approve {b1} lets a marketplace move every NFT you own in a collection, so give the narrowest permission you can and {b2} it when you're done.
nfts-approve-done-explain: Approve all is convenient but covers the whole collection, now and later. Give only the permission you need, and revoke it once you've finished.
nfts-approve-takeaway-p1: Approve all lets a marketplace move every NFT you own in a collection, including ones you get later. Give the narrowest permission you can, and revoke it when you're done.
nfts-uses-summary: What NFTs are used for, beyond pictures.
nfts-uses-intro-p1: Not every NFT is a picture. Because an NFT has exactly one owner that anyone can check, it works well as proof: of a ticket, of something you did, or of belonging to a group.
nfts-uses-intro-p2: A door scanner, a course or a club can look at the list on Ethereum and see that your address holds the right NFT, without phoning anyone to ask.
nfts-uses-match-prompt: Match each everyday thing to the NFT that does the same job.
nfts-uses-match-match-ticket: An NFT that gets you into a show
nfts-uses-match-match-badge: An NFT for finishing a course
nfts-uses-match-match-card: An NFT that unlocks a club's private chat
nfts-uses-match-match-tag: An NFT that points to your address
nfts-uses-match-explain: Each NFT does the job of something you'd carry around. The difference: anyone can check on Ethereum which address holds it.
nfts-uses-gate-prompt: At a concert, the gate checks NFT tickets. Why can't someone get in with a copy of your ticket's picture?
nfts-uses-gate-opt-blurry: Copies of pictures always come out blurry
nfts-uses-gate-fb-blurry: A copy of a picture can be perfect. Think about what the gate actually checks.
nfts-uses-gate-opt-owner: The gate checks which address owns the ticket, not the picture
nfts-uses-gate-fb-owner: Right. A copied picture doesn't change the list on Ethereum. Only the address that owns the ticket gets in, usually by signing a message to prove the address is yours.
nfts-uses-gate-opt-secret: Each picture hides a secret code
nfts-uses-gate-fb-secret: There's no hidden code in the picture. Think about what the gate actually checks.
nfts-uses-helpers-prompt: People who help with ethereum.org, for example by translating it, can claim a badge NFT. What does holding one show?
nfts-uses-helpers-opt-bought: That its owner paid for it
nfts-uses-helpers-fb-bought: These badges are handed out for helping. Think about what the badge records.
nfts-uses-helpers-fb-staff: It's a thank-you for helping, not a job title. Think about what the badge records.
nfts-uses-helpers-opt-helped: That the address holding it helped out
nfts-uses-helpers-fb-helped: Right. A badge like this is a public record of something you did, and anyone can look it up.
nfts-uses-takeaway-p1: NFTs can work as tickets, badges and passes. Anyone can check on Ethereum which address holds one, so they prove things without anyone having to vouch for you.
nfts-exam-coin-prompt: What makes an NFT different from a coin like a stablecoin?
nfts-exam-coin-opt-unique: Each NFT is one of a kind, with its own token ID
nfts-exam-coin-explain: Coins are interchangeable: any one is as good as another. Each NFT has its own token ID, which makes it one of a kind.
nfts-exam-owners-prompt: How many owners does one NFT have on its contract's list at a time?
nfts-exam-owners-opt-none: None, since NFTs have no owners
nfts-exam-owners-explain: An NFT's contract keeps track of who owns each token ID, and each one has exactly one owner at a time. Saving its picture changes nothing on that list.
nfts-exam-picture-prompt: Where does an NFT's picture usually live?
nfts-exam-picture-opt-chain: On the blockchain, next to its owner
nfts-exam-picture-opt-elsewhere: On another computer, linked from the NFT
nfts-exam-picture-explain: Pictures are usually too big to keep on the blockchain. The NFT holds a link, and the picture sits on a host that the link points to.
nfts-exam-offline-prompt: The host of your NFT's picture shuts down. Who owns the NFT now?
nfts-exam-offline-explain: Ownership is recorded on Ethereum, not on the host. The picture may stop showing, but the list still says the NFT is yours.
nfts-exam-copier-prompt: Can someone make an NFT of a picture they didn't create?
nfts-exam-copier-opt-yes: Yes. Nothing on Ethereum stops them
nfts-exam-copier-explain: Ethereum doesn't check who drew a picture, so anyone can make an NFT of one. That's why buyers check the collection address to know an NFT is the real thing.
nfts-exam-proof-prompt: Which detail proves that an NFT comes from the original collection?
nfts-exam-proof-explain: Names and pictures can be copied. The collection address belongs to the original contract alone, so compare it with the one the creators publish.
nfts-exam-name-prompt: What does an Ethereum name like sam.eth do?
nfts-exam-name-opt-points: Points to an address, like a contact name points to a phone number
nfts-exam-name-opt-hides: Hides an address so nobody can see it
nfts-exam-name-explain: An Ethereum name is a readable nickname for an address. It's easier to check than a long address, but it doesn't hide anything.
nfts-exam-renew-prompt: What can happen if you don't renew your Ethereum name?
nfts-exam-renew-opt-lose: You can lose it, and someone else can register it
nfts-exam-renew-explain: Names are registered for a set time. Let one run out and someone else can register it. Your address itself keeps working either way.
nfts-exam-all-prompt: A marketplace asks you to approve all for a collection you hold. What does that permission cover?
nfts-exam-all-opt-everything: Everything in your wallet, ETH included
nfts-exam-all-opt-collection: Every NFT you hold in that collection
nfts-exam-all-explain: Approve all lets that contract move every NFT you own in the collection, including ones you get later, until you revoke it. It doesn't cover other collections or your ETH.
nfts-exam-revoke-prompt: You gave a marketplace approve all and no longer use it. What should you do?
nfts-exam-revoke-opt-disconnect: Just disconnect your wallet from its website
nfts-exam-revoke-explain: Approvals don't expire, and disconnecting from a website doesn't cancel them. Revoking does, with a small transaction.
nfts-exam-gate-prompt: How can a concert gate check an NFT ticket without calling anyone?
nfts-exam-gate-opt-code: The picture holds a secret code
nfts-exam-gate-opt-list: It looks up which address owns the ticket on Ethereum
nfts-exam-gate-opt-call: It can't: the seller always has to confirm
nfts-exam-gate-explain: Ownership is public on Ethereum, so anyone, a concert gate included, can look up which address holds a ticket. A copied picture doesn't change that.
nfts-exam-badge-prompt: What can an NFT badge for finishing a course show?
nfts-exam-badge-opt-finished: That the address holding it finished the course
nfts-exam-badge-opt-paid: That its owner paid the most
nfts-exam-badge-opt-teaches: That its owner teaches the course
nfts-exam-badge-explain: Badge NFTs are a public record of something you did, like finishing a course or going to an event, that anyone can look up.

trading-and-lending-description: How swapping and borrowing work with no company in the middle, and how to tell where a reward really comes from.
trading-and-lending-apps-summary: Who you're trusting when smart contracts run the shop.
trading-and-lending-apps-intro-p1: At a currency exchange desk, a clerk takes your money and hands you a different currency. You trust the clerk, and the company behind the desk.
trading-and-lending-apps-intro-p2: A trading app on Ethereum has no desk and no clerk. It's a set of smart contracts, programs on Ethereum that run exactly as written. Nobody holds your tokens for you: they stay in your wallet until you swap, which means trading one kind of token for another.
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-prompt: Put the steps of a swap in order, from start to finish.
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-item-conne: Connect your wallet to the trading app
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-item-pick: Pick the token you give and the token you want
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-item-appro: Approve the app's contract to move the token you give
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-item-swap: Sign the swap and pay the fee
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-item-check: Check your wallet for the new tokens
trading-and-lending-apps-swap-explain: The contract can only move your tokens once you've allowed it, so the approval comes before the swap. Afterwards, your wallet shows the new tokens at your own address.
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-prompt: With no clerk and no company holding your tokens, what are you trusting when you swap?
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-opt-clerk: A support team that can undo a bad trade
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-fb-clerk: There's no desk to call. Once a swap goes through, nobody can undo it, just like any other payment on Ethereum.
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-opt-code: The app's code, to do exactly what it should
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-fb-code: Right. The contracts do all the work, so a bug in their code is the main risk. Reviews help, but they can't promise there are no bugs.
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-opt-bank: A bank that guarantees your tokens
trading-and-lending-apps-trust-fb-bank: No bank stands behind a trading app. If something goes wrong, there's usually nobody to pay you back.
trading-and-lending-apps-admin-p1: Some apps also keep a few controls for their team, such as pausing the app or changing its rules. These are called admin controls. They can help fix a problem fast, but they also mean you're trusting whoever holds them.
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-prompt: An app's team holds controls that can change how its contracts work. What does that mean for you?
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-opt-ne: Nothing, because smart contracts can never change
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-fb-nev: A contract's own code can't simply be changed, but an app can be built with controls that let its team swap parts out or pause it.
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-opt-bo: You're trusting the team as well as the code
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-fb-bot: Right. Whoever holds the controls could change how the app treats your tokens. Careful apps say plainly who holds them and what they can do.
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-opt-sa: The app is completely safe, because the team can fix anything
trading-and-lending-apps-controls-fb-saf: Fixes help, but the same controls could be misused, or stolen. More power for the team means more trust in the team.
trading-and-lending-apps-takeaway-p1: A trading app is smart contracts, not a company: your tokens stay in your wallet until you swap, but you're trusting its code, and anyone who holds its admin controls.
trading-and-lending-pool-summary: Why a bigger trade gets a worse price.
trading-and-lending-pool-intro-p1: Picture a fruit stand with no seller, just two crates: one of apples, one of pears. Anyone can swap: drop pears in, take apples out. The stand sets its own price. The fewer apples are left, the more pears each apple costs.
trading-and-lending-pool-intro-p2: Many trading apps work like that stand. A pool is a smart contract holding two kinds of tokens. When you swap, you put one kind in and take the other out, and the price shifts as you go.
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-prompt: You want lots of apples from the stand. Will each apple cost the same as when you take just a few?
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-opt-same: Yes, a price is a price
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-fb-same: At this stand, the price moves with every apple you take. See for yourself in the next step.
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-opt-more: No, each one costs more as the apples run low
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-fb-more: That's the idea. Test it in the next step.
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-opt-less: No, a big order gets a discount
trading-and-lending-pool-guess-fb-less: A shop might offer a bulk discount, but this stand has no seller to offer one. See what happens in the next step.
trading-and-lending-pool-stand-prompt: Slide from a handful of apples to most of the crate, and watch what each apple costs.
trading-and-lending-pool-stand-explain: The more apples you take, the fewer are left, so each one costs more pears. A pool works the same way: a big trade gets a worse price than a small one.
trading-and-lending-pool-size-prompt: Two pools hold the same two tokens. One is tiny, the other is huge. You want to make a big swap. Which gives you the better price?
trading-and-lending-pool-size-fb-tiny: Your trade would take a big share of a tiny pool. Remember what happened when the crate ran low.
trading-and-lending-pool-size-opt-same: Either one, since they hold the same tokens
trading-and-lending-pool-size-fb-same: Same tokens, but not the same amount of them. Think about how much of each pool your trade would use up.
trading-and-lending-pool-size-fb-huge: Right. Your trade takes only a small share of a huge pool, so the price barely moves. The same trade would empty a tiny pool fast and send the price soaring.
trading-and-lending-pool-takeaway-p1: A pool is a smart contract holding two tokens that sets its own price: the more you take, the more each one costs, so big trades in small pools get bad prices.
trading-and-lending-limit-summary: Why you choose a limit before you swap.
trading-and-lending-limit-intro-p1: When you press swap, your trade doesn't happen that very instant. It waits to be added to a block, and other people's swaps from the same pool may go first and move the price.
trading-and-lending-limit-intro-p2: So trading apps let you choose how much the price may change before your swap goes through, often called the slippage setting. If the price moves more than that, the swap is canceled: you keep your tokens, but the fee is still spent.
trading-and-lending-limit-first-prompt: You're about to take apples from the stand. Just before your swap, someone else's big swap takes lots of apples out. What happens to your price?
trading-and-lending-limit-first-opt-same: It stays the price you saw
trading-and-lending-limit-first-fb-same: The price you saw was for the crates as they were. Think about what that other swap did to them.
trading-and-lending-limit-first-opt-wors: It gets worse, because fewer apples are left
trading-and-lending-limit-first-fb-worse: Right. Their swap moved the price before yours, so each apple now costs you more.
trading-and-lending-limit-first-opt-bett: It gets better, because the stand is busy
trading-and-lending-limit-first-fb-bette: A busy stand doesn't mean a better price. Think about how many apples are left for you.
trading-and-lending-limit-set-prompt: Choose a price limit for your swap. Then see what happens if the price wiggles a little, and if it suddenly jumps.
trading-and-lending-limit-set-explain: A small limit lets everyday wiggles through but cancels your swap if the price jumps, so you never get a much worse deal than the one you saw.
trading-and-lending-limit-any-prompt: A site tells you to set your limit to "any change", so your swap is never canceled. What's the catch?
trading-and-lending-limit-any-opt-fee: It costs a much bigger fee
trading-and-lending-limit-any-fb-fee: The limit doesn't change the fee. Think about which swaps it lets through.
trading-and-lending-limit-any-opt-never: There's no catch: a swap that's never canceled is the goal
trading-and-lending-limit-any-fb-never: A swap that can never be canceled also can't protect you. Think about what happens if the price jumps.
trading-and-lending-limit-any-opt-worse: Your swap could go through at a terrible price
trading-and-lending-limit-any-fb-worse: Right. With no limit, a sudden jump goes through too, and you could get far fewer tokens than you expected.
trading-and-lending-limit-takeaway-p1: The price can move before your swap goes through, so set a small limit: if the price moves more than that, the swap is canceled instead of going through at a bad price.
trading-and-lending-borrow-summary: How a deposit lets you borrow, and when it gets sold.
trading-and-lending-borrow-intro-p1: At a pawn shop, you leave something valuable, like a guitar, and borrow money for it. You can only borrow less than the guitar is worth. Pay the money back and you get your guitar. If you don't, the shop sells it.
trading-and-lending-borrow-intro-p2: A lending app works much the same way. You put in tokens as a deposit, called collateral, and borrow other tokens worth less than it. Nobody checks who you are: the deposit is your promise to pay back.
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-prompt: Why does a lending app only let you borrow less than your deposit is worth?
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-opt-fee: Because the gap is the app's fee
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-fb-fee: The app doesn't keep the gap: you get your whole deposit back when you repay. Think about what could happen to the deposit's value.
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-opt-cush: So there's still enough to repay the loan if the deposit's value drops
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-fb-cushi: Right. Token prices go up and down. The gap is a cushion that protects whoever lent the tokens.
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-opt-trus: Because the app doesn't trust you personally
trading-and-lending-borrow-less-fb-trust: The app never knows who you are, so trust doesn't come into it. It's the deposit's value it has to worry about.
trading-and-lending-borrow-cushion-promp: Choose how much to borrow, then let your deposit's value drop. Find out when it gets sold.
trading-and-lending-borrow-cushion-expla: If your deposit's value falls too far compared with your loan, some or all of it is sold to repay the lenders. You keep what you borrowed, but lose that part of your deposit. Borrowing less leaves a bigger cushion.
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-promp: You've borrowed against a deposit, and its value is falling fast toward the sell line. What can you do?
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-opt-w: Nothing yet: the app will call you before it sells
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-fb-wa: There's nobody to call you. The contract follows its rules the moment the line is crossed, so keep an eye on it yourself.
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-opt-s: Ask the app's support team to pause the sale
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-fb-su: The sale follows the contract's rules, not a person who can be asked to wait. Think about what you can change yourself.
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-opt-r: Repay part of the loan, or add more to your deposit
trading-and-lending-borrow-falling-fb-re: Right. Either one moves you away from the line: the loan gets smaller, or the deposit gets bigger.
trading-and-lending-borrow-takeaway-p1: Borrowing on Ethereum works like a pawn shop: you borrow less than your deposit is worth, and if its value drops too far, the deposit is sold to repay the loan.
trading-and-lending-rewards-summary: Every real reward comes from someone. Learn to name who.
trading-and-lending-rewards-intro-p1: When your piggy bank grows, someone put the money in: a neighbor who paid you to walk their dog, or a birthday card from your grandma. Money doesn't appear from nowhere.
trading-and-lending-rewards-intro-p2: Real rewards on Ethereum always come from someone too: interest that borrowers pay to lenders, a share of the fee every swap pays, for the people who filled the pool, or rewards from Ethereum itself for staking ETH, the deposit validators put up to help run the network. If nobody can tell you who pays, be careful.
trading-and-lending-rewards-sort-prompt: Sort each reward by who pays it.
trading-and-lending-rewards-sort-explain: Lenders earn interest from borrowers, people who fill a pool share the fees traders pay, and stakers are paid by Ethereum for helping run it. A reward nobody can explain is a warning sign.
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-promp: A site promises a big reward every day for depositing your tokens. When you ask who pays it, they say it's "a secret strategy". What's most likely?
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-opt-s: A clever strategy that's too good to share
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-fb-st: Real rewards can be explained: who pays, and why. A secret is a reason to be careful, not to trust.
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-opt-n: It's paid from newer people's deposits, until the money runs out
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-fb-ne: Most likely. Paying earlier people with newer people's money only works while new money keeps coming. When it stops, the last ones in lose.
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-opt-e: Ethereum pays extra to new apps
trading-and-lending-rewards-secret-fb-et: Ethereum itself only pays rewards for staking to help run the network, never for depositing into an app.
trading-and-lending-rewards-takeaway-p1: Every real reward is paid by someone: borrowers, traders or Ethereum itself. If you can't say who pays, be careful.
trading-and-lending-exam-keep-prompt: You've connected your wallet to a trading app but haven't swapped yet. Where are your tokens?
trading-and-lending-exam-keep-opt-app: Held by the company behind the app
trading-and-lending-exam-keep-explain: Until you swap, your tokens stay in your wallet. A trading app is a set of smart contracts, not a company that holds your tokens for you.
trading-and-lending-exam-admin-prompt: A trading app's team can pause it and change its rules. What are you trusting when you use it?
trading-and-lending-exam-admin-opt-nothi: Nothing at all, because smart contracts need no trust
trading-and-lending-exam-admin-opt-both: Its code, and the people who hold those controls
trading-and-lending-exam-admin-explain: Admin controls can fix problems fast, but whoever holds them could change how the app treats your tokens. So you trust them as well as the code.
trading-and-lending-exam-big-prompt: You make two swaps from the same pool: a small one and a huge one. Which gets the better price for each token?
trading-and-lending-exam-big-explain: Each token you take leaves fewer in the pool, so the next one costs more. A huge swap pushes the price much further than a small one.
trading-and-lending-exam-depth-prompt: A token's only pool is tiny. What happens if you make a big swap in it?
trading-and-lending-exam-depth-opt-worse: The price moves a lot against you
trading-and-lending-exam-depth-explain: A big swap uses up a large share of a tiny pool, so each token costs far more. In a huge pool, the same swap barely moves the price.
trading-and-lending-exam-canceled-prompt: Your swap is canceled because the price moved more than your limit. What happened?
trading-and-lending-exam-canceled-opt-ha: Half of your tokens were swapped
trading-and-lending-exam-canceled-opt-ke: You keep your tokens, but the fee is spent
trading-and-lending-exam-canceled-explai: A canceled swap changes nothing, so your tokens stay where they were. The fee is still paid, as it is for any transaction that fails.
trading-and-lending-exam-limit-prompt: Which price limit protects you best on an everyday swap?
trading-and-lending-exam-limit-explain: A small limit lets ordinary wiggles through and cancels the swap if the price jumps. No room at all cancels too often, and any change lets a terrible price through.
trading-and-lending-exam-pawn-prompt: Why can you only borrow less than your deposit is worth?
trading-and-lending-exam-pawn-opt-cushio: It leaves a cushion in case the deposit's value drops
trading-and-lending-exam-pawn-opt-profit: So the app can keep the difference
trading-and-lending-exam-pawn-opt-identi: Because the app hasn't checked who you are yet
trading-and-lending-exam-pawn-explain: Prices go up and down. Borrowing less than the deposit is worth leaves enough to repay the lenders even if its value falls.
trading-and-lending-exam-drop-prompt: Your deposit's value falls so far that your loan crosses the sell line. What happens?
trading-and-lending-exam-drop-opt-remind: You get a reminder to pay
trading-and-lending-exam-drop-opt-sold: Some or all of the deposit is sold to repay the loan
trading-and-lending-exam-drop-opt-nothin: Nothing until you choose to repay
trading-and-lending-exam-drop-explain: The contract's rules let the deposit be sold to pay back the lenders once the line is crossed. Repaying part of the loan or adding to the deposit beforehand keeps you away from the line.
trading-and-lending-exam-interest-prompt: You lend tokens through a lending app. Who pays the interest you earn?
trading-and-lending-exam-interest-opt-ap: The app, from its own savings
trading-and-lending-exam-interest-opt-bo: The people who borrow those tokens
trading-and-lending-exam-interest-explai: Lenders put tokens in, and borrowers take them out and pay interest for doing so. Ethereum's own rewards are for staking, not lending.
trading-and-lending-exam-secret-prompt: A site promises a guaranteed reward every day but won't say who pays it. What should you think?
trading-and-lending-exam-secret-opt-care: Be careful: a reward nobody can explain is a warning sign
trading-and-lending-exam-secret-explain: Real rewards come from someone, like borrowers, traders or Ethereum itself, and they're never guaranteed. If nobody can say who pays, the money most likely comes from other people's deposits.
scams-description: The tricks scammers use again and again, how to see through them, and what to do if one gets you.
scams-playbook-summary: Four marks that most scams share.
scams-playbook-intro-p1: Scams come in many costumes: a prize, a new friend, a helpful stranger, an urgent warning. Underneath, most of them use the same few tricks.
scams-playbook-intro-p2: Watch for four marks: hurry (act now), secrecy (don't tell anyone), too good to be true (big rewards, no risk), and a request to send or sign something. Spot even one, and slow down.
scams-playbook-sort-prompt: Sort each message by the scam mark it shows.
scams-playbook-sort-explain: Hurry stops you from thinking, secrecy stops you from asking anyone, a too-good offer makes you want to believe, and the request is where the theft happens.
scams-playbook-one-prompt: A friendly person you met online never rushes you and never asks you to keep secrets. Today they ask you to sign one quick message for them. What do you do?
scams-playbook-one-opt-sign: Sign it, since they show none of the other marks
scams-playbook-one-fb-sign: Being patient and friendly can be part of the trick. Look again at what they're asking for.
scams-playbook-one-opt-stop: Stop and check: a request to sign is a mark by itself
scams-playbook-one-fb-stop: Right. Any one mark is enough to slow down. Don't sign anything you didn't expect, for anyone.
scams-playbook-one-opt-free: Sign it, as long as signing is free
scams-playbook-one-fb-free: A signature can be free and still hand something over. You'll see how later in this course.
scams-playbook-takeaway-p1: Hurry, secrecy, too good to be true, and a request to send or sign: spot any one of these marks and stop.
scams-lookalike-summary: Copycat sites, and why a bookmark beats them.
scams-lookalike-intro-p1: A copycat site can look exactly like the real one: same logo, same colors, same buttons. What it can't copy is the real web address, so it uses one that looks close, with a swapped letter, an extra word or a dash.
scams-lookalike-intro-p2: Copycats often reach people through ads at the top of search results and links in direct messages. Once you're there, they ask you to connect your wallet and sign, or to type your recovery phrase. The safest habit is to open important sites from a bookmark you saved yourself.
scams-lookalike-copy-prompt: A copycat site can copy the real one's look perfectly. What can't it copy?
scams-lookalike-copy-fb-logo: A logo is just a picture, and anyone can copy a picture. Look for something only the real site can have.
scams-lookalike-copy-fb-address: Right. Only the real site lives at the real address, so that's the thing to check.
scams-lookalike-copy-fb-design: Copying a design is quick and easy. What belongs to the real site alone?
scams-lookalike-pick-prompt: You saved ethereum.org as a bookmark. Four links you were sent all claim to be it. Which one is the real site?
scams-lookalike-pick-explain: Each copycat changes one small thing: swapped letters, the real name followed by more words, or a dash in place of a dot. Only an exact match with your bookmark is the real site.
scams-lookalike-ad-prompt: You search for a wallet app, and the top result is an ad with the right name and logo. What's the safest way to reach the app's site?
scams-lookalike-ad-opt-ad: Click the ad, since it has the right name
scams-lookalike-ad-fb-ad: Scammers can buy ads too, with any name and logo they like. Think about a way in that you control.
scams-lookalike-ad-opt-dm: Use the link a helpful stranger sent you in a chat
scams-lookalike-ad-fb-dm: Links in direct messages are one of the most common ways copycats find people. Where could you get the address yourself?
scams-lookalike-ad-opt-bookmark: Use a bookmark you saved from the real site
scams-lookalike-ad-fb-bookmark: Right. A bookmark you saved yourself takes you to the real site every time, with no ad or stranger in between.
scams-lookalike-takeaway-p1: Copycat sites can look perfect but can't use the real address. Open important sites from a bookmark you saved, never from an ad or a message.
scams-signatures-summary: Why a signature with no fee can still cost you.
scams-signatures-intro-p1: Signing a message costs no fee, so it can feel harmless, like writing your name on a card. But some messages are permissions: one signature can let someone else's contract move your tokens, just like an approval.
scams-signatures-intro-p2: The scammer then hands that signature to a contract themselves and moves your tokens away. So before you sign, read who's asking, what it lets them do, and how much.
scams-signatures-free-prompt: A message costs nothing to sign. Does that mean signing it can't cost you anything?
scams-signatures-free-opt-safe: Right, no fee means no risk
scams-signatures-free-fb-safe: The fee isn't where the danger is. Think about what the message might let someone do afterwards.
scams-signatures-free-opt-depends: No, it depends on what the message allows
scams-signatures-free-fb-depends: Right. A sign-in message grants nothing, but a permission can hand over your tokens. Try spotting one in the next step.
scams-signatures-free-opt-eth: It can only ever cost you ETH
scams-signatures-free-fb-eth: Your tokens matter too. Think about what the message might let someone do with them.
scams-signatures-spot-prompt: A site you reached from a link offers free tokens and asks you to sign this. Tap every part that should worry you.
scams-signatures-spot-explain: The danger was in the details: a site you didn't choose, a permission to spend, an address you don't know, and no limit. The missing fee is part of the bait.
scams-signatures-login-prompt: You open a site you trust from your bookmark. It asks you to sign a message that says "Sign in to this site", with no permission and no amount. What do you do?
scams-signatures-login-fb-never: Signing is part of using Ethereum, so you'll need to sometimes. The trick is to read what each request asks for.
scams-signatures-login-opt-phrase: Type your recovery phrase instead, to be safe
scams-signatures-login-fb-phrase: No site ever needs your recovery phrase. Anyone who has it controls your wallet.
scams-signatures-login-opt-sign: Sign it: it grants nothing, and you chose the site yourself
scams-signatures-login-fb-sign: Right. Many sites use a signature to log you in. Reading is what matters: no permission, no amount, a site you opened yourself.
scams-signatures-takeaway-p1: A signature costs no fee but can still hand over your tokens. Before you sign, read who's asking, what it allows and how much.
scams-bait-summary: Where the tokens you never asked for are trying to lead you.
scams-bait-intro-p1: Anyone can create a token and send it to any address, so tokens you never asked for can turn up in your wallet. Many carry a web address in their name, or a message like "You won! Claim at the link". Follow one, and you land on a claim page built to look friendly.
scams-bait-spot-prompt: You followed a free token's link to this claim page. Tap every part that's a trick.
scams-bait-spot-explain: The page stacks the scam marks: hurry, a too-good promise, an address you didn't choose. Connecting only shares your address, but the signature after it is the real trap.
scams-bait-trail-p1: Connecting shows the site your address, and nothing moves yet. The trap is the next step: the "claim" is a signature or approval that lets the scammer move your real tokens.
scams-bait-trail-p2: The free token was never worth anything. It was the hook, and the tokens you already had were the catch.
scams-bait-signed-prompt: You already signed on a claim page, but nothing seems to have happened yet. What should you do?
scams-bait-signed-opt-fine: Nothing: if your tokens are still there, the claim didn't work
scams-bait-signed-fb-fine: A permission like this can stay usable for a long time, and the scammer can use it whenever they like, maybe much later. Think about how to cancel it.
scams-bait-signed-opt-revoke: Revoke the permission it gave, right away
scams-bait-signed-fb-revoke: Right. Revoking cancels the permission before the scammer gets around to using it. If you can't find a way to revoke it, move your tokens to a new wallet.
scams-bait-signed-opt-again: Go back and sign again, in case the claim got stuck
scams-bait-signed-fb-again: Signing again only hands over more. The claim never existed. Think about how to cancel what you already gave.
scams-bait-takeaway-p1: A free token's link leads to a claim page whose real goal is your signature. Never claim, and if you already signed, revoke it.
scams-too-good-summary: Guaranteed rewards, magic bots and online friends with a tip.
scams-too-good-intro-p1: Real rewards come from someone, and they're never guaranteed. So a promise of big, sure profits is a mark of a scam, whether it comes from a site, a "trading bot" that never loses, or someone you met online.
scams-too-good-intro-p2: The slowest scam is the friendship scam. A stranger becomes a friend, then coaches you onto a new trading site where your money seems to grow. The growth is only numbers on their screen, and the money is already gone.
scams-too-good-stages-prompt: Put the stages of a friendship scam in order.
scams-too-good-stages-item-hello: A stranger messages you, as if by mistake
scams-too-good-stages-item-friends: You chat often and become friends
scams-too-good-stages-item-tip: They mention the money they make on a special trading site
scams-too-good-stages-item-join: They help you sign up and put in a little
scams-too-good-stages-item-grow: Your balance seems to grow, so you put in more
scams-too-good-stages-item-fee: To take money out, you're told to pay a fee first
scams-too-good-stages-explain: Each stage builds trust for the next. The fake growth gets you to put in more, and the fee to withdraw is one last grab. When someone you've only met online starts talking about investing, that's the moment to stop.
scams-too-good-bot-prompt: An ad offers a trading bot that "never loses" and promises a profit every day. What's wrong with it?
scams-too-good-bot-opt-cheap: Nothing, as long as the bot is cheap
scams-too-good-bot-fb-cheap: The price isn't the problem. Could anyone really keep that promise?
scams-too-good-bot-opt-guarantee: Nobody can promise trading profits, so the promise itself is the mark
scams-too-good-bot-fb-guarantee: Right. Prices go down as well as up, for everyone. The promise is there to stop you asking questions.
scams-too-good-bot-opt-screenshots: Nothing, if it shows screenshots of its wins
scams-too-good-bot-fb-screenshots: Screenshots are easy to fake, and they only ever show the wins. Could anyone really keep that promise?
scams-too-good-tax-prompt: The trading site your online friend recommended shows big gains. To withdraw, you must first pay a "tax". What's going on?
scams-too-good-tax-opt-pay: Pay it, so you can get the gains out
scams-too-good-tax-fb-pay: Paying sends more money to the same people. Think about whether those gains were ever real.
scams-too-good-tax-opt-wait: Wait a while, then try to withdraw again
scams-too-good-tax-fb-wait: Waiting won't change anything, because nothing is really there to withdraw. Think about what the site actually is.
scams-too-good-tax-opt-scam: It's a scam: the gains aren't real, and paying only loses more
scams-too-good-tax-fb-scam: Right. The site only ever showed numbers. Stop paying, stop chatting, and report it.
scams-too-good-takeaway-p1: Guaranteed profits, bots that never lose and online friends with a trading tip are all scams. Real rewards come from someone, and they're never sure.
scams-response-summary: What to do if a scam gets you, and the second scam to watch for.
scams-response-intro-p1: Scams fool careful people too, so it helps to know the plan ahead of time. If you signed something bad, revoke the permission it gave. If your recovery phrase leaked, that wallet can't be made safe again: move what's left to a new wallet with a new phrase.
scams-response-intro-p2: Then report the scam, to help warn others. And watch for the second scam: people who offer to get your tokens back for a fee. Nobody can reverse a payment on Ethereum.
scams-response-phrase-prompt: You typed your recovery phrase into a copycat site. Then you revoke every permission your wallet has given. Is that enough?
scams-response-phrase-fb-enough: Revoking cancels permissions, but the thief doesn't need one. Think about what the phrase gives them.
scams-response-phrase-opt-password: No, you also need to change the wallet app's password
scams-response-phrase-fb-password: A password only locks the app on your device. With the phrase, the thief can open your wallet anywhere.
scams-response-phrase-opt-new: No: the thief has your key, so move what's left to a new wallet
scams-response-phrase-fb-new: Right. The phrase brings back your private key, so whoever has it can move anything, any time. Only a new wallet with a new phrase is safe.
scams-response-steps-prompt: Your recovery phrase leaked. Put what you do in order.
scams-response-steps-item-stop: Close the copycat site and type nothing more
scams-response-steps-item-new: Make a new wallet with a new recovery phrase
scams-response-steps-item-move: Move everything that's left into the new wallet
scams-response-steps-item-report: Report the copycat site so others are warned
scams-response-steps-explain: First stop the damage, then make a safe place, then move what's left before the thief does. Reporting comes once your tokens are safe.
scams-response-recovery-prompt: After you post about the scam, someone messages you. They say they're a "recovery expert" who can trace and return your tokens for a fee paid up front. What is it?
scams-response-recovery-fb-help: Nobody can reverse a payment on Ethereum, whatever they charge. Think about who reaches out to people who just lost money.
scams-response-recovery-opt-scam: A second scam that targets people who just lost money
scams-response-recovery-fb-scam: Right. Recovery scammers look for people who post about their losses. Ignore them, and report them too.
scams-response-recovery-opt-police: Fine, if they say they work with the police
scams-response-recovery-fb-police: Anyone can claim that. Nobody can reverse a payment on Ethereum, whoever they say they work with.
scams-response-takeaway-p1: If a scam gets you: revoke what you signed, move to a new wallet if your phrase leaked, report it, and ignore anyone selling recovery.
scams-exam-marks-prompt: A message says: "Today only! Send some ETH to this address and we'll send back even more." Which scam marks does it show?
scams-exam-marks-opt-ask: A request to send or sign
scams-exam-marks-explain: "Today only" is hurry, "send back even more" is too good to be true, and "send some ETH" is the request. It doesn't ask for secrecy, but three marks are already far more than enough.
scams-exam-one-prompt: A message shows just one scam mark. What should you do?
scams-exam-one-opt-fine: Carry on: real scams always show all four
scams-exam-one-opt-stop: Slow down and check: one mark is enough
scams-exam-one-opt-reply: Reply and ask the sender whether it's a scam
scams-exam-one-explain: Scams don't need every mark to work. Any one of them is a reason to stop and check, and the sender is the last person to ask.
scams-exam-copycat-prompt: A copycat site has the same logo, colors and buttons as the real one. What gives it away?
scams-exam-copycat-explain: Only the real site can use the real address. Copycats use one that looks close, so compare it with an address you saved, all the way to the end.
scams-exam-bookmark-prompt: What's the safest way to open a site you use with your wallet?
scams-exam-bookmark-opt-search: Search for it and click the top result
scams-exam-bookmark-opt-message: Use the link in a message from its team
scams-exam-bookmark-opt-bookmark: Use a bookmark you saved from the real site
scams-exam-bookmark-explain: Ads and messages are favorite ways to reach copycats. A bookmark you saved yourself always goes to the real address.
scams-exam-free-prompt: Why can a signature with no fee still be risky?
scams-exam-free-opt-later: Because the fee is charged later
scams-exam-free-opt-permission: Because it can give someone permission to move your tokens
scams-exam-free-opt-twice: It's only risky if you sign it twice
scams-exam-free-explain: Some messages are permissions. Once signed, the scammer can use them to move your tokens, with no fee ever showing up on your side.
scams-exam-read-prompt: Before you sign a request, what should you read?
scams-exam-read-explain: Who's asking, what it allows and how much tell you whether a request is a sign-in or a permission over your tokens. The look of the button tells you nothing.
scams-exam-lead-prompt: A token you never asked for shows up with a web address in its name. Where does that address lead?
scams-exam-lead-opt-gift: To a real gift from a project
scams-exam-lead-opt-drain: To a site that asks you to sign or approve something that lets it take your tokens
scams-exam-lead-opt-nowhere: Nowhere: the token is a mistake
scams-exam-lead-explain: Tokens that show up unasked are bait. The site they point to asks you to connect and sign or approve, which hands over your real tokens.
scams-exam-trap-prompt: On a claim page for a free token, which step actually hands over your tokens?
scams-exam-trap-explain: Connecting only shares your address. The claim is a signature or approval that gives the scammer permission to move your tokens.
scams-exam-guarantee-prompt: Someone you met online promises a guaranteed profit from a trading site they know. What is it most likely to be?
scams-exam-guarantee-opt-tip: A good tip from someone who knows
scams-exam-guarantee-explain: Nobody can guarantee trading profits. An online friend steering you onto a new trading site is how friendship scams work.
scams-exam-withdraw-prompt: A trading site shows big gains, but says you must pay a fee before you can withdraw. What does that tell you?
scams-exam-withdraw-opt-normal: Fees are normal, so pay it
scams-exam-withdraw-opt-scam: It's a scam, and the gains aren't real
scams-exam-withdraw-opt-wait: The site is busy, so try again later
scams-exam-withdraw-explain: Scam sites show made-up gains to get more money in, then ask for a fee to let it out. Paying only loses more.
scams-exam-phrase-prompt: Your recovery phrase leaked. What keeps what's left safe?
scams-exam-phrase-opt-rename: Renaming the account in your wallet
scams-exam-phrase-opt-move: Moving it to a new wallet with a new phrase
scams-exam-phrase-explain: Whoever has the phrase has your private key, so revoking permissions won't stop them. Only moving to a wallet with a new phrase puts your tokens out of reach.
scams-exam-recovery-prompt: Someone offers to recover your stolen tokens for a fee paid up front. What should you do?
scams-exam-recovery-opt-ignore: Ignore them: nobody can reverse a payment on Ethereum
scams-exam-recovery-opt-pay: Pay, since getting your tokens back is worth it
scams-exam-recovery-explain: Recovery offers are a second scam aimed at people who just lost money. Nobody can reverse a payment on Ethereum, whatever they charge.
page-courses-widget-pool-note-handful: A handful barely changes the crate, so each apple costs about the usual price.
page-courses-widget-pool-note-scoop: The apples are running lower, so each one costs a few more pears.
page-courses-widget-pool-note-half: Now each apple costs many more pears than before.
page-courses-widget-pool-note-most: Most of the apples are gone, so the last ones cost a pile of pears. Big trades get bad prices.
page-courses-widget-slippage-label: How much price change you'll accept
page-courses-widget-slippage-case-wiggle: The price wiggles a little, as it often does
page-courses-widget-slippage-case-jump: Someone's big swap goes first, and the price jumps
page-courses-widget-slippage-outcome-can: Canceled. You keep your tokens, but the fee is spent.
page-courses-widget-slippage-outcome-thr: Goes through, close to the price you saw.
page-courses-widget-slippage-outcome-wor: Goes through at a much worse price. You get far fewer tokens.
page-courses-widget-slippage-hint-none: With no room at all, even an everyday wiggle cancels your swap, and every try costs a fee. Allow a little change.
page-courses-widget-slippage-hint-any: Any change means a sudden jump goes through too, at a much worse price. Pick a smaller limit.
page-courses-widget-slippage-hit: A small limit lets everyday wiggles through and cancels the sudden jumps.
page-courses-widget-collateral-line: Sell line: if what you borrowed passes it, your deposit is sold
page-courses-widget-collateral-safe: Plenty of cushion. Your deposit is safe for now.
page-courses-widget-collateral-close: Close to the line. A small drop could get your deposit sold.
page-courses-widget-collateral-sold: Over the line. Your deposit is sold to repay the loan.
page-courses-widget-reward-sort-bucket-t: Traders pay it, through swap fees
page-courses-widget-reward-sort-bucket-n: Ethereum pays it, for helping run the network
page-courses-widget-reward-sort-bucket-u: Nobody can say who pays: be careful
