layer-2-description: Cheaper networks built on top of Ethereum. Learn how they share costs, how to move ETH between them and how to make sure a payment lands on the right one.
layer-2-lanes-summary: Why most payments now travel on networks built on top of Ethereum.
layer-2-lanes-picture-p1: When lots of people use Ethereum at once, it gets crowded, like a main road at rush hour. Everyone wants the same space, so fees go up.
layer-2-lanes-picture-p2: A layer 2 is like an express lane next to that road. It's a separate network that carries lots of payments for much smaller fees, then reports back to Ethereum.
layer-2-lanes-predict-prompt: It's rush hour on Ethereum. Where do you think a payment costs less to send?
layer-2-lanes-predict-fb-main: When Ethereum is crowded, everyone competes for the same space and fees climb. Test it in the next step.
layer-2-lanes-predict-fb-layer-2: Good guess. Test it in the next step, on a quiet day and on a busy one.
layer-2-lanes-predict-opt-same: It costs the same on both
layer-2-lanes-predict-fb-same: The two networks charge very different fees. Test it in the next step.
layer-2-lanes-try-prompt: Send a payment in each lane. Then switch to the other kind of day and send again.
layer-2-lanes-try-explain: On a busy day, Ethereum's fee jumped. The layer 2's fee stayed tiny either way, because it shares its costs among lots of payments. The next lesson shows how.
layer-2-lanes-today-p1: Today, most payments and app actions happen on layer 2s. They aren't cut off from Ethereum: each one regularly reports what happened on it back to Ethereum, where that record can't be secretly changed.
layer-2-lanes-why-prompt: Why does a layer 2 report back to Ethereum?
layer-2-lanes-why-opt-safe: So its record is kept on Ethereum, where nobody can secretly change it
layer-2-lanes-why-fb-safe: Right. The layer 2 does the everyday work cheaply, and Ethereum keeps the record safe.
layer-2-lanes-why-opt-fees: So Ethereum can pay the layer 2's fees for it
layer-2-lanes-why-fb-fees: Ethereum doesn't pay anyone's fees. Reporting to Ethereum actually costs a fee. Think about what Ethereum is good at keeping.
layer-2-lanes-why-opt-permission: So Ethereum can approve each payment before it happens
layer-2-lanes-why-fb-permission: Payments on a layer 2 happen right there, without waiting for Ethereum. Think about what happens after them.
layer-2-lanes-takeaway-p1: A layer 2 is an express lane for Ethereum: a separate network that carries lots of payments for small fees and reports back to Ethereum.
layer-2-parcels-summary: How a layer 2 shares the cost of reporting to Ethereum.
layer-2-parcels-picture-p1: A courier could drive across town once for every parcel. Or they could pack lots of parcels into one crate and make a single trip, so each parcel pays only a small share of the drive.
layer-2-parcels-try-prompt: Pack parcels into the crate and send it to Ethereum. Then send a crate with a different number of parcels and compare each parcel's share of the trip.
layer-2-parcels-try-explain: Every trip has a cost, full crate or not. The more parcels share it, the smaller each one's share.
layer-2-parcels-reveal-p1: A layer 2 works the same way. It gathers lots of payments, packs them into one bundle and sends the bundle to Ethereum in a single transaction. Everyone in the bundle shares that one fee, so each payment pays only a little.
layer-2-parcels-reveal-p2: The bundle lists every payment inside it, so anyone can look on Ethereum and check what happened on the layer 2.
layer-2-parcels-share-prompt: A layer 2 is about to send payments to Ethereum. Which way gives each payment the smallest share of the fee?
layer-2-parcels-share-opt-few: A bundle with just a few payments
layer-2-parcels-share-fb-few: A few payments split the fee only a few ways, so each share is still big. Think about how to split it more ways.
layer-2-parcels-share-opt-many: A bundle with lots of payments
layer-2-parcels-share-fb-many: Right. The fee to reach Ethereum is split across every payment in the bundle, so the fuller it is, the less each one pays.
layer-2-parcels-share-opt-alone: Each payment sent to Ethereum on its own
layer-2-parcels-share-fb-alone: That's one trip per parcel: each payment pays the whole fee by itself. Think about the courier's crate.
layer-2-parcels-recap-prompt: Fill the gaps to sum up how a layer 2 keeps fees low.
layer-2-parcels-recap-text: A layer 2 packs lots of {b1} into one {b2} and sends it to {b3}.
layer-2-parcels-recap-explain: Payments go into one bundle, and the bundle goes to Ethereum in one trip, so they all share one fee.
layer-2-parcels-takeaway-p1: A layer 2 packs lots of payments into one bundle and sends it to Ethereum in one go, so each payment pays only a small share of the fee.
layer-2-networks-summary: Why the sender and the receiver have to use the same network.
layer-2-networks-picture-p1: Imagine your name is on a locker at every swimming pool in town. It's your locker everywhere, but each one is separate: a towel you leave at one pool isn't waiting for you at another.
layer-2-networks-picture-p2: Your address works the same way. It's the same on Ethereum and on most layer 2s, but each network keeps its own balances. ETH you have on one network shows up only on that network.
layer-2-networks-wrong-prompt: Your friend Sam asks you to send ETH on a layer 2. You send it to Sam's address, but on Ethereum by mistake. Where does it end up?
layer-2-networks-wrong-opt-anyway: On the layer 2 anyway, since the address is the same
layer-2-networks-wrong-fb-anyway: The address is the same, but each network keeps its own balances. Think about which network you sent it on.
layer-2-networks-wrong-opt-ethereum: At Sam's address on Ethereum, not on the layer 2
layer-2-networks-wrong-fb-ethereum: Right. It arrived, just on the wrong network. With most wallets, Sam can still reach it by switching to Ethereum. Some special wallets only work on certain networks, though, so a payment on the wrong one can be hard to get back.
layer-2-networks-wrong-fb-vanish: It doesn't vanish. Sam's address exists on more than one network. Think about which one you used.
layer-2-networks-try-prompt: Each friend told you which network to pay them on. Pick the right network for every payment.
layer-2-networks-try-explain: Each friend has the same address on every network, but only the network they asked for puts the ETH where they expect it.
layer-2-networks-receive-prompt: You want a friend to send you ETH on a layer 2. Besides your address, what should you tell them?
layer-2-networks-receive-opt-network: Which network to send it on
layer-2-networks-receive-fb-network: Right. Your address is the same on many networks, so naming the network is what makes the ETH land where you expect it.
layer-2-networks-receive-opt-key: Your private key, so it lands safely
layer-2-networks-receive-fb-key: Never share your private key: whoever has it can spend everything at your address. Receiving needs something much less secret.
layer-2-networks-receive-opt-nothing: Nothing else: the address is enough
layer-2-networks-receive-fb-nothing: The same address works on many networks, so the address alone doesn't say where to send. Think about what's missing.
layer-2-networks-takeaway-p1: Your address is the same on Ethereum and most layer 2s, but each network keeps its own balances, so the sender and the receiver must use the same network.
layer-2-bridge-summary: How a bridge carries your ETH across, and why you have to trust it.
layer-2-bridge-picture-p1: At a coat check, you hand over your coat and get a ticket. The ticket is worth something only because your coat is hanging safely behind the counter, and you trust the people there to keep it.
layer-2-bridge-try-prompt: Move some ETH from Ethereum to the layer 2, then move some back.
layer-2-bridge-try-explain: Each time, ETH was locked on one side and the same amount came out on the other. Nothing was lost, but the bridge held your ETH the whole time.
layer-2-bridge-reveal-p1: That's a bridge: an app that moves your ETH between networks. It locks your ETH on one side and gives you the same amount on the other, like a coat check handing you a ticket.
layer-2-bridge-reveal-p2: A bridge is one more app holding your ETH, so you have to trust it. Use well-known bridges, like the one a layer 2 offers itself, and go to them yourself instead of following links sent to you.
layer-2-bridge-link-prompt: Someone in a group chat shares a link to a super fast bridge, with a bonus for anyone who uses it today. What's the safe move?
layer-2-bridge-link-opt-hurry: Use it quickly, before the bonus ends
layer-2-bridge-link-fb-hurry: A rush and a bonus are classic tricks to stop you from thinking. Fake bridges can look just like real ones.
layer-2-bridge-link-opt-known: Ignore the link and use a well-known bridge you find yourself
layer-2-bridge-link-fb-known: Right. Going to a well-known bridge yourself means a stranger never picks the app that holds your ETH.
layer-2-bridge-link-opt-small: Try it with a little ETH first
layer-2-bridge-link-fb-small: A fake bridge doesn't care how much you send. It may ask your wallet for permission to take far more than your test. Think about who picked this app.
layer-2-bridge-takeaway-p1: A bridge moves your ETH between networks by locking it on one side and giving you the same amount on the other. It's another app you have to trust, so use well-known bridges you find yourself.
layer-2-check-summary: Find the network on your wallet screen before you send.
layer-2-check-picture-p1: Before you board a train, you check the sign on the platform. Same station, same ticket, but the wrong platform takes you somewhere else.
layer-2-check-picture-p2: Your wallet has a sign like that: it always shows which network it's using. Payments you send go out on that network.
layer-2-check-try-prompt: This wallet is about to send ETH. Which part of the screen tells you the network it will use?
layer-2-check-try-explain: The network name is your wallet's platform sign. Your address and the ETH look the same on every network.
layer-2-check-mismatch-prompt: Your friend asked for ETH on a layer 2, but your wallet screen shows Ethereum. What do you do?
layer-2-check-mismatch-opt-switch: Switch your wallet to the layer 2 your friend named, then send
layer-2-check-mismatch-fb-switch: Right. Switching changes the network, not your address. Check that you have ETH on that network too, since each one keeps its own balance.
layer-2-check-mismatch-opt-send: Send anyway: same address, same result
layer-2-check-mismatch-fb-send: Same address, but a different network. The ETH would arrive somewhere your friend didn't ask for.
layer-2-check-mismatch-opt-new: Ask your friend for a different address
layer-2-check-mismatch-fb-new: Your friend's address is fine. The problem is on your screen, not theirs.
layer-2-check-steps-prompt: Put the steps for paying a friend on a layer 2 in order.
layer-2-check-steps-item-ask: Ask your friend which network they want
layer-2-check-steps-item-switch: Switch your wallet to that network
layer-2-check-steps-item-paste: Paste their address and check it
layer-2-check-steps-item-send: Check the network one last time and send
layer-2-check-steps-explain: Find out the network first, switch to it, check the address, then glance at the network once more before you send.
layer-2-check-takeaway-p1: Your wallet always shows which network it's on. Check it before every payment, so your ETH lands on the network your friend asked for.
layer-2-exam-lane-prompt: Ethereum is crowded and fees are high. Where does a small payment usually cost much less?
layer-2-exam-lane-opt-ethereum: On Ethereum, by sending a smaller amount
layer-2-exam-lane-explain: Layer 2s carry lots of payments for much smaller fees than Ethereum, like an express lane beside a crowded main road. A smaller amount doesn't lower Ethereum's fee.
layer-2-exam-report-prompt: What does a layer 2 do with the payments it carries?
layer-2-exam-report-explain: A layer 2 regularly reports its payments back to Ethereum, where that record can't be secretly changed.
layer-2-exam-trip-prompt: A courier packs lots of parcels into one crate so they share one trip. What does a layer 2 do that's like this?
layer-2-exam-trip-opt-split: Splits one payment into lots of small ones
layer-2-exam-trip-opt-wallets: Keeps lots of wallets on one phone
layer-2-exam-trip-opt-bundle: Sends lots of payments to Ethereum together, in one bundle
layer-2-exam-trip-explain: A layer 2 bundles lots of payments and sends them to Ethereum together, so they share one trip.
layer-2-exam-share-prompt: Why does a fuller bundle make each payment on a layer 2 cheaper?
layer-2-exam-share-opt-share: More payments share the one fee to reach Ethereum
layer-2-exam-share-opt-skip: Full bundles don't pay Ethereum's fee at all
layer-2-exam-share-opt-discount: Ethereum gives full bundles a discount
layer-2-exam-share-explain: Sending a bundle to Ethereum costs one fee, and every payment inside shares it. The more payments, the smaller each share.
layer-2-exam-address-prompt: You use the same wallet on Ethereum and on a layer 2. What's true about your address?
layer-2-exam-address-opt-new: Each network gives you a different one
layer-2-exam-address-opt-same: It's usually the same on both
layer-2-exam-address-opt-wallet: You need a new wallet for each network
layer-2-exam-address-explain: With most wallets, your address is the same on Ethereum and most layer 2s. Each network still keeps its own balances.
layer-2-exam-balance-prompt: All your ETH is on a layer 2. You open your wallet while it's set to Ethereum. What balance does it show?
layer-2-exam-balance-opt-split: Half of it on each network
layer-2-exam-balance-opt-none: No ETH, because each network keeps its own balance
layer-2-exam-balance-explain: Each network keeps its own balances. Your ETH on the layer 2 shows up only when your wallet is on that layer 2.
layer-2-exam-bridge-opt-moves: Moves your ETH from one network to another
layer-2-exam-bridge-opt-copies: Copies your ETH so you have it on both networks
layer-2-exam-bridge-explain: A bridge locks your ETH on one network and gives you the same amount on the other. Nothing is copied: the locked ETH backs what you get.
layer-2-exam-giveaway-prompt: A message says a layer 2 is giving away free ETH to anyone who bridges through the link inside. What should you do?
layer-2-exam-giveaway-opt-quick: Bridge through the link before the giveaway ends
layer-2-exam-giveaway-opt-phrase: Share your recovery phrase so the bridge can send the gift
layer-2-exam-giveaway-opt-known: Ignore the link and use a well-known bridge you find yourself
layer-2-exam-giveaway-explain: A bridge holds your ETH, so a stranger should never pick it for you. Free-money offers with a link are a common trick. Go to a well-known bridge yourself.
layer-2-exam-screen-prompt: Where can you see which network your wallet will send a payment on?
layer-2-exam-screen-opt-network: In the network name on the wallet screen
layer-2-exam-screen-opt-balance: In the ETH next to your balance
layer-2-exam-screen-explain: Your wallet shows the network it's on. Your address is the same on many networks, and ETH can sit on many networks, so neither tells you.
layer-2-exam-before-prompt: Your friend wants ETH on Ethereum, but your wallet shows a layer 2. What's the right move?
layer-2-exam-before-opt-send: Send it anyway, since the address is the same
layer-2-exam-before-opt-address: Ask your friend for a different address
layer-2-exam-before-opt-switch: Switch your wallet to Ethereum, then send
layer-2-exam-before-explain: Payments go out on the network your wallet is set to. Switch to the network your friend asked for, then check it again before sending.
rollups-description: What rollups post to Ethereum, how optimistic and zero-knowledge rollups keep each other honest, and what to weigh when you bridge out.
rollups-posted-summary: The data that lets anyone rebuild a rollup from Ethereum alone.
rollups-posted-intro-p1: Most layer 2s, the cheaper networks built on top of Ethereum, are rollups. A rollup runs transactions on its own network, then posts them to Ethereum in batches: hundreds of transactions, compressed and sent together in one Ethereum transaction.
rollups-posted-intro-p2: What it posts is the transaction data itself, who sent what to whom, not just the results. Today most rollups post it in blobs: cheaper space attached to Ethereum blocks, which the network keeps for about 18 days.
rollups-posted-offline-prompt: A rollup's operator, the company that runs it, shuts down overnight. Can anyone still work out every balance on the rollup?
rollups-posted-offline-opt-gone: No, the balances were on the operator's servers
rollups-posted-offline-fb-gone: The servers ran the rollup, but they weren't the only record of what happened. Test it in the next step.
rollups-posted-offline-opt-replay: Yes, by replaying the transaction data it posted to Ethereum
rollups-posted-offline-fb-replay: That's the idea. Test it in the next step.
rollups-posted-offline-opt-list: Yes, by reading the list of balances it posts to Ethereum
rollups-posted-offline-fb-list: Rollups don't post a readable balance list, only a hash of their balances. What they do post is enough, though. Test it in the next step.
rollups-posted-replay-prompt: The rollup's operator is offline. Starting from everyone's earlier balances, replay the batch it posted to Ethereum to rebuild its state: the balance of every account.
rollups-posted-replay-explain: The earlier balances plus every posted transaction gave back the exact state, with no help from the operator. That's why rollups post the data, not just the results.
rollups-posted-blobs-prompt: Today, nodes delete blob data after about 18 days. Why doesn't that put a rollup's users at risk?
rollups-posted-blobs-opt-proof: Once a proof is posted, nobody needs the data again
rollups-posted-blobs-fb-proof: Proofs check results, but people still need the data to rebuild balances and make withdrawals. Think about who else could keep it.
rollups-posted-blobs-opt-window: About 18 days is plenty of time for anyone who wants the data to download a copy
rollups-posted-blobs-fb-window: Right. Ethereum's job is to make sure the data was published for everyone to see. After that, the rollup, its users and anyone else can keep copies.
rollups-posted-blobs-opt-forever: Ethereum quietly keeps a backup of every blob forever
rollups-posted-blobs-fb-forever: Nodes really do delete blobs, which is what makes them cheaper. Think about who could keep copies instead.
rollups-posted-terms-prompt: Match each term to what it means.
rollups-posted-terms-match-rollup: Layer 2 posting its data to Ethereum
rollups-posted-terms-match-blob: Cheap data space kept about 18 days
rollups-posted-terms-match-state: Every account's balance at one moment
rollups-posted-terms-explain: A rollup posts batches of transaction data, usually in blobs, and anyone can replay that data to rebuild its state.
rollups-posted-takeaway-p1: A rollup posts its transaction data to Ethereum, so anyone can rebuild its state from Ethereum alone, even if the rollup's operator disappears.
rollups-optimistic-summary: How optimistic rollups catch bad batches, and why their withdrawals wait about a week.
rollups-optimistic-intro-p1: An optimistic rollup posts each batch with its claimed new state but no proof that it's right. Ethereum treats the batch as valid unless someone shows it isn't.
rollups-optimistic-intro-p2: Anyone can replay the posted data to check. If a result is wrong, they have a challenge period, usually about seven days, to submit a fraud proof. A successful one undoes the bad result and costs whoever posted it the deposit they put up.
rollups-optimistic-challenge-prompt: You're watching an optimistic rollup. One of these batches claims a result its transaction doesn't add up to. Challenge it while the period is still open.
rollups-optimistic-challenge-explain: Replaying each transaction against the balances before it exposes the batch that created ETH from nothing.
rollups-optimistic-honest-prompt: How many honest watchers does an optimistic rollup need to catch a bad batch?
rollups-optimistic-honest-opt-one: Just one, who replays the data and challenges in time
rollups-optimistic-honest-fb-one: Right. Ethereum checks a fraud proof itself, so there's no vote. One honest watcher with the data is enough, as long as they act within the challenge period.
rollups-optimistic-honest-opt-majority: More than half of the rollup's users
rollups-optimistic-honest-fb-majority: Nobody votes on a challenge: Ethereum checks the fraud proof itself. Think about how many people it takes to submit one.
rollups-optimistic-honest-opt-validators: Every one of Ethereum's validators, who stake ETH to run the network
rollups-optimistic-honest-fb-validators: Validators include a challenge like any other transaction. They don't watch the rollup themselves. Think about who has to spot the problem.
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-prompt: You withdraw ETH from an optimistic rollup through the rollup's own bridge. Why does it take about a week to arrive on Ethereum?
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-opt-queue: Ethereum only processes withdrawals once a week
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-fb-queue: Ethereum adds blocks all the time and has no weekly schedule. Think about what has to run out first.
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-opt-window: The batch with your withdrawal has to get through its challenge period first
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-fb-window: Right. Until the challenge period ends, that batch could still be undone, so the bridge waits before releasing your ETH on Ethereum.
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-opt-fee: Waiting a week keeps the fee low
rollups-optimistic-withdraw-fb-fee: The wait isn't about the fee. Think about what could still happen to the batch.
rollups-optimistic-takeaway-p1: An optimistic rollup's batches count as valid unless someone proves fraud within the challenge period, about a week, which is why withdrawals through its own bridge take that long.
rollups-zk-summary: How zero-knowledge rollups prove every batch to Ethereum.
rollups-zk-intro-p1: A zero-knowledge rollup, or ZK rollup, sends each batch with a validity proof: a short piece of cryptography showing that the new state really follows from the batch's transactions.
rollups-zk-intro-p2: A contract on Ethereum checks the proof, which costs far less than replaying every transaction. A batch whose proof fails is simply rejected, so there's nothing to challenge and no challenge period to wait out. Despite the name, the proof is about correctness, not privacy: the data to rebuild the state is still posted.
rollups-zk-verify-prompt: A batch reaches the rollup's contract on Ethereum with its validity proof. Verify it, then change a balance in the batch and verify again.
rollups-zk-verify-explain: The proof only fits the honest result. Changing a balance made it fail, so the contract rejected the batch and the false result never counted.
rollups-zk-journey-prompt: Put a ZK rollup batch's journey in order.
rollups-zk-journey-item-run: The rollup runs the batch's transactions
rollups-zk-journey-item-prove: It creates a validity proof for the result
rollups-zk-journey-item-post: It posts the batch data and proof to Ethereum
rollups-zk-journey-item-check: A contract on Ethereum checks the proof
rollups-zk-journey-item-accept: The new state is accepted on Ethereum
rollups-zk-journey-explain: The proof is made after running the transactions and checked on Ethereum before the new state is accepted, with no wait for challenges in between.
rollups-zk-exit-prompt: You withdraw ETH from a ZK rollup through its own bridge. When can you claim it on Ethereum?
rollups-zk-exit-opt-week: After the same seven-day challenge period as an optimistic rollup
rollups-zk-exit-fb-week: A ZK rollup doesn't wait for challenges, because nothing is accepted without a proof. Think about what the bridge waits for instead.
rollups-zk-exit-opt-operator: When the rollup's operator approves it
rollups-zk-exit-fb-operator: The bridge doesn't need the operator's approval: its contract follows what Ethereum has verified. Think about what that is.
rollups-zk-exit-opt-verified: Once a batch with your withdrawal has its proof verified on Ethereum
rollups-zk-exit-fb-verified: Right. In practice that can still take hours, because proofs take time to make and some rollups add safety delays, but there's no week-long challenge period.
rollups-zk-takeaway-p1: A ZK rollup proves every batch with a validity proof that Ethereum checks, so a bad batch is simply rejected and withdrawals don't wait out a challenge period.
rollups-exits-summary: A rollup's own bridge or a fast bridge, and what each asks you to trust.
rollups-exits-intro-p1: A rollup's own bridge, often called its canonical bridge, is part of the rollup's contracts on Ethereum. It relies only on Ethereum and the rollup itself, but leaving an optimistic rollup that way takes about a week.
rollups-exits-intro-p2: A fast bridge skips the wait. A liquidity provider pays you on Ethereum within minutes, for a fee, then collects your withdrawal from the rollup when the challenge period ends. In return, you're also trusting the fast bridge's contracts and the people running it.
rollups-exits-race-prompt: You have ETH on an optimistic rollup and need it on Ethereum. Try both ways out and slide through time to see when your ETH arrives.
rollups-exits-race-explain: The rollup's own bridge paid out in full once the challenge period ended. The fast bridge paid within minutes, minus its fee: the provider waited out the week instead of you, and you trusted one more party.
rollups-exits-trust-prompt: Compared with the rollup's own bridge, what do you also have to trust when you use a fast bridge?
rollups-exits-trust-opt-validators: Ethereum's validators, which the rollup's own bridge doesn't need
rollups-exits-trust-fb-validators: Both ways rely on Ethereum, so that isn't the difference. Think about who pays you early.
rollups-exits-trust-opt-provider: The fast bridge's contracts and the provider who pays you
rollups-exits-trust-fb-provider: Right. A bug in those contracts or a provider that misbehaves puts your ETH at a risk the rollup's own bridge doesn't add.
rollups-exits-trust-opt-nothing: Nothing extra: it's the same, just faster
rollups-exits-trust-fb-nothing: The speed comes from somewhere: someone pays you before the challenge period ends. Think about who that is.
rollups-exits-month-prompt: You're moving 10 ETH off an optimistic rollup and won't need it for a month. Which way out makes the most sense?
rollups-exits-month-opt-fast: A fast bridge, because faster is always safer
rollups-exits-month-fb-fast: Faster isn't safer: it adds a fee and another party to trust. Think about whether you need the speed.
rollups-exits-month-opt-own: The rollup's own bridge: the week doesn't matter, and there's no extra fee or party
rollups-exits-month-fb-own: Right. When you can wait, the rollup's own bridge avoids the fee and the extra trust.
rollups-exits-month-opt-split: Many small withdrawals, so each one arrives sooner
rollups-exits-month-fb-split: Every withdrawal waits the same challenge period whatever its size, and you'd pay gas for each one.
rollups-exits-takeaway-p1: A rollup's own bridge relies only on Ethereum and the rollup but can take a week. A fast bridge saves the wait for a fee, by adding a provider and contracts you also have to trust.
rollups-risk-summary: Why a bridge exploit can leave bridged ETH with nothing behind it.
rollups-risk-intro-p1: When you bridge ETH, the ETH itself stays locked in the bridge's contract on Ethereum. What you get on the other network is a claim on it: it's worth ETH only because the bridge will hand that ETH back.
rollups-risk-intro-p2: So bridged ETH is only as safe as the pile behind it. If attackers find a bug, or the people who control the bridge turn on its users, the pile can be drained, and every claim loses its backing at once. Many of the biggest crypto hacks have hit bridges.
rollups-risk-backing-prompt: This bridge's locked ETH backs the bridged ETH out on another network. Redeem some of yours, let attackers drain the bridge, then try to redeem again.
rollups-risk-backing-explain: Before the exploit, every bridged ETH could be swapped back. After it, the bridged ETH still existed, but there was nothing left to hand back.
rollups-risk-signers-prompt: A bridge lets a group of 5 signers approve every transfer, and any 3 of their signatures are enough. What's the biggest risk?
rollups-risk-signers-fb-slow: Signers can approve quickly, so speed isn't the worry. Think about what 3 signatures can do.
rollups-risk-signers-opt-keys: Anyone who controls 3 of those keys can approve a fake transfer and drain the locked ETH
rollups-risk-signers-fb-keys: Right. Whether attackers steal the keys or 3 signers work together, the bridge follows their signatures, not Ethereum's or the rollup's rules.
rollups-risk-signers-opt-fees: Fees are higher than on other bridges
rollups-risk-signers-fb-fees: Fees vary for many reasons. The bigger question is who can move the locked ETH. Think about what 3 signatures can do.
rollups-risk-judge-prompt: You're choosing a bridge. Which of these are good signs?
rollups-risk-judge-opt-native: Transfers are checked by Ethereum and the rollup's own proofs, not a small group of signers
rollups-risk-judge-fb-native: Yes. It adds no new group you have to trust.
rollups-risk-judge-opt-record: It has run for years, is widely used and has never been drained
rollups-risk-judge-fb-record: Yes. A long, clean record isn't a guarantee, but it means many attackers have tried and failed.
rollups-risk-judge-opt-bonus: It offers a bonus to anyone who bridges today
rollups-risk-judge-fb-bonus: A bonus says nothing about how safe the locked ETH is, and rushing you is a classic scam trick.
rollups-risk-judge-opt-audited: Its contracts are public and have been audited
rollups-risk-judge-fb-audited: Yes. An audit lowers the risk of bugs, though it can't promise there are none.
rollups-risk-judge-explain: Look at who checks transfers, how the contracts were reviewed and how long the bridge has held up. Bonuses and urgency are red flags, not good signs.
rollups-risk-takeaway-p1: Bridged ETH is only a claim on the ETH locked in the bridge, so an exploit can leave it with nothing behind it. Prefer bridges checked by Ethereum and the rollup itself, with a long, clean record.
rollups-exam-data-prompt: What does a rollup post to Ethereum so that anyone can check or rebuild it?
rollups-exam-data-opt-balances: Only a readable list of everyone's final balances
rollups-exam-data-opt-nothing: Nothing: its data stays on its own servers
rollups-exam-data-explain: Rollups post their transaction data to Ethereum in batches. Earlier balances plus that data are enough to rebuild the rollup's state without the operator.
rollups-exam-blob-prompt: A rollup posts its batches in blobs, which nodes delete after about 18 days. Why is that acceptable?
rollups-exam-blob-opt-copies: The data stays up long enough for anyone who needs it to download a copy
rollups-exam-blob-opt-unused: Nobody ever needs a rollup's old data
rollups-exam-blob-opt-proof: Each blob turns into a proof when it's deleted
rollups-exam-blob-explain: Blobs only need to be available long enough for anyone to download and check them. After that, the rollup, its users and others can keep copies, which is why blobs can be cheaper.
rollups-exam-assume-prompt: An optimistic rollup posts a new batch. How does Ethereum treat it?
rollups-exam-assume-opt-replays: It replays every transaction before accepting it
rollups-exam-assume-opt-valid: As valid, unless someone proves fraud during the challenge period
rollups-exam-assume-opt-proof: It checks a validity proof first
rollups-exam-assume-explain: Optimistic rollups post no proof up front. A batch counts as valid unless a fraud proof shows otherwise within the challenge period.
rollups-exam-week-prompt: Your withdrawal from an optimistic rollup through its own bridge is taking about a week. Why?
rollups-exam-week-opt-busy: Ethereum is too busy to process it sooner
rollups-exam-week-opt-fee: A longer wait keeps the fee low
rollups-exam-week-opt-challenge: The batch with your withdrawal has to get through the challenge period
rollups-exam-week-explain: Until the challenge period of about seven days ends, a fraud proof could still undo the batch, so the bridge waits before releasing your ETH.
rollups-exam-validity-prompt: What does a ZK rollup send to Ethereum with each batch that an optimistic rollup doesn't?
rollups-exam-validity-opt-proof: A validity proof, checked by a contract on Ethereum
rollups-exam-validity-opt-same: Nothing: both send exactly the same
rollups-exam-validity-explain: A ZK rollup attaches a validity proof to each batch, and a contract on Ethereum checks it before the new state is accepted.
rollups-exam-bad-prompt: A ZK rollup's operator posts a batch with a false result, and its proof doesn't check out. What happens?
rollups-exam-bad-opt-week: It counts for about a week unless someone challenges it
rollups-exam-bad-opt-rejected: The contract on Ethereum rejects it, so it never counts
rollups-exam-bad-opt-counts: It counts, because the data was posted
rollups-exam-bad-explain: A ZK rollup's new state is accepted only once its proof is verified on Ethereum, so a batch with a failing proof is rejected outright.
rollups-exam-fast-prompt: How does a fast bridge get you ETH on Ethereum within minutes of leaving an optimistic rollup?
rollups-exam-fast-opt-provider: A provider pays you now, for a fee, and collects your withdrawal after the challenge period
rollups-exam-fast-opt-skip: It lets everyone skip the challenge period
rollups-exam-fast-opt-mint: It creates new ETH on Ethereum for you
rollups-exam-fast-explain: The challenge period still applies. A liquidity provider pays you early on Ethereum and takes over your pending withdrawal, keeping a fee.
rollups-exam-tradeoff-prompt: What do you give up by using a fast bridge instead of a rollup's own bridge?
rollups-exam-tradeoff-opt-none: Nothing: it's the same, only faster
rollups-exam-tradeoff-opt-trust: You pay a fee and also trust the bridge's contracts and its provider
rollups-exam-tradeoff-explain: A fast bridge trades a fee and extra trust for speed. The rollup's own bridge relies only on Ethereum and the rollup, but makes you wait.
rollups-exam-backing-prompt: Attackers drain the ETH locked in a bridge. What happens to the bridged ETH people hold on the other network?
rollups-exam-backing-opt-safe: Nothing: it's on another network, so it's safe
rollups-exam-backing-opt-unbacked: It loses its backing and may become worthless
rollups-exam-backing-explain: Bridged ETH is a claim on the ETH locked in the bridge. Once that's gone, the claims have nothing behind them.
rollups-exam-safer-prompt: Which bridge is generally the safer choice?
rollups-exam-safer-opt-signers: A new one where a small group of signers approves transfers
rollups-exam-safer-opt-message: One a stranger recommends in a direct message
rollups-exam-safer-opt-native: One whose transfers are checked by Ethereum and the rollup itself, with a long record
rollups-exam-safer-explain: Bridges checked by the chains they connect add no new group to trust, and a long, clean record means they've held up under attack. A small group of signers is a single point of failure.

everyday-description: Never touched crypto? Start here. Every lesson begins with something you already know, like a notebook, a mailbox or a vending machine.
everyday-notebook-summary: Why a notebook with thousands of copies is hard to cheat.
everyday-notebook-picture-p1: Imagine a notebook that thousands of people keep identical copies of. A new line goes into every copy, but if someone changes an old line in theirs, the other copies still show the real one.
everyday-notebook-try-prompt: Add a new line to the notebook. Then change an old line in your copy and see what the other copies do.
everyday-notebook-try-explain: The new line reached every copy. Your change stayed in your copy alone, so the others still show the real line and ignore yours.
everyday-notebook-reveal-p1: No single copy is in charge. Every copy checks each new line, and the version they agree on is the real one.
everyday-notebook-reveal-p2: Ethereum works like that notebook, shared by computers all over the world. Its notebook is called a blockchain.
everyday-notebook-change-prompt: Someone changes an old line in their copy of Ethereum's blockchain to give themselves extra money. What happens?
everyday-notebook-change-opt-counts: The change counts, because it's in their copy
everyday-notebook-change-fb-counts: Only their own copy says so. Think about what all the other copies show.
everyday-notebook-change-opt-ignored: Nothing: the other copies still show the real line
everyday-notebook-change-fb-ignored: Right. Every other copy still has the real line, so a secret change gets nowhere.
everyday-notebook-change-opt-copied: Every other copy updates to match
everyday-notebook-change-fb-copied: Copies don't simply take on each other's edits. Think about what the other copies still show.
everyday-notebook-takeaway-p1: A blockchain is like a notebook that computers all over the world keep identical copies of, so nobody can secretly change it.
everyday-cash-summary: Ethereum's own money, and sending it without a bank.
everyday-cash-picture-p1: Hand a friend cash, and it goes straight from you to them. Pay by bank transfer, and you ask your bank to move it for you.
everyday-cash-try-prompt: Sort each way of paying: does the money go hand to hand, or does a bank move it for you?
everyday-cash-try-explain: Hand to hand, the money goes straight across and nobody's permission is needed. Through a bank, the bank moves it for you, when it's open and willing.
everyday-cash-reveal-p1: Ethereum has its own money, called ETH. Sending it works like handing over cash: no bank in the middle, just a new line on the blockchain.
everyday-cash-approve-prompt: You send ETH to a friend in another country at midnight. Does a bank have to approve it before it goes through?
everyday-cash-approve-opt-bank: Yes, your bank, once it opens
everyday-cash-approve-fb-bank: ETH doesn't move through your bank. Think about how cash changes hands.
everyday-cash-approve-opt-both: Yes, a bank in each country
everyday-cash-approve-fb-both: Borders don't matter here: there's one blockchain for the whole world. Think about how cash changes hands.
everyday-cash-approve-opt-none: No: no bank is involved at all
everyday-cash-approve-fb-none: Right. Like cash, ETH needs no bank's permission, at any hour. The computers keeping the blockchain check it and add it as a new line.
everyday-cash-takeaway-p1: ETH is Ethereum's own money. Like cash, it goes straight from you to someone else, with no bank in the middle.
everyday-mailbox-summary: Where people send you ETH, and the key that lets you spend it.
everyday-mailbox-picture-p1: Picture a mailbox with a glass door. Anyone can drop money through the slot and see what's inside, but only your key opens the door to take it out.
everyday-mailbox-try-prompt: This is your mailbox. Drag or tap each payment into the slot, then try every key in the lock.
everyday-mailbox-try-explain: Anyone could drop money in, and anyone can see it through the glass, but only your own key opened the door.
everyday-mailbox-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, your mailbox is an address: anyone can send ETH to it and see what it holds. Its key is your private key, the only way to spend that ETH.
everyday-mailbox-reveal-p2: A wallet is an app that keeps your key. Your ETH stays at your address on the blockchain.
everyday-mailbox-phone-prompt: Losing your key doesn't empty your mailbox. So if the phone with your wallet app breaks, where is your ETH?
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-gone: The phone only held your key. Think about where your mailbox is.
everyday-mailbox-phone-opt-maker: With the company that made the wallet app
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-maker: This app only kept your key. The company that made it never had your ETH.
everyday-mailbox-phone-opt-address: Still at your address on the blockchain
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-address: Right. Your ETH never left your address. But to reach it again you need a backup of your key, so always make one. A later lesson shows how.
everyday-mailbox-takeaway-p1: Your address is a glass mailbox anyone can send ETH to and see into. Your private key is the only way to spend it, and your wallet keeps that key, not your ETH.
everyday-stamp-summary: Why every payment carries a small fee, and why its price changes.
everyday-stamp-picture-p1: Every letter needs a stamp to pay for its delivery, and heavier mail needs more stamps. Without them, the post office would be buried in junk mail.
everyday-stamp-try-prompt: Stamp each parcel so it gets delivered. Some carry a check for a small amount, and some a check for a huge one.
everyday-stamp-try-explain: Stamps pay for the work of carrying a parcel. A crate takes more work than a letter, but a huge check weighs no more than a small one.
everyday-stamp-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, the stamp is a small fee paid in ETH, often called gas. Bigger jobs need more gas, and the fee stops anyone from flooding Ethereum with junk.
everyday-stamp-reveal-p2: Unlike a real stamp, the price of gas moves. It goes up when lots of people are using Ethereum at once, and back down when it's quieter.
everyday-stamp-amount-prompt: A check for a tiny amount and a check for a huge amount need the same envelope and the same stamp. So which pays the bigger fee: sending a little ETH, or a lot?
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-more: A bigger check doesn't need more stamps. Think about whether the work changes with the amount.
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-same: Right. The fee pays for the work of adding your payment, not for how much it moves. Sending a lot takes the same work as sending a little.
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-less: Small payments don't get cheaper stamps. Think about whether the work changes with the amount.
everyday-stamp-busy-prompt: Lots of people are using Ethereum right now, so fees are high. Your payment isn't urgent. What's a smart way to save?
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-skip: Every payment needs a fee, like every letter needs a stamp. Think about when fees cost less.
everyday-stamp-busy-opt-wait: Send it later, when Ethereum is quieter
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-wait: Right. Fees drop when fewer people are using Ethereum, so waiting can save you money.
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-small: Too small a fee leaves your payment waiting until fees drop that low, and if they never do, it never goes through. Think about a way to save that doesn't leave it stuck.
everyday-stamp-takeaway-p1: Every payment on Ethereum pays a small fee in ETH, like a stamp. The fee follows the work, not the amount you send, and it rises when Ethereum is busy.
everyday-machine-summary: Programs on Ethereum that follow their rules exactly.
everyday-machine-picture-p1: A vending machine sells snacks without a shopkeeper. It follows the same rules for everyone: pay the right amount and the snack drops, or nothing happens.
everyday-machine-try-prompt: Buy a snack. Then try paying the wrong amount, or picking one that's sold out.
everyday-machine-try-explain: The machine followed its rules every time. Nobody behind a counter had to say yes or no.
everyday-machine-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, a program that works like this is called a smart contract: it follows its rules exactly, with no person in the middle. Apps on Ethereum are built from smart contracts.
everyday-machine-tickets-prompt: A smart contract sells concert tickets for ETH. You try to pay a little less than the price. What happens?
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-anyway: It sells you the ticket anyway, since you were close
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-anyway: Close isn't enough. The contract follows its rules exactly, the same way for everyone.
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-staff: Someone at the box office decides whether to let it slide
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-staff: There's no box office. The rules decide, with no person in the middle.
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-refused: It turns you down, and your ETH stays with you
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-refused: Right. Like the vending machine, it follows its rules for everyone. The payment never goes through, so your ETH stays at your address. Only the small fee is spent.
everyday-machine-takeaway-p1: A smart contract is like a vending machine on Ethereum: a program that follows its rules exactly, with no shopkeeper in the middle.
everyday-undo-summary: Why there are no take-backs, and how to keep your key safe.
everyday-undo-picture-p1: Once you hand someone cash, there's no undo button. And if you lose every copy of the key to an unbreakable safe, no help desk can make you a new one.
everyday-undo-try-prompt: Your safe has one key. You can copy it, but if every copy is lost, nobody can ever make another. How do you avoid getting locked out for good?
everyday-undo-try-opt-spare: Make a copy of the key and hide it where only you know
everyday-undo-try-fb-spare: Right. With a copy kept somewhere safe and secret, losing one key isn't the end.
everyday-undo-try-opt-stranger: Give a copy to a friendly stranger who offers to hold it
everyday-undo-try-fb-stranger: Whoever holds a copy can open your safe whenever they like. Think about who should know where it is.
everyday-undo-try-opt-maker: Call the safe maker if it happens
everyday-undo-try-fb-maker: Once every copy is gone, nobody can make another, not even the safe's maker. Make your copy before you need it.
everyday-undo-hide-prompt: You made a spare copy of your safe's key. Sort these hiding places: which keep it safe, and which are risky?
everyday-undo-hide-explain: A good hiding place is one only you know about or can open. Anywhere others might look, or anything others can see, lets someone copy your key.
everyday-undo-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, a payment is like cash: once sent, nobody can undo it. Your hidden copy of the key is a recovery phrase, a list of words that brings back your private key, so write it on paper and never share it.
everyday-undo-support-prompt: You'd never hand a stranger a copy of your safe's key. A message says: "Hi, I'm from wallet support. Send me your recovery phrase and I'll fix your account." What is it?
everyday-undo-support-opt-send: Real help, so you send the phrase
everyday-undo-support-fb-send: Real support never asks for your recovery phrase. Think about what anyone holding it could do.
everyday-undo-support-opt-half: Fine, as long as you send only half the words
everyday-undo-support-fb-half: Even part of the phrase helps a thief. Think about who really needs it.
everyday-undo-support-opt-scam: A scam: anyone with the phrase can take your ETH
everyday-undo-support-fb-scam: Right. Nobody genuine ever needs your recovery phrase. Anyone who asks for it is trying to take your ETH.
everyday-undo-takeaway-p1: Payments on Ethereum can't be undone, and no help desk can reset your key. Keep your recovery phrase safe, and never share it with anyone.
everyday-story-summary: One payment from start to finish, step by step.
everyday-story-picture-p1: Alex owes Sam for lunch and decides to pay Sam back in ETH. Follow the payment from start to finish.
everyday-story-try-item-address: Sam shares an address: the mailbox slot
everyday-story-try-item-fee: Alex enters it and sees the fee: the stamp
everyday-story-try-item-key: Alex approves with Alex's private key
everyday-story-try-item-notebook: A new line goes on the blockchain: the global notebook
everyday-story-try-item-arrives: Sam sees the ETH at Sam's address
everyday-story-try-explain: Every step had an everyday twin: a mailbox slot to send to, a stamp to pay for delivery, a key only Alex has, and a notebook the whole world shares.
everyday-story-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, that whole trip is called a transaction. A transaction is any change added to the notebook. Once it's on the blockchain, nobody can undo it, and anyone can see it.
everyday-story-twins-prompt: Match each Ethereum word to its everyday twin.
everyday-story-twins-match-blockchain: A notebook everyone keeps a copy of
everyday-story-twins-match-address: A mailbox slot anyone can use
everyday-story-twins-match-fee: A stamp that pays for delivery
everyday-story-twins-explain: Each everyday picture stands for one part of Ethereum, and every payment uses all of them.
everyday-story-takeaway-p1: A transaction brings it together: an address to send to, a fee, your private key to approve it, and the blockchain to record it for good.
everyday-exam-notebook-prompt: In Ethereum, what plays the part of the notebook that everyone keeps an identical copy of?
everyday-exam-notebook-explain: The blockchain is Ethereum's shared notebook. Computers all over the world keep identical copies of it, so an old line can't be quietly changed.
everyday-exam-change-prompt: Someone secretly edits an old line in their own copy of the blockchain. What happens?
everyday-exam-change-opt-counts: Their edit becomes the new record
everyday-exam-change-opt-spreads: Every other copy updates to match
everyday-exam-change-opt-ignored: The other copies still show the real line, so the edit is ignored
everyday-exam-change-explain: Every other copy still holds the real line, so an edit in one copy gets nowhere.
everyday-exam-cash-prompt: Sending ETH is most like which everyday way of paying?
everyday-exam-cash-opt-cash: Handing over cash, with no bank in between
everyday-exam-cash-opt-card: Paying by card, through your bank
everyday-exam-cash-opt-check: Writing a check that a bank has to clear
everyday-exam-cash-explain: Like cash, ETH goes straight from you to the other person, with no bank in the middle.
everyday-exam-slot-prompt: A mailbox slot lets anyone drop money in. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-slot-explain: Your address is like the slot: anyone can send ETH to it. Moving that ETH takes your private key.
everyday-exam-wallet-prompt: You have a wallet app on your phone. What does it keep for you?
everyday-exam-wallet-explain: Your wallet keeps your private key. Your ETH stays at your address on the blockchain.
everyday-exam-stamp-prompt: A stamp pays for delivering a letter, and heavier mail needs more of them. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-stamp-explain: Every payment on Ethereum carries a small fee in ETH. Bigger jobs cost more, and the price goes up when Ethereum is busy.
everyday-exam-machine-prompt: A vending machine follows its rules with no shopkeeper. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-machine-explain: A smart contract is a program on Ethereum that follows its rules exactly, with no person in the middle.
everyday-exam-undo-prompt: You sent ETH to the wrong address by mistake. Who can undo it?
everyday-exam-undo-opt-nobody: Nobody: once it's on the blockchain, it can't be undone
everyday-exam-undo-explain: A payment can't be undone once it's on the blockchain, so check the address before you send.
everyday-exam-spare-prompt: A hidden copy of your key gets you back into your safe. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-spare-explain: Your recovery phrase is a list of words that brings back your private key. Write it on paper and never share it.
everyday-exam-support-prompt: Someone online says they're from wallet support and asks for your recovery phrase to fix a problem. What is it?
everyday-exam-support-opt-send: Real help, so you share it
everyday-exam-support-opt-scam: A scam to take your ETH
everyday-exam-support-opt-half: Safe, as long as you share only half
everyday-exam-support-explain: Real support never asks for your recovery phrase. Anyone who has it can take your ETH.
wallets-description: Find out what a wallet really holds, why your recovery phrase matters, how to keep both safe, and how to get and use your first ETH.
wallets-keys-title: Your wallet doesn't hold your ETH
wallets-keys-summary: Keys, addresses and where your money actually lives.
wallets-keys-intro-p1: Most people picture a wallet as a pouch that holds money. An Ethereum wallet works differently: your ETH, Ethereum's own money, never leaves the blockchain, a shared record of who owns what that thousands of computers keep in sync.
wallets-keys-intro-p2: Think of a glass mailbox. Your address is the mailbox: anyone can send ETH to it and see what's inside. Your private key is the only key that opens it to spend, and that key is what your wallet holds. Unlike a real mailbox and key, these two are tied together by math.
wallets-keys-made-prompt: Your private key and your address come as a pair. Which one is made from the other?
wallets-keys-made-opt-address: The address is made from the private key
wallets-keys-made-fb-address: Right. Your wallet picks a secret key first, then works out its address from it. Next, see what that means for anyone trying to go the other way.
wallets-keys-made-opt-key: The private key is made from the address
wallets-keys-made-fb-key: If keys came from addresses, anyone could take a public address and make its key. Test which way it goes in the next step.
wallets-keys-made-opt-separate: Neither: they're picked separately, and the wallet links them
wallets-keys-made-fb-separate: They aren't picked separately: one is worked out from the other. Test which way it goes in the next step.
wallets-keys-generate-prompt: Generate a private key and its address using the same math every Ethereum wallet uses. Then change a single character of the private key and watch what happens to the address.
wallets-keys-generate-explain: Your address is calculated from your private key, but the math only runs one way. Anyone can see your address, and nobody can work backwards to your key.
wallets-keys-share-prompt: A friend wants to send you some ETH. What should you give them?
wallets-keys-share-fb-key: Never share this. Anyone with your private key controls everything at your address.
wallets-keys-share-fb-address: Right. Your address is public by design, so anyone can send to it. Just know that anyone who has it can also see its balance and history.
wallets-keys-share-opt-both: Both, so the transfer goes through faster
wallets-keys-share-fb-both: A transfer only ever needs the recipient's address. Sharing your key would hand over control of your funds.
wallets-keys-takeaway-p1: Your address is made from your private key, and nobody can work back from the address to the key. Share your address like a glass mailbox anyone can see into, and keep your key to yourself.
wallets-recovery-summary: The words that can bring your wallet back, or give it away.
wallets-recovery-intro-p1: Private keys are long strings of characters that are easy to copy wrong. So most wallets show you a recovery phrase (also called a seed phrase) instead: a list of ordinary words, in order.
wallets-recovery-intro-p2: Those words can recreate every key in your wallet, on any device, in any compatible wallet app.
wallets-recovery-lost-prompt: Your phone falls in a lake, but you wrote your recovery phrase on paper. You type it into a wallet app on a new phone. Which address will the new wallet show?
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-same: Right. The same words make the same keys, and the same keys make the same address. Try it in the next step.
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-new: A new address would mean new keys. Think about what the words bring back, then try it in the next step.
wallets-recovery-lost-opt-empty: The same address, but with no ETH in it
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-empty: Your ETH was never on the phone. Think about where it's recorded, then try it in the next step.
wallets-recovery-restore-prompt: Set up a wallet, then lose its phone in the lake. Copy your paper phrase into a new wallet, word by word, and restore it. Then change one word.
wallets-recovery-restore-explain: The same words, in the same order, always bring back the same keys and the same address. Change one word and you get a different wallet with nothing in it, so copy your phrase carefully.
wallets-recovery-storage-prompt: Sort these backups of a recovery phrase: which stay offline, and which could end up online?
wallets-recovery-storage-explain: Offline backups can't be stolen over the internet. Photos, emails and chats can copy themselves to online accounts, where anyone who breaks in could find the phrase.
wallets-recovery-scam-prompt: A website says your wallet is out of date and must be synced. To sync it, you have to type in your recovery phrase. What do you do?
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-type: Type it in, since keeping a wallet up to date matters
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-type: Wallets never need your phrase to stay up to date. Whoever gets it can take everything in your wallet.
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-half: Type in only the first half of the words
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-half: Even part of a phrase makes the rest far easier to guess. Think about where a phrase ever needs to go.
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-close: Close the site. The phrase only goes into a wallet app, to restore your own wallet
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-close: Right. A recovery phrase only goes into a wallet app you trust, when you choose to restore your own wallet. Any website asking for it is a scam, however official it looks.
wallets-recovery-takeaway-p1: Your recovery phrase brings back your keys, and your address, on any device. Keep it offline and private, and only ever type it into a wallet app to restore your own wallet.
sending-description: Follow a payment from the moment you press send: what its fee pays for, why it waits in line, what happens when it fails, and how to check it arrived.
sending-lifecycle-title: What happens when you hit send
sending-lifecycle-summary: From a signature in your wallet to a permanent record on the blockchain.
sending-lifecycle-intro-p1: Sending ETH isn't like sending an email. Your wallet builds a message that says who's sending, who's receiving and how much, then signs it with your private key.
sending-lifecycle-intro-p2: That signature proves the transaction came from you, without revealing your key. Your wallet then broadcasts it: sends it out to the computers that run the network.
sending-lifecycle-order-prompt: Put the life of a transaction in order.
sending-lifecycle-order-item-create: You enter an address and an amount
sending-lifecycle-order-item-sign: Your wallet signs the transaction with your private key
sending-lifecycle-order-item-broadcast: The signed transaction is broadcast to the network
sending-lifecycle-order-item-include: A validator, one of the computers that run the network, adds it to a new block
sending-lifecycle-order-item-confirm: The block joins the chain and balances update
sending-lifecycle-order-explain: Each step depends on the one before it: no signature, no broadcast. No block, no balance change.
sending-lifecycle-done-prompt: Your friend asks whether your payment has arrived yet. At which point is it actually done?
sending-lifecycle-done-fb-signed: Signing only proves the payment came from you. At that point it hasn't even reached the network.
sending-lifecycle-done-opt-sent: When your wallet says it was sent
sending-lifecycle-done-fb-sent: Sent means it was shared with the network. It's still waiting, and your friend's balance hasn't changed yet.
sending-lifecycle-done-opt-block: When a validator adds it to a block
sending-lifecycle-done-fb-block: Right. Until then it's pending: shared, but waiting. Once it's in a block, the balances update and your friend has the ETH.
sending-lifecycle-takeaway-p1: A transaction is a signed instruction. Your wallet signs it and shares it with the network, and it's only done once a validator adds it to a block.
sending-fees-summary: What your fee pays for, and what happens when you offer too little.
sending-fees-intro-p1: Every payment carries a fee, paid in ETH and often called gas. It pays for the work of handling your payment, so a bigger job, like a trade in an app, costs more than a simple payment.
sending-fees-intro-p2: The price of that work rises when lots of people are using Ethereum and falls when it's quiet. Your wallet suggests a fee that matches the price right now, but the fee you offer is up to you.
sending-fees-predict-prompt: Ethereum is busy, and you offer a fee lower than the price right now. What do you think happens to your payment?
sending-fees-predict-opt-fails: It fails, and you lose the fee
sending-fees-predict-fb-fails: A low offer doesn't make a payment fail. Test your idea in the next step.
sending-fees-predict-opt-waits: It waits until the price drops to your offer
sending-fees-predict-fb-waits: Good thinking. Test it in the next step, and see what happens when an offer is far too low.
sending-fees-predict-opt-less: It goes through, but your friend gets less ETH
sending-fees-predict-fb-less: The fee never comes out of what your friend receives. Test your idea in the next step.
sending-fees-meter-prompt: Try different jobs, busy and quiet times, and fees. Find a payment that goes in right away, one that waits, and one that's too low.
sending-fees-meter-explain: A payment goes in once your fee reaches the price right now. Offer less and it waits for the price to drop. Offer less than even quiet times cost, and it may never go through.
sending-fees-urgent-prompt: You need to pay a friend back right away, and Ethereum is busy. What fee should you offer?
sending-fees-urgent-opt-lowest: The lowest fee possible, since it goes through eventually
sending-fees-urgent-fb-lowest: A low offer waits for the price to drop, and on a busy day that might not be soon. Think about what gets a payment in now.
sending-fees-urgent-opt-going: At least the price right now, like your wallet suggests
sending-fees-urgent-fb-going: Right. Meeting the price right now lets your payment go in without waiting for it to drop.
sending-fees-urgent-opt-amount: A fee that matches how much ETH you're sending
sending-fees-urgent-fb-amount: The fee follows the work and the price right now, not the amount you send. Think about what gets a payment in now.
sending-fees-takeaway-p1: Your fee pays for the work of handling your payment. Offer at least the price right now and it goes in. Offer less and it waits for the price to drop, or may never go through.
sending-line-summary: Why payments wait for a block, and how a tip moves yours up.
sending-line-intro-p1: Payments don't go onto the blockchain one at a time. A validator, one of the computers that run the network, gathers them into a block, and each block only has room for so many. When more are waiting than will fit, the rest wait in line for a later block.
sending-line-intro-p2: You can add a tip to your fee: an extra that goes to the validator who adds your payment. Validators keep the tips, so they usually pick the biggest ones first. A bigger tip works like the express line at a theme park.
sending-line-build-prompt: You're the validator, and you keep every tip. The next block only has room for a few payments. Fill it with the ones you'd pick.
sending-line-build-explain: Validators keep the tips, so they fill each block with the biggest tips first. When a payment was sent doesn't matter, and payments with small tips wait for a later block.
sending-line-jump-prompt: The line for the next block is long, and you want your payment in it. What helps most?
sending-line-jump-fb-first: The line isn't first come, first served. Think about what the validator gets to keep.
sending-line-jump-fb-tip: Right. A bigger tip moves you up the line, because the validator keeps it.
sending-line-jump-fb-amount: The amount you send doesn't move you up. Think about what the validator gets to keep.
sending-line-recap-prompt: Complete the sentences about waiting in line.
sending-line-recap-text: When blocks are full, payments wait in {b1} for space in a later {b2}. A bigger {b3} moves yours up.
sending-line-recap-explain: Each block has limited space, so payments wait in line. Validators keep the tips, so a bigger tip gets yours picked sooner.
sending-line-takeaway-p1: Blocks have limited space, so payments wait in line. Validators keep the tips, so a bigger tip moves yours up, like an express line.
sending-failed-summary: Why a payment can fail, and what it still costs.
sending-failed-intro-p1: Sometimes a payment can't do what it asked. Say you pay for the last spot in an online chess tournament, but while your payment waits in line, someone else's takes the spot first.
sending-failed-intro-p2: Your payment still goes into a block, but the tournament's rules turn it down, so it fails.
sending-failed-predict-prompt: Your payment for that tournament spot failed. What did it cost you?
sending-failed-predict-opt-both: The ETH for the spot, and the fee
sending-failed-predict-fb-both: Think about whether you got the spot. Test your idea in the next step.
sending-failed-predict-fb-fee: Good thinking. Test it in the next step.
sending-failed-predict-fb-nothing: Something did happen: your payment went into a block. Test your idea in the next step.
sending-failed-sort-prompt: Your payment for the tournament spot failed. Sort each thing: did it change, or is it the same as before?
sending-failed-sort-explain: A failed payment changes nothing it asked for: you keep your ETH, and the tournament's list stays the same. But the fee is spent, because validators did the work of trying it, and the blockchain keeps a record that it failed.
sending-failed-retry-prompt: Your payment failed, and your ETH is still with you. A friend says to press send again right away. What should you do first?
sending-failed-retry-opt-again: Send it again right away, a few times to be safe
sending-failed-retry-fb-again: Each send is a new payment with its own fee. If the same thing stops them, each one fails and costs a fee.
sending-failed-retry-fb-why: Right. If the spot is gone, the same payment would fail again and cost another fee. Fix the reason first.
sending-failed-retry-opt-refund: Wait for the fee to come back
sending-failed-retry-fb-refund: The fee doesn't come back. Validators did the work of trying the payment, so it stays spent.
sending-failed-takeaway-p1: When a payment can't do what it asked, it fails: nothing it asked for changes, but the fee is still spent.

wallets-signing-summary: How your key approves things without ever leaving your wallet.
wallets-signing-intro-p1: Every time you approve something in your wallet, it creates a digital signature: a code that only your private key could have produced.
wallets-signing-intro-p2: Anyone can check a signature against your address, but nobody can use it to work out your key or sign something new.
wallets-signing-proves-prompt: When you sign a message, what does the signature prove?
wallets-signing-proves-fb-identity: A signature proves control of a key, not who you are in the real world.
wallets-signing-proves-opt-key: That whoever holds the key for your address approved this exact message
wallets-signing-proves-fb-key: Right. And it covers this exact message only. Let's see what happens if someone changes it.
wallets-signing-proves-opt-secret: That the message is encrypted and hidden
wallets-signing-proves-fb-secret: Signing doesn't hide anything. The message stays readable; the signature proves who approved it.
wallets-signing-sign-prompt: Sign a message with a demo key. Then change the message as if you were an attacker and see whether the signature still checks out.
wallets-signing-sign-explain: A signature is tied to the exact message. Change a single character and it no longer matches your address, so anyone checking it can tell.
wallets-signing-blind-prompt: A site you've never heard of asks you to sign a message full of unreadable code to "claim a free prize". What do you do?
wallets-signing-blind-opt-sign: Sign it. Signing doesn't send anything, so it's harmless
wallets-signing-blind-fb-sign: Some signatures give a site permission to move your assets. Signing something you can't read can hand them over.
wallets-signing-blind-opt-reject: Reject it. Never sign anything you can't read or didn't expect
wallets-signing-blind-fb-reject: Exactly. If you can't tell what you're approving, the safe answer is no.
wallets-signing-blind-opt-padlock: Sign it, since the site looks professional and has a padlock in the address bar
wallets-signing-blind-fb-padlock: Scam sites can look polished and use a padlock too. The padlock only means the connection is private, not that the site is honest.
wallets-signing-takeaway-p1: A signature is your key saying yes to one exact message. Only sign things you can read, understand and expect.
wallets-addresses-summary: One phrase, many accounts, and how to be sure you're sending to the right one.
wallets-addresses-intro-p1: Your recovery phrase can create more than one key. Most wallets let you add extra accounts from the same phrase, each with its own private key and its own address.
wallets-addresses-intro-p2: Any of those addresses is safe to share, in that nobody can spend from it. It isn't private, though: anyone who has it can look up its balance and every transfer, one reason people keep separate accounts for different uses. Sending is where care matters most: once ETH goes to the wrong address, nobody can undo the transfer for you.
wallets-addresses-spot-prompt: Sam sends you their address so you can pay them back. Which address below matches it exactly?
wallets-addresses-spot-explain: All four addresses start and end the same way, so the shortened view can't tell them apart. Only checking the whole address catches a look-alike.
wallets-addresses-poison-prompt: A tiny amount arrives in your wallet from an address that starts and ends just like your friend Ana's. Later, you want to pay Ana. What should you do?
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-history: Copy Ana's address from your recent activity, since that's quickest
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-history: That's what the sender is counting on. The look-alike now sits in your activity, easy to copy by mistake.
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-ends: Check that the first and last few characters match, then send
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-ends: Those are exactly the characters the look-alike copied. A glance at the ends will happily approve the fake.
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-source: Use the address Ana gave you, or a contact you saved earlier, and check it in full
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-source: Right. This trick is called address poisoning: a look-alike planted in your activity in the hope you'll copy it. Going back to a source you trust avoids it.
wallets-addresses-wrong-prompt: You send ETH, then notice the address was wrong. What can you do?
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-support: Ask Ethereum's support team to reverse it
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-support: Ethereum has no central authority that can reverse a transfer. Anyone who says they can is probably running a scam.
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-bounce: Wait. It bounces back if nobody uses that address
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-bounce: Transfers don't bounce. ETH sent to a valid address stays there, whether anyone uses it or not.
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-owner: Ask whoever owns that address to send it back, if you know who they are
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-owner: That's the only way. Only the holder of that address's private key can move the ETH, which is why checking before you send matters so much. Never type an address by hand: copy it from a source you trust.
wallets-addresses-verify-text: A look-alike address copies the {b1} of a real one, so check the {b2} address against one you trust before you send.
wallets-addresses-verify-explain: Look-alikes are made to match the few characters a wallet shows at each end. Only checking every character against an address you trust catches the difference in the middle.
wallets-addresses-takeaway-p1: Sharing your address lets people see its activity, but never spend from it. Sending is final: check the whole address against one you trust, not just the start and end.
wallets-custody-summary: Exchanges, phone apps and hardware wallets: who's really in control.
wallets-custody-intro-p1: So far, this course has assumed you hold your own keys. Many people start on an exchange instead: a company that lets you buy and sell ETH. There, the company holds the keys for you. That's a custodial account: an account with the company, where someone else holds your keys.
wallets-custody-intro-p2: It's convenient. You sign in with a password, and support can help if you forget it. But the company controls the funds: it can freeze your account, and exchanges have failed and lost their customers' money.
wallets-custody-control-prompt: Your exchange suddenly stops letting customers take their ETH out. Who can move the ETH in your account there?
wallets-custody-control-opt-password: You can, with your exchange password
wallets-custody-control-fb-password: Your password only signs you in to the company's website. It isn't a private key, so it can't move anything on its own.
wallets-custody-control-opt-exchange: Only the exchange, because it holds the keys
wallets-custody-control-fb-exchange: Right. Whoever holds the keys controls the funds, and here that's the company.
wallets-custody-control-opt-phrase: You can, using your recovery phrase
wallets-custody-control-fb-phrase: A custodial account doesn't give you a recovery phrase for those funds. The keys stay with the company.
wallets-custody-storage-p1: Holding your own keys comes with choices too. A wallet app on your phone or computer is a hot wallet: its keys live on a device that's connected to the internet. That's handy for everyday use, but a hacked device could expose them.
wallets-custody-storage-p2: A hardware wallet is a small device made to keep keys offline, which makes it a cold wallet. It signs on the device itself, so your private key never touches the internet, even while it's plugged into a computer.
wallets-custody-sort-prompt: Sort each situation by who holds the keys, and whether they're kept online or offline.
wallets-custody-sort-explain: Custodial means someone else holds the keys. When you hold them yourself, a hot wallet keeps them on an internet-connected device, and a hardware wallet keeps them offline, even while it's plugged in.
wallets-custody-savings-prompt: You're saving ETH for years and will rarely touch it. Which setup fits best?
wallets-custody-savings-opt-exchange: Leave it on the exchange where you bought it
wallets-custody-savings-fb-exchange: Easy, but the exchange stays in control the whole time. If it freezes your account or fails, your savings go with it.
wallets-custody-savings-opt-hardware: A hardware wallet, with its recovery phrase written down and stored offline
wallets-custody-savings-fb-hardware: Right. Offline keys are much harder to steal, and the recovery phrase brings everything back if the device breaks or gets lost.
wallets-custody-savings-opt-phone: A wallet app on your phone, since it's always with you
wallets-custody-savings-fb-phone: Great for everyday spending, but those keys live on an internet-connected device. For savings you rarely touch, offline keys are safer.
wallets-custody-takeaway-p1: Whoever holds the keys controls the ETH. Hold your own, and keep the keys to long-term savings offline.
wallets-first-eth-summary: The easiest way to get some ETH, and how to receive it safely.
wallets-first-eth-intro-p1: The easiest way to get your first ETH is from someone who already has some, like a friend or family member. You share your address, and they send ETH straight to it, with nobody's permission needed.
wallets-first-eth-intro-p2: Exchanges, the companies that sell ETH, are another way. But you have to sign up first, they may check your ID, most only accept adults, and they can limit or freeze your account.
wallets-first-eth-easiest-prompt: You'd like some ETH, and you don't want to sign up for anything. What's the simplest way?
wallets-first-eth-easiest-opt-friend: Ask a friend or relative who has ETH to send some to your address
wallets-first-eth-easiest-fb-friend: Right. Anyone with ETH can send some to your address. All you share is the address, never your key.
wallets-first-eth-easiest-opt-exchange: Sign up to an exchange and buy some
wallets-first-eth-easiest-fb-exchange: That works for many adults, but it means signing up, which is what you wanted to skip.
wallets-first-eth-easiest-opt-app: Ask your wallet app to make some for you
wallets-first-eth-easiest-fb-app: A wallet app keeps your key. It can't make ETH. Think about who already has some.
wallets-first-eth-steps-prompt: Your aunt is sending you your first ETH. Put the steps in a safe order.
wallets-first-eth-steps-item-copy: Copy your address from your wallet app
wallets-first-eth-steps-item-share: Send the address to your aunt
wallets-first-eth-steps-item-test: She sends a tiny test amount
wallets-first-eth-steps-explain: A tiny test first proves the address works before the rest goes out. Payments can't be undone, so if something is wrong, only a little is lost.
wallets-first-eth-exchange-prompt: Exchanges also sell ETH. Which of these might an exchange ask for or do?
wallets-first-eth-exchange-opt-signup: Ask you to sign up for an account
wallets-first-eth-exchange-fb-signup: Yes. An exchange is a company, and buying from it starts with an account.
wallets-first-eth-exchange-opt-id: Check your ID, and turn you away if you're under its age limit
wallets-first-eth-exchange-fb-id: Yes. Most exchanges check who you are, and most only accept adults.
wallets-first-eth-exchange-fb-freeze: Yes. The exchange holds the keys, so it can stop you from moving the ETH in your account.
wallets-first-eth-exchange-fb-phrase: Never. An exchange holds its own keys and has no use for your phrase. Anyone asking for it is trying to take your ETH.
wallets-first-eth-exchange-explain: Buying from an exchange takes a company's permission: an account, maybe ID and age checks, and rules that can limit your account. No real exchange ever asks for your recovery phrase.
wallets-first-eth-keep-prompt: You've spent most of the ETH your aunt sent. Why keep a little in your wallet?
wallets-first-eth-keep-opt-fee: So you can pay the fee on your next payment
wallets-first-eth-keep-fb-fee: Right. Every payment pays a small fee in ETH, like a stamp. With no ETH left, you can't send anything.
wallets-first-eth-keep-fb-open: Addresses never close, even when they're empty. Think about what every payment needs.
wallets-first-eth-keep-opt-bank: So your bank doesn't charge you
wallets-first-eth-keep-fb-bank: No bank is involved with ETH at all. Think about what every payment on Ethereum needs.
wallets-first-eth-takeaway-p1: The easiest way to get your first ETH is from someone you know: share your address, take a tiny test payment first, and keep a little ETH for fees.
wallets-connect-summary: What your wallet's pop-ups ask, and which ones move your ETH.
wallets-connect-intro-p1: When you use an app on Ethereum, your wallet pops up to ask you to do one of three things. Connecting shares your address with the app, so it can see your address and what it holds. Nothing moves.
wallets-connect-intro-p2: Signing approves a message, often to prove an address is yours, and costs no fee. Sending moves ETH from your address, and pays a small fee in ETH.
wallets-connect-game-prompt: A game's website asks you to connect your wallet. Once you say yes, what does the game get?
wallets-connect-game-opt-address: Your address, so it can see what it holds
