wallets-connect-game-fb-address: Right. Connecting shares your address, and with it anything anyone can see about that address. Nothing moves.
wallets-connect-game-fb-key: Your key never leaves your wallet, not even when you connect. Think about what's already public.
wallets-connect-game-fb-spend: Connecting alone can't move anything. Spending would need a separate pop-up that you approve.
wallets-connect-sort-prompt: Sort these wallet pop-ups: is each one asking you to connect, sign or send?
wallets-connect-sort-explain: Connecting shares your address. Signing approves a message and costs no fee. Sending moves ETH and pays a fee.
wallets-connect-surprise-prompt: You only meant to log in to a website, but your wallet pops up asking you to send ETH. What do you do?
wallets-connect-surprise-opt-approve: Approve it. The website must need it to log you in
wallets-connect-surprise-fb-approve: Logging in never needs you to send ETH. A pop-up that doesn't match what you meant to do is a warning sign.
wallets-connect-surprise-opt-reject: Reject it. It doesn't match what you meant to do
wallets-connect-surprise-fb-reject: Right. Every pop-up should match what you meant to do. If it doesn't, say no and find out why.
wallets-connect-surprise-opt-smaller: Approve it, but lower the amount
wallets-connect-surprise-fb-smaller: ETH you send can't be taken back, however little. Think about whether this pop-up should be there at all.
wallets-connect-takeaway-p1: Connecting shares your address, signing approves a message, and sending moves ETH and pays a fee. Read every pop-up, and only approve one that matches what you meant to do.
wallets-exam-made-prompt: How are your private key and your address connected?
wallets-exam-made-opt-separate: They're picked separately, and your wallet links them
wallets-exam-made-opt-address: Your address is made from your private key, and the math can't run backward
wallets-exam-made-opt-key: Your private key is made from your address
wallets-exam-made-explain: Your wallet works out your address from your private key. The math only runs one way, so nobody can use your address to find your key.
wallets-exam-public-prompt: You post your address on a public page so people can pay you. What can a stranger do with it?
wallets-exam-public-opt-move: Move the ETH recorded at it
wallets-exam-public-opt-key: Work out your private key from it
wallets-exam-public-explain: An address is public by design, so anyone can send to it. Moving ETH takes the private key, and the math that turns a key into an address only runs one way. Anyone who has your address can also see its balance and history.
wallets-exam-restore-prompt: Your laptop stops working for good. You type your written-down recovery phrase into a wallet app on a new laptop. What does the new wallet show?
wallets-exam-restore-opt-same: Your old address, with your ETH still there
wallets-exam-restore-opt-empty: Your old address, but with the ETH gone
wallets-exam-restore-explain: The same phrase brings back the same keys, and so the same address. Your ETH never left the blockchain, so it's still there.
wallets-exam-website-prompt: A pop-up on a website warns that your wallet is at risk and asks you to type in your recovery phrase to secure it. What should you do?
wallets-exam-website-opt-type: Type it in. The pop-up is there to protect your wallet
wallets-exam-website-opt-close: Close the page. Nobody legitimate ever needs your phrase
wallets-exam-website-opt-part: Type in only the first few words, to be safe
wallets-exam-website-explain: Whoever has your recovery phrase owns your wallet, so any request for it is an attempt to take your funds. Even part of the phrase makes the rest far easier to guess.
wallets-exam-signature-prompt: Which of these are true of a digital signature?
wallets-exam-signature-opt-identity: It proves your real name and identity
wallets-exam-signature-opt-key: Only your private key could have produced it
wallets-exam-signature-opt-reveal: Anyone who sees it can use it to work out your private key
wallets-exam-signature-opt-exact: It covers one exact message, and stops matching if the message changes
wallets-exam-signature-explain: A signature is made by your private key and tied to one exact message. It proves control of a key, not who you are, and nobody can use it to work out the key.
wallets-exam-unreadable-prompt: A site you don't know asks you to sign a request you can't make sense of, to unlock a "free bonus". It says signing is harmless because nothing is being sent. What do you do?
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-reject: Reject it. Don't sign anything you can't read or didn't expect
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-sign: Sign it. A signature can't give anyone access to your assets
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-padlock: Sign it, since the site looks professional and has a padlock in the address bar
wallets-exam-unreadable-explain: Some signatures give a site permission to move your assets, so signing something you can't read could hand them over. If you can't tell what you're approving, the safe answer is no.
wallets-exam-lookalike-prompt: You want to pay your landlord, Jo, in ETH. Your recent activity shows an address that starts and ends just like Jo's. Where should the address you pay come from?
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-recent: Your recent activity, since it's already in your wallet
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-trusted: The address Jo gave you, or a contact you saved earlier, checked in full
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-ends: Any copy you find, as long as its first and last few characters match Jo's
wallets-exam-lookalike-explain: Look-alike addresses copy the start and end of a real one, and address poisoning plants them in your activity. Going back to a source you trust and checking the whole address avoids paying a stranger.
wallets-exam-mistake-prompt: You sent ETH to an address with one wrong character. Who can move that ETH now?
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-holder: Only whoever holds the private key for that address
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-support: Ethereum's support team, if you ask quickly
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-bounce: Nobody needs to. It returns to you if the address is never used
wallets-exam-mistake-explain: Transfers are final: they don't bounce, and no central authority can reverse them. Only the holder of that address's private key can move the ETH, and for a mistyped address that is almost certainly nobody, so it's lost for good. Never type an address by hand: copy it from a source you trust.
wallets-exam-frozen-prompt: You keep ETH on an exchange, and it freezes every customer's account. What can you do with your ETH there?
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-password: Move it out by signing in with your password
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-phrase: Move it out with your recovery phrase
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-exchange: Nothing on your own. The exchange holds the keys
wallets-exam-frozen-explain: An exchange account is custodial: the company holds the keys, so it controls the funds. Your password only signs you in to its website, and you have no recovery phrase for that ETH.
wallets-exam-savings-prompt: You keep a little ETH for everyday payments and a larger amount you won't touch for years. Which setup fits best?
wallets-exam-savings-opt-phone: Everything in a wallet app on your phone, so it's all in one place
wallets-exam-savings-opt-split: A phone wallet app for everyday spending, and a hardware wallet for the savings
wallets-exam-savings-opt-exchange: Everything on an exchange, so support can help if you forget your password
wallets-exam-savings-explain: A hot wallet on your phone is handy for spending, but its keys sit on an internet-connected device. Savings you rarely touch are safer on a hardware wallet, which keeps your own keys offline.
wallets-exam-peer-prompt: You want some ETH without signing up for anything. What's the simplest way?
wallets-exam-peer-opt-app: Ask your wallet app to create some
wallets-exam-peer-opt-friend: Share your address with a friend or relative who has ETH, so they can send some
wallets-exam-peer-explain: Anyone who has ETH can send some straight to your address, with nobody's permission. Exchanges need you to sign up, and a wallet app can't create ETH.
wallets-exam-signup-prompt: Your older cousin wants to buy ETH from an exchange. What should they expect?
wallets-exam-signup-opt-account: To sign up first, and maybe show ID, before they can buy
wallets-exam-signup-opt-instant: To buy straight away, with no account
wallets-exam-signup-opt-phrase: To hand over their recovery phrase
wallets-exam-signup-explain: An exchange is a company, so it needs an account and may check ID and age before it sells ETH. No real exchange ever needs a recovery phrase.
wallets-exam-connect-prompt: You connect your wallet to a drawing app's website. What does the site get?
wallets-exam-connect-explain: Connecting only shares your address, so the site can see it, along with the balance and history anyone can look up. Moving ETH still needs your approval in your wallet.
wallets-exam-fee-prompt: Your wallet can ask you to connect, sign or send. Which of these costs a fee?
wallets-exam-fee-explain: Sending ETH adds a payment to the blockchain, so it pays a fee. Connecting just shares your address, and signing a message adds nothing to the blockchain, so neither costs a fee.
sending-explorer-summary: Look up any transaction yourself and see whether it really worked.
sending-explorer-intro-p1: Everything on Ethereum is public. A block explorer is a website that shows what's on the chain: every block, every address and every transaction, for anyone to look up.
sending-explorer-intro-p2: Each transaction has a transaction hash: its unique ID, made by hashing the transaction's data into a short fingerprint. Your wallet can show it once you send, and searching for it on an explorer brings up the record.
sending-explorer-proof-prompt: A seller won't ship until your payment arrives, and you've just sent it. What's the most trustworthy thing to give them?
sending-explorer-proof-opt-screenshot: A screenshot of your wallet saying it was sent
sending-explorer-proof-fb-screenshot: Screenshots are easy to fake, and "sent" only means broadcast. It doesn't show the transaction made it into a block, or that it worked.
sending-explorer-proof-fb-hash: Right. Anyone can look the hash up on a block explorer and check the result themselves, instead of trusting your screenshot.
sending-explorer-proof-opt-balance: A screenshot of your lower balance
sending-explorer-proof-fb-balance: A lower balance doesn't say where the ETH went, and even a failed transaction lowers it, because the fee is still paid.
sending-explorer-read-prompt: Your wallet says your trade was sent, but nothing came back from the trading app. Which field on this page proves the trade failed?
sending-explorer-read-explain: Status is the field to trust. Being in a block, showing a value and charging a fee all happen to failed transactions too.
sending-explorer-pending-prompt: You look up your transaction hash and the status says Pending. What does that mean?
sending-explorer-pending-fb-failed: Failure has its own status, and a failed transaction is already in a block. Pending comes earlier than that.
sending-explorer-pending-opt-waiting: It's been broadcast but isn't in a block yet
sending-explorer-pending-fb-waiting: Right. It's waiting in line for a validator to add it to a block. When Ethereum is busy, that can take a while.
sending-explorer-pending-opt-lost: The network lost it, so you should send it again
sending-explorer-pending-fb-lost: Pending isn't lost. Sending again makes a second transaction, and if both go through, you pay twice.
sending-explorer-public-prompt: Who can look up your transactions on a block explorer?
sending-explorer-public-opt-you: Only you, using your private key
sending-explorer-public-fb-you: Your private key is for signing, not reading. Looking up a transaction needs no key at all.
sending-explorer-public-opt-both: Only you and the people you've paid
sending-explorer-public-fb-both: There's no list of who's allowed to look. Ethereum's records aren't shared only with the people involved.
sending-explorer-public-fb-anyone: Right. The chain is public, so anyone who knows your address can see its whole history. That's worth remembering before you share it.
sending-explorer-takeaway-p1: To find out whether a transaction worked, look up its hash on a block explorer and read the status. Don't settle for a screenshot.
sending-exam-sign-prompt: What has to happen before your transaction can be broadcast to the network?
sending-exam-sign-opt-block: A validator puts it in a block
sending-exam-sign-opt-key: Your wallet attaches your private key so the network knows it's you
sending-exam-sign-opt-sign: Your wallet signs it with your private key
sending-exam-sign-explain: Your wallet signs the transaction first, which proves it came from you without revealing your key. Only then is it broadcast, and later a validator includes it in a block.
sending-exam-sent-prompt: Your wallet says your payment was sent a moment ago, but it isn't in a block yet. What's true?
sending-exam-sent-opt-arrived: Your friend already has the ETH
sending-exam-sent-opt-waiting: It's waiting, and your friend's balance hasn't changed yet
sending-exam-sent-opt-cancelled: It was turned down, because it isn't in a block
sending-exam-sent-explain: Sent means your wallet shared the payment with the network. It's only done once a validator adds it to a block, and that's when the balances update.
sending-exam-job-prompt: At the same moment, which carries the bigger fee: a simple payment to a friend, or a trade in an app?
sending-exam-job-explain: The fee pays for the work of handling a transaction. A trade is a bigger job than a simple payment, so at the same moment it costs more.
sending-exam-offer-prompt: Ethereum is busy, and you offer a fee below the price right now. What happens to your payment?
sending-exam-offer-opt-less: It goes through, but your friend receives less ETH
sending-exam-offer-opt-waits: It waits until the price drops to your offer, and may never go through if it doesn't
sending-exam-offer-opt-fails: It fails at once, and you lose the fee
sending-exam-offer-explain: A payment only goes in once its fee reaches the price right now. Until the price drops that far, it waits. The fee never comes out of what your friend receives.
sending-exam-space-prompt: Lots of payments are waiting, and only some make it into the next block. Why?
sending-exam-space-opt-bank: A bank has to approve the rest first
sending-exam-space-opt-space: Each block has limited space, so the rest wait for a later one
sending-exam-space-opt-small: Small payments always have to wait until last
sending-exam-space-explain: A block can only hold so much, so when more payments are waiting than will fit, some wait for a later block. No bank is involved, and the amount sent doesn't decide the order.
sending-exam-tip-prompt: Two payments are waiting, and the next block has room for just one of them. Which will the validator most likely pick?
sending-exam-tip-opt-first: The one that was sent first
sending-exam-tip-opt-tip: The one with the bigger tip
sending-exam-tip-explain: Validators keep the tips, so they pick the biggest tips first. When a payment was sent and how much it moves don't change its place in line.
sending-exam-outcome-prompt: You pay for the last spot in a cooking class, but someone else's payment gets it first, so yours fails. Which are true?
sending-exam-outcome-opt-kept: You still have the ETH you tried to pay for the spot
sending-exam-outcome-opt-item: You get the spot anyway, since you paid
sending-exam-outcome-opt-refund: The fee comes back, since the payment failed
sending-exam-outcome-explain: A failed payment changes nothing it asked for, so the ETH you tried to pay stays with you and you don't get the spot. Validators still did the work of trying it, so the fee stays spent.
sending-exam-retry-prompt: Your payment failed because what you were buying sold out. What's the smart next step?
sending-exam-retry-opt-spam: Send the same payment again and again until one works
sending-exam-retry-opt-nothing: Send it again right away, since failing costs nothing
sending-exam-retry-opt-why: Check why it failed before sending anything again
sending-exam-retry-explain: A failed payment still costs its fee, so sending the same one again would likely fail again and cost another fee. Find out why it failed first.
sending-exam-proof-prompt: You paid a friend back, and they want to check for themselves that the payment worked. What should you send them?
sending-exam-proof-opt-screenshot: A screenshot of your wallet showing it was sent
sending-exam-proof-opt-key: Your private key, so they can look inside your wallet
sending-exam-proof-explain: Anyone can look up a transaction hash on a block explorer and read the result straight from the chain. Screenshots are easy to fake, and looking up a transaction needs no key at all.
sending-exam-status-prompt: You look up a trade on a block explorer. Which field tells you whether it actually worked?
sending-exam-status-explain: Status is the field to trust. Failed transactions are in a block too, still show the value they tried to send and still charge a fee.
gas-description: Work out fees in gwei, watch the base fee rise and fall, pack a block, and rescue a failed or stuck transaction.
gas-units-summary: Gas units, the price of each one, and how they make a fee.
gas-units-intro-p1: Every step a transaction makes the network do has a fixed cost in gas, the unit that measures computing work. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas today, though upgrades can change these costs. Calling a smart contract makes the network do more, so it uses more gas.
gas-units-intro-p2: You pay for every unit at the gas price, quoted in gwei: one billionth of an ETH. So the fee is gas used × gas price. At 10 gwei, a plain transfer costs 21,000 × 10 = 210,000 gwei, or 0.00021 ETH. Your wallet also sets a gas limit: the most gas the transaction is allowed to use.
gas-units-calculator-prompt: A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. Set the gas price so the fee matches the goal.
gas-units-calculator-explain: Fee = gas used × gas price. The work fixes the gas used; the gas price is what you pay for each unit, in gwei.
gas-units-compare-prompt: Trading one token for another through a smart contract often uses more than 100,000 gas, while a plain transfer uses 21,000. At the same gas price, which costs more?
gas-units-compare-fb-transfer: The plain transfer uses the least gas of any transaction, so at the same price it's the cheapest.
gas-units-compare-fb-swap: Right. The trade does far more computing work, so it buys far more units of gas. At the same price, its fee is about five times bigger.
gas-units-compare-fb-same: The price per unit is the same, but the fee is gas used × gas price. Compare how many units each one buys.
gas-units-rank-prompt: Put these in order, from the one that usually uses the least gas to the one that usually uses the most.
gas-units-rank-item-token: Send a token to a friend
gas-units-rank-explain: A plain transfer is the cheapest, at 21,000 gas. Sending a token asks its smart contract to update a list of balances, often around 50,000. A trade runs several contracts, often 100,000 or more, and publishing a contract stores all its code, which can take millions.
gas-units-takeaway-p1: Fee = gas used × gas price. The work decides the gas used, so a plain ETH transfer is the cheapest thing you can send, and every contract call costs more.
gas-fees-summary: The two parts of the gas price, and why one of them is burned.
gas-fees-intro-p1: The gas price has two parts. The base fee is set by the network for each block, and every transaction in that block pays the same one. The priority fee, or tip, is extra you choose to add, and it goes to the validator who adds your transaction to a block.
gas-fees-intro-p2: The base fee isn't paid to anyone: it's burned, destroyed for good. It also moves after every block. Each block aims to be half full. A fuller block raises the next base fee, by up to 12.5%, and an emptier one lowers it, by up to 12.5%.
gas-fees-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: block after block is completely full. What happens to the base fee?
gas-fees-predict-opt-climb: It climbs with every full block
gas-fees-predict-fb-climb: Good thinking. Test it in the next step.
gas-fees-predict-opt-same: It stays the same, and only tips go up
gas-fees-predict-fb-same: Tips do rise when it's busy, but they aren't the only thing that moves. Test it in the next step.
gas-fees-predict-opt-top: It jumps to the highest price anyone offers
gas-fees-predict-fb-top: The base fee isn't an auction price. It follows a fixed rule based on how full blocks are. Test it in the next step.
gas-fees-meter-prompt: Add blocks of different fullness and watch what each one does to the next base fee.
gas-fees-meter-explain: A block more than half full raises the next base fee, and one less than half full lowers it, by up to 12.5% a block. A rush of full blocks makes the base fee climb fast, until enough people wait and blocks empty out again.
gas-fees-split-prompt: You send ETH using 21,000 gas, at a base fee of 10 gwei plus a 2 gwei tip, so the fee is 252,000 gwei. How much of it does the validator receive?
gas-fees-split-fb-all: The fee has two parts, and only one of them is paid to anyone. The other is destroyed.
gas-fees-split-fb-tip: Right. 21,000 × 2 = 42,000 gwei goes to the validator. The other 210,000 gwei, the base fee, is burned.
gas-fees-split-fb-base: That's the part nobody receives. Work out the part that's paid to the validator instead.
gas-fees-takeaway-p1: Gas price = base fee + tip. The base fee is burned and follows how full blocks are; the tip goes to the validator who adds your transaction.
gas-blocks-summary: Play block builder and decide which transactions make the cut.
gas-blocks-intro-p1: Transactions don't land on the blockchain one at a time. Validators, who stake ETH to run the network, take turns adding blocks, with a chance for a new block every 12 seconds today.
gas-blocks-intro-p2: Each block has room for a limited amount of gas, so when more transactions are waiting than will fit, someone has to choose. Today most blocks are put together by specialist builders, who compete to offer the validator the most profitable block. Either way, the validator, or a builder working for it, picks the transactions that pay the best tips.
gas-blocks-build-prompt: You're building the block. Fill it from the waiting pool to hit the tip goal without overfilling it.
gas-blocks-build-explain: Tips go to whoever fills the block, so the transactions paying the most per unit of gas are picked first. The base fee is burned no matter who includes it, so it doesn't sway the choice.
gas-blocks-per-gas-prompt: Two transactions are waiting. A pays 100,000 gwei in tips and uses 100,000 gas. B pays 63,000 gwei in tips and uses 21,000 gas. For the block space it takes, which pays the builder more?
gas-blocks-per-gas-opt-a: A, since its total tip is bigger
gas-blocks-per-gas-fb-a: A bigger total isn't the whole story: A also takes almost five times the space. Divide each tip by the gas it uses.
gas-blocks-per-gas-opt-b: B, at 3 gwei per gas against A's 1
gas-blocks-per-gas-fb-b: Right. Space is what's scarce, so builders compare tips per unit of gas. B pays 63,000 ÷ 21,000 = 3 gwei per gas, while A pays only 1.
gas-blocks-per-gas-fb-same: Work out each one's tip per unit of gas: total tip ÷ gas used.
gas-blocks-builder-prompt: A builder is choosing between two transactions that each use 21,000 gas. One sends 50 ETH with a 1 gwei tip. The other sends 0.01 ETH with a 3 gwei tip. Which does it pick first?
gas-blocks-builder-opt-big: The 50 ETH one, since bigger payments come first
gas-blocks-builder-fb-big: The amount sent goes to the recipient, not to the builder. Look at what each transaction offers whoever includes it.
gas-blocks-builder-opt-tip: The 0.01 ETH one, with the bigger tip
gas-blocks-builder-fb-tip: Right. Builders earn tips, not a share of what's sent, so a small payment with a bigger tip goes first.
gas-blocks-builder-fb-order: There's no first-come, first-served line between different senders. Builders choose by what pays them.
gas-blocks-match-up-prompt: Match each term to the right description.
gas-blocks-match-up-match-base: Burned, so no one receives it
gas-blocks-match-up-explain: Tips reward whoever fills the block and the base fee is burned, so tips decide who gets the limited space. Specialist builders do that packing for most validators today.
gas-blocks-takeaway-p1: Block space is limited, so the validator, or a builder working for it, packs the transactions with the best tips first.
gas-failed-summary: Why a failed transaction still costs a fee, and how the gas limit protects you.
gas-failed-intro-p1: Making it into a block doesn't always mean a transaction worked. A failed transaction is included in a block but doesn't finish: for example, it runs out of gas partway through, or a smart contract it calls rejects it.
gas-failed-intro-p2: When that happens, everything the transaction tried to change is undone, as if it had never run. The trade doesn't happen, and the amount you tried to send stays put.
gas-failed-cost-prompt: Your trade had a gas limit of 150,000 at a gas price of 10 gwei. The smart contract rejected it after it had used 90,000 gas. What did it cost you?
gas-failed-cost-fb-free: Failing undoes the changes, not the work. The network ran the trade until it was rejected, and that work is paid for.
gas-failed-cost-opt-used: 900,000 gwei: the 90,000 gas it used × 10 gwei
gas-failed-cost-fb-used: Right. You pay for the gas used before it stopped, and the rest of the limit comes back.
gas-failed-cost-fb-limit: The limit is a ceiling, not a price. This trade stopped well below it, and gas left under the limit comes back.
gas-failed-limit-prompt: This trade's exact gas need is hidden. Find the lowest gas limit at which it goes through.
gas-failed-limit-explain: The trade needs 130,000 gas. Any lower limit runs out partway, and you pay for all the gas it used anyway. Any limit at or above it costs the same, because gas left unused under the limit is refunded.
gas-failed-headroom-prompt: Your wallet suggests a gas limit of 200,000 for a trade that usually uses about 120,000. What should you do?
gas-failed-headroom-opt-lower: Lower it to 100,000 to cut the fee
gas-failed-headroom-fb-lower: The fee depends on the gas used, not the limit, so this saves nothing. Below what the trade needs, it fails and you still pay.
gas-failed-headroom-opt-exact: Set it to exactly 120,000 so you don't overpay
gas-failed-headroom-fb-exact: There's nothing to overpay: unused gas is refunded. And if the trade needs a little more than usual this time, it fails and you still pay.
gas-failed-headroom-fb-keep: Right. The extra room adds nothing to the fee, because you only pay for the gas actually used, and it keeps the trade from running out.
gas-failed-recap-prompt: Fill in what happens when a transaction fails.
gas-failed-recap-text: When a transaction fails, its changes are {b1}, but you still pay for the gas it {b2}. Any gas left over under the limit is {b3}.
gas-failed-recap-explain: Failing undoes the changes but not the work, so the gas used is still paid. Leftover gas under the limit comes back, which is why headroom in the limit is free.
gas-failed-takeaway-p1: A failed transaction is undone but still costs the gas it used. Leave room in the gas limit: unused gas is refunded, so the headroom is free.
gas-stuck-summary: Why one underpriced transaction holds up the rest, and how to fix it.
gas-stuck-intro-p1: Every transaction from your account carries a number called its nonce: 0 for the first, then 1, 2, 3 and so on. The network takes them strictly in that order, and each number only once. So if one offers less than the base fee, it can't go into a block until the base fee drops that low, and every later transaction from your account waits behind it, however much it pays.
gas-stuck-intro-p2: Wallets set fees for you, so this is rare today. It mostly happens when fees jump suddenly, or when someone sets a fee by hand. The fix is to replace the stuck transaction: send a new one with the same nonce and a higher fee. Only one transaction per nonce can ever go in, so the new one takes the old one's place.
gas-stuck-predict-prompt: Your transaction with nonce 4 is stuck because its fee is too low. You send nonce 5 with a big tip. What happens?
gas-stuck-predict-opt-first: Nonce 5 goes in first, and 4 follows later
gas-stuck-predict-fb-first: A builder would love that tip, but the network won't accept 5 before 4. Think about what the numbers are for.
gas-stuck-predict-fb-waits: Right. Nonces go strictly in order, so a big tip on 5 can't jump the line. Test it in the next step.
gas-stuck-predict-fb-replaces: Only a transaction with the same nonce can replace another one. Nonce 5 is a new transaction, further back in the line.
gas-stuck-queue-prompt: Nonce 7 offers less than the base fee, and nonces 8 and 9 are stuck behind it. Try the buttons and get all three into a block.
gas-stuck-queue-explain: Speeding up re-sends nonce 7 with the same number and a higher fee, so it replaces the stuck one. A new transaction gets the next number and joins the back of the line, and raising the fee on a later one doesn't help either.
gas-stuck-cancel-prompt: You sent 1 ETH to the wrong address, and luckily it's still pending. How can you stop it?
gas-stuck-cancel-opt-self: Send 0 ETH to yourself with the same nonce and a higher fee
gas-stuck-cancel-fb-self: Right. That replaces the payment with one that moves nothing, so the 1 ETH stays put. It only works while the payment is pending: once it's in a block, it's too late.
gas-stuck-cancel-opt-again: Send 1 ETH to the right address
gas-stuck-cancel-fb-again: That's a new transaction with the next nonce. It waits behind the wrong one, and once fees drop, both could go through.
gas-stuck-cancel-opt-wait: Wait, since pending transactions expire after an hour
gas-stuck-cancel-fb-wait: There's no expiry time you can count on. It can sit for a long while and still go through later, when fees drop.
gas-stuck-terms-prompt: Match each term to what it means.
gas-stuck-terms-match-nonce: A transaction's place in your account's line
gas-stuck-terms-explain: Both fixes work by replacing. The network accepts only one transaction per nonce, so a new one with the same number and a higher fee takes the old one's place.
gas-stuck-takeaway-p1: Your transactions go in nonce order, so one stuck transaction holds up the rest. Replace it with the same nonce and a higher fee to speed it up, or with 0 ETH to yourself to cancel it.
gas-exam-fee-prompt: A trade on an app uses 100,000 gas, and the gas price is 2 gwei. What's the fee?
gas-exam-fee-explain: Fee = gas used × gas price, so 100,000 × 2 = 200,000 gwei. The trade does more work than a plain ETH transfer, which uses 21,000 gas today, so it costs more at the same price.
gas-exam-token-prompt: Sending ETH to a friend uses 21,000 gas today. Why does sending them a token use more?
gas-exam-token-opt-contract: The token's smart contract has to update its list of balances, which is extra work
gas-exam-token-opt-creator: Every token adds a fee that goes to the person who created it
gas-exam-token-opt-value: Gas grows with the value sent, and tokens are worth more
gas-exam-token-explain: A token is a balance kept by a smart contract, so sending one runs that contract's code. More work means more gas. Gas follows the work done, never the value sent.
gas-exam-burn-prompt: A transaction uses 21,000 gas at a base fee of 20 gwei plus a 1 gwei tip. How much of its fee is burned?
gas-exam-burn-explain: Only the base fee is burned: 21,000 × 20 = 420,000 gwei. The tip, 21,000 × 1 = 21,000 gwei, goes to the validator, and the two add up to the whole fee of 441,000 gwei.
gas-exam-rise-prompt: A popular event fills block after block to the brim. What happens to the base fee?
gas-exam-rise-opt-fixed: Nothing, since the base fee is fixed for the day
gas-exam-rise-opt-drop: It falls, since validators earn more in tips
gas-exam-rise-opt-climb: It rises after each full block, by up to 12.5% a block
gas-exam-rise-explain: Each block aims to be half full. A full block raises the next base fee by 12.5%, so a run of full blocks makes it climb quickly, and emptier blocks bring it back down.
gas-exam-tip-prompt: The network is busy and your transaction is still waiting. Why does raising your tip help?
gas-exam-tip-opt-keep: Tips go to whoever fills the block, so the best-paying transactions are picked first
gas-exam-tip-opt-burn: The tip is burned, and the network moves transactions that burn more to the front
gas-exam-tip-opt-limit: A higher tip raises your gas limit, giving the transaction more room
gas-exam-tip-explain: The validator, or a builder working for it, earns the tip on every transaction it includes. When more are waiting than will fit, the ones paying the most per unit of gas go first. The base fee is burned, so it doesn't sway the choice.
gas-exam-builder-prompt: Who usually puts together the list of transactions in a block today?
gas-exam-builder-opt-server: A central Ethereum server that sorts every transaction
gas-exam-builder-opt-builder: A specialist builder, working for the validator who adds the block
gas-exam-builder-opt-sender: Whoever sent the biggest payment in that block
gas-exam-builder-explain: Most validators take their blocks from specialist builders, who compete to offer the most profitable one. The validator still adds the block, and no central server sorts transactions.
gas-exam-outcome-prompt: Your trade on an app was included in a block, but it failed. What happened?
gas-exam-outcome-opt-sent: The ETH you were trading still went to the app
gas-exam-outcome-opt-fee: You paid for the gas it used
gas-exam-outcome-opt-refund: The fee was refunded, because the trade failed
gas-exam-outcome-opt-undone: Everything the trade tried to change was undone
gas-exam-outcome-explain: A failed transaction is undone as if it never ran, so your ETH stays put. Validators still did the work of running it, so you pay for the gas it used.
gas-exam-headroom-prompt: A trade needs exactly 130,000 gas. At the same gas price, how does its fee with a 200,000 gas limit compare to its fee with a 130,000 limit?
gas-exam-headroom-opt-higher: Higher, because you pay for the whole limit
gas-exam-headroom-opt-same: The same, because unused gas is refunded
gas-exam-headroom-opt-fails: The 200,000 limit makes the trade fail, because the limit has to match its need exactly
gas-exam-headroom-explain: You only pay for the gas the trade actually uses, and gas left unused under the limit is refunded. That makes extra room in the limit free, and it keeps the trade from running out.
gas-exam-order-prompt: Your transaction with nonce 12 is stuck. You send a new one, nonce 13, with a big tip. What happens to nonce 13?
gas-exam-order-opt-jumps: It goes in first, thanks to the tip
gas-exam-order-opt-waits: It waits until nonce 12 goes in
gas-exam-order-explain: The network takes each account's transactions strictly in nonce order, so 13 can't go in before 12, whatever its tip. Only a transaction with nonce 12 can replace 12.
gas-exam-cancel-prompt: A payment you just sent is still pending, and you want to call it off. What does your wallet's cancel button actually send?
gas-exam-cancel-opt-delete: A request asking validators to delete the payment
gas-exam-cancel-opt-self: 0 ETH to yourself, with the same nonce and a higher fee
gas-exam-cancel-opt-next: The same payment again, with the next nonce
gas-exam-cancel-explain: Cancel works by replacing: a 0 ETH transaction to yourself with the same nonce and a higher fee takes the payment's place. Nobody can delete a transaction, and one with the next nonce would only wait in line behind it.
blockchains-description: Fingerprints, pages and copies: see how any blockchain stays honest, and why there are so many of them.
blockchains-hashing-summary: Why one tiny change gives data a whole new fingerprint.
blockchains-hashing-intro-p1: Your fingerprint belongs to you alone. Computers can make a fingerprint for any piece of data too, from a single word to a whole book.
blockchains-hashing-intro-p2: That fingerprint is called a hash, and the tool that makes it is a hash function. The same text always gets the same hash, on every computer in the world.
blockchains-hashing-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: you change one letter of the text. How much of its hash changes?
blockchains-hashing-predict-fb-one: It feels like it should. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-hashing-predict-fb-few: Good guess. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-hashing-predict-fb-most: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-hashing-playground-prompt: Type anything and watch its fingerprint. Then change just one letter.
blockchains-hashing-playground-explain: One tiny change made an almost completely different fingerprint. Put the text back and the old fingerprint returns, because the same text always gets the same hash.
blockchains-hashing-reverse-prompt: Someone shows you a hash. Can you work out the text it came from?
blockchains-hashing-reverse-opt-backward: Yes, by running the hash function backwards
blockchains-hashing-reverse-fb-backwards: A hash function only works one way. There's no button that runs it backwards.
blockchains-hashing-reverse-fb-supercomp: Even the fastest computers can't undo a good hash. That's exactly what makes it useful.
blockchains-hashing-reverse-opt-no: No, a hash only works one way
blockchains-hashing-reverse-fb-no: Right. A hash is one-way. The only trick is guessing texts one at a time until one matches, which takes far too long.
blockchains-hashing-takeaway-p1: A hash is a one-way fingerprint for data: the same text always gets the same one, and even a tiny change gives a completely different one.
blockchains-chain-summary: Why changing an old page breaks the chain.
blockchains-chain-intro-p1: Picture a blockchain as a notebook that fills up one page at a time. Each page holds a batch of new records and is called a block.
blockchains-chain-intro-p2: Every page also carries the hash of the page before it. That links the pages together like a chain, all the way back to the very first one.
blockchains-chain-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: someone changes a record on an old page. What happens to the link stored on the next page?
blockchains-chain-predict-opt-nothing: Nothing: the next page doesn't notice
blockchains-chain-predict-fb-nothing: Remember what a tiny change does to a hash. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-chain-predict-fb-breaks: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-chain-predict-fb-fixes: Pages don't update each other on their own. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-chain-tamper-prompt: Here's a short blockchain. Change the record in block 1 and watch the links. Then try to repair them.
blockchains-chain-tamper-explain: Changing one page broke the link after it. You can repair the links in your own copy, but every other copy still has the real pages, so they won't accept yours.
blockchains-chain-detect-prompt: Someone edits an old page in their copy of a blockchain, then repairs every link after it. Why don't the other copies accept it?
blockchains-chain-detect-opt-accepted: They do accept it, because every link matches
blockchains-chain-detect-fb-accepted: Matching links only show that the copy agrees with itself. The others compare it with their own pages too.
blockchains-chain-detect-opt-old: Nobody looks at old pages, so they never find out
blockchains-chain-detect-fb-old: A changed old page changes every link after it, right up to the newest page. That's easy to spot.
blockchains-chain-detect-opt-rejected: It doesn't match the pages in their own copies
blockchains-chain-detect-fb-rejected: Right. Every other copy still has the real pages and their hashes, so the edited copy stands out.
blockchains-chain-takeaway-p1: Each block carries the hash of the block before it, so changing an old page breaks the chain, and the other copies won't accept the change.
blockchains-nodes-summary: Switch computers off and watch the blockchain carry on without them.
blockchains-nodes-intro-p1: Where does a blockchain live? Not on one company's computer. Thousands of computers around the world each keep their own copy of it.
blockchains-nodes-intro-p2: Each of those computers is called a node. When a new block arrives, every node checks it against the rules for itself, adds it to its copy, then passes it on to other nodes.
blockchains-nodes-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: a few nodes suddenly switch off. What happens to the blockchain?
blockchains-nodes-predict-opt-stops: It stops until they come back
blockchains-nodes-predict-fb-stops: That would be true if one server ran everything. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-nodes-predict-opt-lost: The blocks stored on those nodes are lost
blockchains-nodes-predict-fb-lost: Think about how many copies of each block exist. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-nodes-predict-opt-continues: The other nodes carry on without them
blockchains-nodes-predict-fb-continues: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
blockchains-nodes-network-prompt: Switch a node off, add a few blocks, then switch it back on.
blockchains-nodes-network-explain: The other nodes didn't wait. When the node came back, it caught up: it fetched the blocks it missed from the others and checked each one itself before adding it.
blockchains-nodes-who-prompt: On a blockchain like Ethereum, who's allowed to run a node?
blockchains-nodes-who-opt-approval: Only computers a company has approved
blockchains-nodes-who-fb-approval: Nobody has to sign off. The software is free for anyone to download and run.
blockchains-nodes-who-opt-company: Only big companies with special computers
blockchains-nodes-who-fb-company: Big companies can run nodes, but they aren't the only ones. Think about what kind of computer the software needs.
blockchains-nodes-who-fb-anyone: Right. Nobody needs permission, and the software is made to run on an ordinary computer. The more people run nodes, the harder the blockchain is for anyone to control.
blockchains-nodes-why-prompt: Your wallet app shows your balance by asking someone else's node. Why might you run your own node instead?
blockchains-nodes-why-opt-faster: To make the whole blockchain faster
blockchains-nodes-why-fb-faster: One more node doesn't speed anything up. Every node still waits for the same new blocks.
blockchains-nodes-why-opt-check: To check the blockchain yourself instead of trusting someone else
blockchains-nodes-why-fb-check: Exactly. Your own node checks every block itself, so you don't have to take anyone's word for what's on the chain.
blockchains-nodes-why-opt-earn: To get paid for every block it checks
blockchains-nodes-why-fb-earn: Keeping and checking a copy doesn't pay anything by itself. Think about what having your own copy gives you.
blockchains-nodes-takeaway-p1: Thousands of nodes each keep and check their own copy of the blockchain, so no single computer is in charge, and the blockchain keeps going when some switch off.
blockchains-consensus-summary: How all the copies settle on the same next page.
blockchains-consensus-intro-p1: New records arrive all the time. If every node wrote its own next page, the copies would soon stop matching, and nobody could tell which one is real.
blockchains-consensus-intro-p2: So the nodes follow shared rules to agree on which page comes next. Agreeing like this is called consensus.
blockchains-consensus-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: two nodes each suggest a different next page at the same moment. What should happen?
blockchains-consensus-predict-opt-both: Each node keeps whichever page it likes
blockchains-consensus-predict-fb-both: Then the copies would stop matching, and nobody could tell which one is real.
blockchains-consensus-predict-opt-agree: The nodes use shared rules to settle on one of them
blockchains-consensus-predict-fb-agree: Right. Everyone follows the same rules, so every copy ends up with the same next page.
blockchains-consensus-predict-opt-boss: A boss computer picks the winner
blockchains-consensus-predict-fb-boss: A blockchain has no boss computer. The nodes have to settle it among themselves.
blockchains-consensus-ways-p1: Blockchains have two main ways to choose who writes the next page. In proof of work, computers race to solve a hard puzzle, and the winner writes the page. That's how Bitcoin, the first blockchain, works, and how Ethereum used to.
blockchains-consensus-ways-p2: In proof of stake, people lock up some of their own ETH as a promise to play fair, and they lose some of it if they cheat. They're called validators, and this is how Ethereum works today.
blockchains-consensus-try-prompt: Try both ways of choosing who writes the next page. In proof of stake, also try to cheat.
blockchains-consensus-try-explain: Either way, one writer adds the page and everyone else checks it before adding it to their copy. A fake page gets turned down, and in proof of stake the cheater loses some of their locked-up ETH.
blockchains-consensus-takeaway-p1: Every copy has to agree on each next page. Proof of work picks the writer with a puzzle race, and proof of stake picks people who locked up ETH as a promise to play fair.
blockchains-many-summary: The same big ideas, with different rules.
blockchains-many-intro-p1: Think of board games. Most of them have a board, pieces and turns, but each game has its own rules.
blockchains-many-intro-p2: Blockchains are like that. Bitcoin was the first, made for sending digital money with no bank in the middle. Since then, people have built many more, each with its own rules. Ethereum is one of them.
blockchains-many-rules-prompt: Two blockchains both link their pages with hashes. Does that mean they follow the same rules?
blockchains-many-rules-opt-same: Yes, every blockchain follows one shared set of rules
blockchains-many-rules-fb-same: They share the big ideas, like the board and pieces in a game. The rules on top can be very different.
blockchains-many-rules-opt-own: No, each blockchain sets its own rules
blockchains-many-rules-fb-own: Right. Like board games, they share the basics, but each one decides what it keeps track of and how it agrees on the next page.
blockchains-many-rules-opt-copy: Yes, because they keep copies of each other
blockchains-many-rules-fb-copy: Each blockchain keeps its own pages. Its nodes keep its copy, not another blockchain's.
blockchains-many-sort-prompt: Sort each fact: is it true of Bitcoin, of Ethereum, or of both?
blockchains-many-sort-explain: Both link their pages with hashes and are kept by computers all over the world. Bitcoin came first and uses a puzzle race. Ethereum uses locked-up ETH and was built to run programs.
blockchains-many-fee-prompt: You want to send something on the Bitcoin blockchain. Can you pay its fee with ETH?
blockchains-many-fee-opt-any: Yes, any blockchain's money works on any other
blockchains-many-fee-fb-any: Each blockchain has its own rules, and that includes what its fees are paid in.
blockchains-many-fee-opt-own: No, Bitcoin's fees are paid in its own money
blockchains-many-fee-fb-own: Right. Bitcoin's fees are paid in bitcoin, and Ethereum's are paid in ETH. Each blockchain has its own money.
blockchains-many-fee-opt-swap: Yes, the blockchain swaps it for you
blockchains-many-fee-fb-swap: A blockchain doesn't swap in another blockchain's money on its own. Each one only follows its own rules.
blockchains-many-takeaway-p1: There are many blockchains. They share the same big ideas, but each one has its own rules, and Ethereum is one of them.
blockchains-exam-tiny-change-prompt: You make the hash of a sentence, then add a single comma and make its hash again. How do the two hashes compare?
blockchains-exam-tiny-change-opt-one: They differ in just one small part
blockchains-exam-tiny-change-opt-none: They're identical, because the meaning didn't change
blockchains-exam-tiny-change-explain: A hash function scrambles everything, so even the smallest change gives an entirely different hash. That's why a hash works as a fingerprint for spotting changed data.
blockchains-exam-work-back-prompt: A friend sends you a hash and dares you to find the message it came from. What's your best option?
blockchains-exam-work-back-opt-reverse: Run the hash function backwards on it
blockchains-exam-work-back-opt-power: Borrow the world's fastest computer to undo it
blockchains-exam-work-back-opt-guess: Guess messages and make each one's hash until one matches
blockchains-exam-work-back-explain: A hash function only works one way, and no computer can undo a good one. Guessing messages and comparing their hashes is the only approach.
blockchains-exam-link-prompt: What does each block carry that links it to the block before it?
blockchains-exam-link-opt-hash: The hash of the block before it
blockchains-exam-link-opt-time: A copy of every block before it
blockchains-exam-link-opt-name: The name of whoever wrote the block before it
blockchains-exam-link-explain: Each block carries the hash of the block before it. Change an old block and its hash changes, so the link stored in the next block stops matching.
blockchains-exam-repair-prompt: Someone changes an old page in their copy of a blockchain and repairs every link after it. Why doesn't their change count?
blockchains-exam-repair-opt-company: A company that owns the blockchain deletes it
blockchains-exam-repair-opt-counts: It does count, because all of its links match
blockchains-exam-repair-opt-others: The other copies still have the real pages and won't accept it
blockchains-exam-repair-explain: Repaired links only show that one copy agrees with itself. Every other copy still has the real pages, so the changed copy doesn't match and isn't accepted.
blockchains-exam-back-online-prompt: Your node is switched off for a while, and new blocks keep arriving. What happens when you switch it back on?
blockchains-exam-back-online-opt-broken: It's broken and has to start again from an empty copy
blockchains-exam-back-online-opt-trust: It adds the missed blocks without checking them, since other nodes already did
blockchains-exam-back-online-opt-catch-u: It fetches the blocks it missed from other nodes, checks each one and catches up
blockchains-exam-back-online-explain: A node that was switched off is just behind, not broken. It fetches the blocks it missed and checks every one itself before adding it to its copy.
blockchains-exam-who-runs-prompt: Who can run a node on a blockchain like Ethereum?
blockchains-exam-who-runs-opt-approved: Only computers a company has approved
blockchains-exam-who-runs-opt-rich: Only people who own a lot of ETH
blockchains-exam-who-runs-explain: Nobody needs permission or ETH to run a node. The software runs on an ordinary computer, and the more people run one, the harder the blockchain is to control.
blockchains-exam-agree-prompt: Why do the nodes of a blockchain need to agree on each next page?
blockchains-exam-agree-opt-match: So every copy stays the same
blockchains-exam-agree-opt-boss: So one main node can be in charge
blockchains-exam-agree-explain: If each node wrote its own next page, the copies would stop matching. Agreeing on each page, called consensus, keeps every copy the same with no one in charge.
blockchains-exam-today-prompt: How does Ethereum choose who writes the next page today?
blockchains-exam-today-opt-race: Computers race to solve a hard puzzle
blockchains-exam-today-opt-stake: It picks from people who locked up ETH as a promise to play fair
blockchains-exam-today-opt-fee: Whoever pays the biggest fee writes it
blockchains-exam-today-explain: Ethereum uses proof of stake: validators lock up ETH and lose some if they cheat. The puzzle race is proof of work, which Bitcoin uses and Ethereum used to.
blockchains-exam-first-opt-together: They all started at the same time
blockchains-exam-first-explain: Bitcoin was the first blockchain, made for sending digital money with no bank. Many more came later, Ethereum among them.
blockchains-exam-same-prompt: A friend thinks Bitcoin and Ethereum are the same blockchain. What's true?
blockchains-exam-same-opt-one: They're right: it's one blockchain with two names
blockchains-exam-same-opt-separate: They're separate blockchains, each with its own rules
blockchains-exam-same-opt-part: Ethereum is one page of the Bitcoin blockchain
blockchains-exam-same-explain: Bitcoin and Ethereum share the big ideas, like hash-linked pages and many copies, but they're separate blockchains with their own rules and their own money.
proof-of-stake-description: Meet the validators, follow a block from proposal to vote, keep time in slots and epochs, wait out finality, and see what rule breakers lose.
proof-of-stake-validators-summary: What it takes to run a validator, and what it does all day.
proof-of-stake-validators-intro-p1: A validator isn't a person or a company. It's a program running on someone's computer, backed by a deposit of ETH: its stake. Today the minimum is 32 ETH. Anyone with 32 ETH and a computer that stays online can run one, with no sign-up and no permission. With less, people can join a staking pool, which combines ETH from many.
proof-of-stake-validators-intro-p2: Its job never stops: check every new block, vote for the ones that follow the rules, and now and then propose a block of its own. Doing the job well earns rewards in new ETH. The stake is what it puts at risk if it breaks the rules.
proof-of-stake-validators-need-prompt: You want to run your own validator. Which of these do you need?
proof-of-stake-validators-need-opt-stake: At least 32 ETH to deposit as stake
proof-of-stake-validators-need-fb-stake: Needed. The deposit is what the validator puts at risk, and it's what gives its votes their weight.
proof-of-stake-validators-need-opt-permi: Approval from the team that builds Ethereum
proof-of-stake-validators-need-fb-permis: Not needed. Nobody approves validators: the deposit is the only ticket in.
proof-of-stake-validators-need-opt-onlin: A computer that stays online almost all the time
proof-of-stake-validators-need-fb-online: Needed. A validator that's offline can't vote, so it misses out on rewards.
proof-of-stake-validators-need-opt-rig: Special mining hardware that solves puzzles
proof-of-stake-validators-need-fb-rig: Not needed. Puzzle-solving hardware belongs to proof of work, which Ethereum stopped using in 2022. An ordinary computer is enough.
proof-of-stake-validators-need-explain: A validator needs a stake and a reliable computer, and nothing else: no permission and no special hardware.
proof-of-stake-validators-many-prompt: Someone sets up 1,000 validators on one powerful machine, hoping to outvote everyone else. What does that take?
proof-of-stake-validators-many-opt-cheap: Very little, since running more programs is cheap
proof-of-stake-validators-many-fb-cheap: Votes don't count per program. Each validator's vote weighs as much as its stake, so look at what every one of them needs.
proof-of-stake-validators-many-opt-stake: At least 32,000 ETH, since every validator needs its own stake
proof-of-stake-validators-many-fb-stake: Right. 1,000 validators need at least 32 ETH each. Influence costs stake, not computers.
proof-of-stake-validators-many-opt-banne: Nothing works: one person may run only one validator
proof-of-stake-validators-many-fb-banned: There's no ID check, so nothing limits how many validators one person runs. Something else keeps this attack expensive.
proof-of-stake-validators-recap-prompt: Fill in what a validator is.
proof-of-stake-validators-recap-text: A validator is a program backed by at least {b1} ETH of stake. It votes on new blocks and sometimes {b2} one, and doing that job earns {b3}.
proof-of-stake-validators-recap-explain: The stake is the ticket in, voting and proposing are the job, and rewards in new ETH are the pay.
proof-of-stake-validators-takeaway-p1: A validator is a program with at least 32 ETH at stake. Anyone can run one, and its vote weighs as much as its stake, not as much as its computer.
proof-of-stake-voting-summary: How one validator proposes a block and a committee votes on it.
proof-of-stake-voting-intro-p1: Every 12 seconds, the network picks one validator at random to propose the next block, with odds that grow with its stake. The proposer puts the block together, or takes one from a builder, then signs it and sends it out.
proof-of-stake-voting-intro-p2: At the same time, a committee of other validators is picked to check that block. Each member runs it, and if it follows the rules, signs a vote for it called an attestation. Committees rotate, so every validator gets to vote once every few minutes.
proof-of-stake-voting-round-prompt: Put one round of proposing and voting in order.
proof-of-stake-voting-round-item-pick: One validator is picked at random to propose
proof-of-stake-voting-round-item-send: It signs the block and sends it out
proof-of-stake-voting-round-item-check: Committee members run the block and check it
proof-of-stake-voting-round-item-attest: They sign and send their attestations
proof-of-stake-voting-round-item-include: A later block records those votes
proof-of-stake-voting-round-explain: The proposer goes first, then the committee checks its work. Their votes are recorded in later blocks, where they decide which chain everyone builds on and, later, count toward finality.
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-prompt: Your validator has voted every few minutes for months, but it has never proposed a block. Is something wrong?
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-opt-hourly: Yes. Every validator should propose about once an hour
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-fb-hourly: With so many validators sharing one block every 12 seconds, no single validator gets picked anywhere near that often.
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-opt-lottery: No. Proposing is a lottery, and voting is the everyday job
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-fb-lottery: Right. With so many validators sharing one block every 12 seconds, a turn to propose can take months to come up. Voting is what every validator does all the time.
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-opt-weekly: Yes. It should have proposed within its first week
proof-of-stake-voting-rare-fb-weekly: Nothing schedules a turn. The pick is random, so a validator might wait days, or many months.
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-prompt: A committee member runs a newly proposed block and finds that it breaks the rules. What does it do?
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-opt-fix: Fixes the block and sends out a corrected copy
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-fb-fix: Validators never edit someone else's block. A changed block wouldn't carry the proposer's signature anymore.
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-opt-vote: Votes for the last valid block it knows instead
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-fb-vote: Right. An attestation says which block a validator sees as the newest valid one. A broken block gets no votes, and the chain carries on without it.
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-opt-retry: Asks the proposer to try again
proof-of-stake-voting-broken-fb-retry: There's no back and forth. Each validator votes on what it sees and moves on.
proof-of-stake-voting-takeaway-p1: In each round, one validator proposes a block, and a committee checks it and votes. Those votes, weighed by stake, decide which blocks the network builds on.
proof-of-stake-slots-summary: The 12-second beat that every validator keeps time to.
proof-of-stake-slots-intro-p1: Ethereum keeps a steady beat. Today, time is split into slots of 12 seconds, each a chance for exactly one block. Every 32 slots make an epoch: 32 × 12 = 384 seconds, or 6.4 minutes.
proof-of-stake-slots-intro-p2: The epoch is the voting cycle. Each validator sits on one committee, in one slot, in every epoch, so all of them vote once per epoch, spread across its 32 slots. The first slot of each epoch is also a checkpoint, which finality builds on.
proof-of-stake-slots-hour-prompt: At most, how many blocks can Ethereum add in one hour?
proof-of-stake-slots-hour-fb-minute: That would be one block a minute. A slot is much shorter than that.
proof-of-stake-slots-hour-fb-slots: Right. An hour is 3,600 seconds, and 3,600 ÷ 12 = 300 slots, each with room for one block.
proof-of-stake-slots-hour-fb-second: That would be one block every second. Each slot lasts longer than that.
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-prompt: The validator picked to propose in a slot is offline. What happens?
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-opt-wait: The network waits until that validator comes back
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-fb-wait: Slots tick by on a fixed clock, whatever happens. Nobody waits for one validator.
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-opt-backup: Another validator proposes in its place, in the same slot
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-fb-backup: Each slot has exactly one chosen proposer and no stand-in. Think about what the clock does.
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-opt-empty: The slot passes with no block, and the next slot carries on
proof-of-stake-slots-missed-fb-empty: Right. The clock never waits. The slot stays empty, and the next proposer builds on the last block there is.
proof-of-stake-slots-recap-prompt: Fill in the beat of the network.
proof-of-stake-slots-recap-text: A slot lasts {b1} seconds. {b2} slots make an epoch, and in each epoch every validator votes {b3}.
proof-of-stake-slots-recap-explain: 32 slots of 12 seconds make a 6.4-minute epoch. Spreading the votes across all 32 slots means no single slot has to carry every validator's vote.
proof-of-stake-slots-takeaway-p1: Today a slot is 12 seconds and holds at most one block. 32 slots make a 6.4-minute epoch, and every validator votes once in each one.
proof-of-stake-finality-title: Finality: when it's set in stone
proof-of-stake-finality-summary: Two checkpoints, and the wait until a block can't be undone.
proof-of-stake-finality-intro-p1: A shop sees your payment in a brand-new block. Should it hand over the goods right away? Not yet. Until a block is final, there's a small chance it gets replaced by a different one.
proof-of-stake-finality-intro-p2: Finality builds on checkpoints, the first slot of every epoch, so there's one about every 6.4 minutes. Validators vote on each checkpoint. Once two checkpoints in a row are each backed by validators holding two-thirds of all staked ETH, the earlier one becomes final, along with every block before it.
proof-of-stake-finality-clock-prompt: The shop ships once your payment is final. It's in the last block before a checkpoint. Find the earliest moment it's final.
proof-of-stake-finality-clock-explain: Validators take about 6.4 minutes to vote on each checkpoint. Once the checkpoint right after your block and the one after that are both backed by two-thirds of staked ETH, your block is final: about 13 minutes after it was added. A block added just after a checkpoint waits longer, up to about 19 minutes.
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-prompt: Someone wants to undo a block that's already final. What would it take?
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-opt-node: Editing the copy on one node
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-fb-node: Other nodes check every block themselves, so an edited copy is simply rejected.
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-opt-majo: Getting over half of all nodes to agree
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-fb-major: Finality isn't decided by counting nodes. Anyone can run as many nodes as they like.
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-opt-thir: Validators holding at least a third of all staked ETH breaking the rules
proof-of-stake-finality-reverse-fb-third: Right. Those rule breaks leave signed proof, so the attackers would be slashed, the punishment that destroys staked ETH, and lose a huge amount of it.
proof-of-stake-finality-recap-prompt: Fill the gaps to sum up how a block becomes final.
proof-of-stake-finality-recap-text: Every 32 {b1} brings a new {b2}, so there's one about every 6.4 minutes. A block is {b3} once the checkpoint after it and the next one are both backed by two-thirds of staked ETH.
proof-of-stake-finality-recap-explain: Each slot lasts 12 seconds, so 32 of them take about 6.4 minutes. A block has to wait for two checkpoints to be backed, which is why finality takes minutes, not seconds.
proof-of-stake-finality-takeaway-p1: Today a block normally becomes final about 13 to 19 minutes after it's added. Undoing it would mean validators breaking the rules and getting slashed, losing a huge amount of staked ETH.
proof-of-stake-penalties-summary: What validators earn for doing the job, and what they lose for skipping it or cheating.
proof-of-stake-penalties-intro-p1: Validators that vote on time and propose when picked earn rewards: new ETH, plus the tips from the blocks they propose. A validator that's offline misses its votes and pays a small penalty, about the size of the rewards it missed. Once it's back online, it earns again. That holds while the network is finalizing as normal: if so many validators are offline that finality stops, the offline ones lose more and more until it recovers.
proof-of-stake-penalties-intro-p2: Cheating is different. Signing two different blocks for the same slot, or casting votes that contradict each other, leaves signed proof, and the validator is slashed: part of its stake is destroyed and it's forced out. Slashed alone, it loses only a small part. The more stake is slashed around the same time, the more each one loses, up to all of it.
proof-of-stake-penalties-sort-prompt: Sort what each validator did by what happens to it.
proof-of-stake-penalties-sort-explain: Doing the job earns rewards, missing it costs about what it would have earned, and only provable cheating gets a validator slashed.
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-prompt: A validator is offline for a whole day, then comes back. Normally, roughly what has it lost?
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-fb-stake: Losing stake on that scale is the punishment for cheating, not for going offline. A missed day costs far less.
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-opt-nothing: Nothing, since it broke no rules
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-fb-nothing: It broke no rules, but it didn't do the job either. Missed votes cost a little.
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-opt-rewards: About a day's worth of rewards
proof-of-stake-penalties-day-fb-rewards: Right. Its balance shrinks by about what it would have earned that day. That's small next to its stake, and it earns again once it's back.
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-prompt: Why does each slashed validator lose more when many are slashed around the same time?
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-opt-sh: The slashed ETH is shared out among the honest validators
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-fb-sha: Almost all slashed ETH is destroyed, not handed out. The reason has to do with what a mass rule break means.
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-opt-at: Many at once looks like an attack, so the cost grows with its size
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-fb-att: Right. A lone slip, like the same validator accidentally running on two machines, costs little. A mass rule break looks like an attack, and it can cost the attackers everything.
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-opt-ra: Penalties are random, and big groups are unlucky
proof-of-stake-penalties-together-fb-ran: Nothing about slashing is random. The rules scale it on purpose.
proof-of-stake-penalties-takeaway-p1: Doing the job earns rewards, and missing it costs about the same small amount. Provable cheating gets a validator slashed, and the more validators cheat together, the more each one loses.
proof-of-stake-exam-deposit-prompt: What does it take to run your own validator?
proof-of-stake-exam-deposit-opt-approval: An application approved by the team behind Ethereum
proof-of-stake-exam-deposit-opt-stake: At least 32 ETH as stake, and a computer that stays online
proof-of-stake-exam-deposit-opt-mining: Mining hardware that solves puzzles faster than others
proof-of-stake-exam-deposit-explain: Anyone can run a validator with at least 32 ETH at stake and a reliable computer. There's no approval process, and puzzle-solving hardware belongs to proof of work, not proof of stake.
proof-of-stake-exam-weight-prompt: Why can't someone take over voting just by running thousands of validators on cheap computers?
proof-of-stake-exam-weight-opt-limit: The network allows only one validator per person
proof-of-stake-exam-weight-opt-ignored: Validators past the first ten on one machine are ignored
proof-of-stake-exam-weight-opt-stake: Each validator needs its own stake, so influence costs ETH, not computers
proof-of-stake-exam-weight-explain: Votes weigh as much as the stake behind them, and every validator needs at least 32 ETH, so a thousand validators means staking at least 32,000 ETH. Nothing checks identities.
proof-of-stake-exam-proposer-prompt: How is the validator that proposes the block in a slot chosen?
proof-of-stake-exam-proposer-opt-random: At random, with odds that grow with its stake
proof-of-stake-exam-proposer-opt-fastest: Whichever validator solves a puzzle first
proof-of-stake-exam-proposer-opt-rota: By a fixed rota, in the order validators joined
proof-of-stake-exam-proposer-explain: One validator per slot is picked at random, weighted by its stake. Racing to solve puzzles was how proof of work chose who added blocks.
proof-of-stake-exam-attest-opt-receipt: A receipt the proposer sends to everyone whose transaction it included
proof-of-stake-exam-attest-opt-fee: The fee a validator pays to join a committee
proof-of-stake-exam-attest-opt-vote: A validator's signed vote for the block it sees as the newest valid one
proof-of-stake-exam-attest-explain: Committee members check each new block and sign a vote for the chain they see as valid. Those votes, weighed by stake, decide which blocks the network builds on and later count toward finality.
proof-of-stake-exam-epoch-prompt: An epoch is 32 slots. How long does it last?
proof-of-stake-exam-epoch-explain: Each slot is 12 seconds today, so 32 slots take 32 × 12 = 384 seconds: 6.4 minutes. Every validator votes once in each epoch.
proof-of-stake-exam-missed-prompt: The validator picked to propose misses its slot. What happens to Ethereum's clock?
proof-of-stake-exam-missed-opt-empty: It keeps ticking: that slot stays empty and the next proposer carries on
proof-of-stake-exam-missed-opt-pause: It pauses until a block arrives
proof-of-stake-exam-missed-opt-repeat: The slot is repeated with a new proposer
proof-of-stake-exam-missed-explain: Slots are fixed 12-second steps that pass whatever happens. A missed slot simply has no block, and the next proposer builds on the last block there is.
proof-of-stake-exam-wait-prompt: A shop waits until your payment is final before shipping. Roughly how long after your payment's block is added will that take?
proof-of-stake-exam-wait-opt-block: About 12 seconds, once the next block arrives
proof-of-stake-exam-wait-opt-thirteen: About 13 to 19 minutes, once two checkpoints in a row are backed
proof-of-stake-exam-wait-opt-checkpoint: About 6.4 minutes, once the next checkpoint is backed
proof-of-stake-exam-wait-explain: A checkpoint comes every 32 slots, about every 6.4 minutes. Your block is final once the two checkpoints after it are each backed by validators holding two-thirds of staked ETH, 13 to 19 minutes after it was added, depending on how close to a checkpoint it landed.
proof-of-stake-exam-undo-prompt: An exchange credited your deposit once its block was final. Someone wants to erase that block. What would it take?
proof-of-stake-exam-undo-opt-third: Validators with a third or more of all staked ETH breaking the rules
proof-of-stake-exam-undo-opt-edit: Editing the block on their own node
proof-of-stake-exam-undo-opt-nodes: Running more than half of all the nodes
proof-of-stake-exam-undo-explain: Finality depends on staked ETH, not on counting nodes, and an edited copy is simply rejected. Breaking the rules leaves signed proof, so those validators would be slashed, and the more staked ETH is slashed at once, the more each one loses.
proof-of-stake-exam-offline-prompt: A solo staker's validator is offline for a weekend because of a power cut. What does it cost them?
proof-of-stake-exam-offline-opt-slash: Slashing: part of the stake destroyed, and removal
proof-of-stake-exam-offline-opt-small: Small penalties, about the rewards it would have earned
proof-of-stake-exam-offline-opt-nothing: Nothing, since the network can't tell
proof-of-stake-exam-offline-explain: Missed votes cost about what they would have earned, and the network sees every missing vote. Slashing is only for provable cheating, like signing two different blocks for the same slot.
proof-of-stake-exam-correlated-prompt: Validators holding a large share of all stake are slashed within the same few weeks. Compared with a lone slashing, what does each one lose?
proof-of-stake-exam-correlated-opt-same: The same small amount as a lone slashing
proof-of-stake-exam-correlated-opt-less: Less, because the penalty is split between them
proof-of-stake-exam-correlated-opt-more: More, up to its whole stake
proof-of-stake-exam-correlated-explain: A lone slashing destroys a small part of a validator's stake. The penalty grows with how much stake was slashed around the same time, up to all of it, so a large coordinated attack is ruinous.
