eth-description: Count ETH down to its smallest unit, follow new ETH in and burned ETH out, and see how wrapping and staking really work.
eth-what-summary: The network, its money and what that money is for.
eth-what-intro-p1: People often say they bought some Ethereum. What they actually bought is ether, or ETH for short: the currency built into Ethereum itself, also called its native currency.
eth-what-intro-p2: Ethereum is the network: the blockchain and the thousands of computers that keep it in sync. ETH is the money built into it from day one. Because it's built in, every node records each account's ETH balance directly, while a token's balances are kept by its own smart contract.
eth-what-price-prompt: A friend says the price of Ethereum went up today. What actually went up in price?
eth-what-price-fb-network: A network isn't something you can buy a slice of. People say Ethereum as shorthand for something else.
eth-what-price-opt-company: Shares in a company called Ethereum
eth-what-price-fb-company: Ethereum isn't a company and has no shares. No single organization owns or runs it.
eth-what-price-fb-eth: Right. When people talk about the price of Ethereum, they mean the price of ETH.
eth-what-sort-prompt: Sort each statement: is it about Ethereum, the network, or ETH, its money?
eth-what-sort-explain: Ethereum is the network: the computers, the shared record and the rules, which upgrades can change. ETH is the money on it: it has a price, pays for gas and is what validators stake.
eth-what-native-prompt: Tokens are balances kept by smart contracts. Where is your ETH balance kept?
eth-what-native-opt-account: In your account itself, recorded by Ethereum's own rules
eth-what-native-fb-account: Right. ETH is built in, so every node tracks each account's ETH balance directly. That's also why only ETH can pay fees and be staked: those rules are part of Ethereum itself.
eth-what-native-opt-contract: On an ETH smart contract's list of balances, like a token
eth-what-native-fb-contract: That's how tokens work, but ETH was there before any smart contract. Think about what built in means.
eth-what-native-fb-wallet: A wallet holds your keys, not your coins. Think about where every node can see the balance.
eth-what-takeaway-p1: Ethereum is the network and ETH is its built-in money. The network records every ETH balance itself, and only ETH can pay fees or back validators.
eth-units-summary: The small units behind every balance and fee.
eth-units-intro-p1: Gas prices are tiny fractions of an ETH, so they're quoted in gwei: one billionth of an ETH. That makes 1 ETH equal to 1,000,000,000 gwei.
eth-units-intro-p2: There's an even smaller unit: the wei, the smallest amount of ETH there is. A billion wei make one gwei, so 1 ETH is a 1 followed by 18 zeros in wei. Behind the scenes, Ethereum records every balance in wei.
eth-units-biggest-prompt: Which of these is the biggest amount?
eth-units-biggest-fb-wei: A million sounds like a lot, but wei are so small that a million of them is only a thousandth of a gwei.
eth-units-biggest-fb-gwei: One gwei is only a billionth of an ETH. Convert each amount into the same unit to compare them.
eth-units-biggest-fb-eth: Right. 0.001 ETH is a million gwei, far bigger than the other two.
eth-units-convert-prompt: A developer tool shows a fee in wei, the unit Ethereum uses behind the scenes. Find the same amount in ETH.
eth-units-convert-explain: Each unit is worth a billion of the next smaller one. 210,000,000,000,000 wei is 210,000 gwei, which is 0.00021 ETH: the fee for a simple transfer at a gas price of 10 gwei.
eth-units-price-prompt: A gas price is 10 gwei. How many wei is that?
eth-units-price-fb-same: That treats gwei and wei as the same size, but a gwei is much bigger than a wei.
eth-units-price-fb-billion: Right. Each gwei is a billion wei, so 10 gwei is ten billion wei. Same amount, smaller unit, bigger number.
eth-units-price-fb-fraction: Switching to a smaller unit makes the number bigger, not smaller. And nothing is smaller than one wei.
eth-units-equal-prompt: Match each amount with the same amount in another unit.
eth-units-equal-explain: Every pair is the same amount written two ways. A gwei is a billionth of an ETH, and a wei is a billionth of a gwei.
eth-units-takeaway-p1: ETH, gwei and wei are the same money in different sizes. Each unit is worth a billion of the next smaller one, so a smaller unit just means a bigger number.
eth-supply-summary: Issuance, burning, and why the supply can shrink.
eth-supply-intro-p1: No company or central bank prints ETH. New ETH is created by the network itself, as rewards for validators, who stake ETH to run the network. Creating new ETH this way is called issuance. How much is issued follows public rules that every node checks, and depends mostly on how much ETH is staked in total.
eth-supply-intro-p2: ETH also disappears. Every transaction pays a base fee, the part of the gas fee set by the network, and that base fee is burned: destroyed for good. Issuance adds ETH and burning removes it, so the total supply can grow or shrink.
eth-supply-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: when the network gets busier, what happens to the amount of ETH burned?
eth-supply-predict-fb-more: Good thinking. More transactions, and a higher base fee when demand is high, both mean more ETH burned. Test it in the next step.
eth-supply-predict-fb-less: Think about what busy times do to the base fee. Test it in the next step.
eth-supply-predict-fb-same: Every transaction burns its own base fee, so the total depends on how much is happening. Test it in the next step.
eth-supply-balance-prompt: In this example, validators receive the same amount of new ETH every day. Find the level of network activity where the ETH burned exactly matches the ETH issued.
eth-supply-balance-explain: When burn matches issuance, the total supply stays flat. Quieter than that and it grows; busier and it shrinks. Real numbers change daily, and issuance depends mostly on how much ETH is staked, not on activity.
eth-supply-who-prompt: The example kept issuance the same every day. On the real network, what mostly decides how much new ETH is issued?
eth-supply-who-opt-stake: How much ETH is staked in total
eth-supply-who-fb-stake: Right. More staked ETH means more new ETH issued in total, though less for each validator. Network activity changes how much is burned, not how much is issued.
eth-supply-who-fb-activity: Busy times change the burn, the other side of the balance. Issuance follows a different number.
eth-supply-who-fb-price: The rules that set issuance don't know ETH's price. They count something recorded on the chain itself.
eth-supply-recap-prompt: Fill in how ETH enters and leaves the supply.
eth-supply-recap-text: New ETH is issued as rewards for {b1}, and every {b2} is burned. When more ETH is burned than issued, the total supply {b3}.
eth-supply-recap-explain: Validators earn the new ETH, and the base fee is the part of each fee that gets destroyed. Burn more than is issued and there's less ETH than before.
eth-supply-takeaway-p1: New ETH is issued to validators and every base fee is burned. Busy times burn more, so the supply can shrink as well as grow.
eth-wrapped-summary: Turning ETH into a token and back again.
eth-wrapped-intro-p1: Besides ETH, Ethereum has thousands of tokens: balances kept by smart contracts, each recording who holds how much and moving amounts when their owners ask.
eth-wrapped-intro-p2: ETH is older than the shared rules tokens follow, so it doesn't follow them, and many apps are built to handle tokens only. Wrapped ETH (WETH) fixes this: a token you get by depositing ETH, 1 for 1, and can always swap back for exactly the same amount of ETH.
eth-wrapped-predict-prompt: You wrap 1 ETH. What do you end up with?
eth-wrapped-predict-fb-both: Wrapping doesn't create money. If it did, everyone would wrap forever. Try it in the next step.
eth-wrapped-predict-opt-one: 1 WETH, with your 1 ETH held by the WETH contract
eth-wrapped-predict-fb-one: Right. Your ETH is locked away and you get the same amount of WETH. Try it in the next step.
eth-wrapped-predict-opt-less: A little less than 1 WETH, after a wrapping cut
eth-wrapped-predict-fb-less: The WETH contract doesn't take a cut. You do pay the usual gas fee, in ETH, to send the transaction. Try it in the next step.
eth-wrapped-wrap-prompt: Wrap some ETH, then unwrap it. Watch both balances and the total.
eth-wrapped-wrap-explain: Every WETH is backed by 1 ETH held in the WETH contract, so nothing is created or lost. In real life each wrap or unwrap is a transaction, so you also pay a small gas fee in ETH.
eth-wrapped-gas-prompt: You wrap all your ETH into WETH, then try to send some WETH to a friend. What's the problem?
eth-wrapped-gas-opt-value: WETH is worth less than ETH
eth-wrapped-gas-fb-value: Each WETH can be unwrapped for exactly 1 ETH, so it's worth the same.
eth-wrapped-gas-opt-fee: You have no ETH left to pay the gas fee
eth-wrapped-gas-fb-fee: Right. Fees are always paid in ETH, never in WETH. When you wrap, keep some ETH back for fees.
eth-wrapped-gas-opt-send: WETH can't be sent to other people
eth-wrapped-gas-fb-send: WETH is a token, and tokens can be sent like any other balance. Something else is in the way.
eth-wrapped-peg-prompt: WETH is bought and sold on trading apps. Why can't real WETH stay far below the price of 1 ETH for long?
eth-wrapped-peg-opt-unwrap: Anyone can buy it cheap and unwrap it for a full ETH
eth-wrapped-peg-fb-unwrap: Right. The WETH contract always swaps 1 WETH back for 1 ETH, so cheap WETH gets bought up until the price is back near 1 ETH. A WETH offered far below that is more likely a copy: check its contract address.
eth-wrapped-peg-opt-company: A company buys it back to hold the price up
eth-wrapped-peg-fb-company: No company stands behind WETH. It's a smart contract, so think about what the contract lets anyone do.
eth-wrapped-peg-opt-fixed: Ethereum's rules fix the price of every token
eth-wrapped-peg-fb-fixed: Ethereum's rules don't set token prices: buyers and sellers do. Something else pulls WETH back toward 1 ETH.
eth-wrapped-takeaway-p1: WETH is ETH in token form: wrap 1 ETH to get 1 WETH, and unwrap it any time to get your ETH back. You still need plain ETH to pay for gas.
eth-staking-summary: How staking earns rewards, and what it risks.
eth-staking-intro-p1: Validators, who propose and vote on new blocks, each lock up ETH as a security deposit. In return they earn staking rewards: newly issued ETH, plus the tips from transactions in the blocks they propose.
eth-staking-intro-p2: Running a validator entirely with your own ETH is called solo staking. Today it takes at least 32 ETH and a computer that stays online around the clock. If you have 32 ETH but no spare computer, a company can run the validator for you. With less, you can join a staking pool, which combines ETH from many people, or stake through an exchange.
eth-staking-small-prompt: You have 1 ETH and want to earn staking rewards. Can you?
eth-staking-small-opt-no: No. Staking needs at least 32 ETH
eth-staking-small-fb-no: 32 ETH is what one validator needs, but there's more than one way to take part.
eth-staking-small-opt-own: Yes, by running your own validator with your 1 ETH
eth-staking-small-fb-own: Solo staking needs at least 32 ETH, so 1 ETH alone can't run a validator.
eth-staking-small-opt-pool: Yes, by joining a staking pool or staking through an exchange
eth-staking-small-fb-pool: Right. Pools and exchanges combine ETH from many people to fill validators, so you can take part with less.
eth-staking-control-prompt: Put these ways to stake in order, from the most control over your ETH to the least.
eth-staking-control-item-solo: Solo: your own 32 ETH on your own computer
eth-staking-control-item-operator: Your own 32 ETH, with a company running the computer
eth-staking-control-item-pool: A staking pool: any amount, combined with other people's ETH
eth-staking-control-item-exchange: An exchange: it holds your ETH and stakes it for you
eth-staking-control-explain: Each step down trades control for convenience. Solo stakers hold every key themselves. Staking through an exchange is custodial: the exchange holds the keys, so you're trusting it with your ETH.
eth-staking-risks-prompt: Which of these are real risks of staking?
eth-staking-risks-opt-slashing: Losing part of the stake if the validator cheats
eth-staking-risks-fb-slashing: Real. A validator that provably cheats, such as by signing two conflicting blocks, has part of its stake destroyed. That's slashing.
eth-staking-risks-opt-offline: Losing small amounts if the validator goes offline
eth-staking-risks-fb-offline: Real. Validators that go offline miss rewards and lose small amounts of ETH, so solo stakers need a reliable computer and connection.
eth-staking-risks-opt-trust: A pool or exchange mishandling your ETH
eth-staking-risks-fb-trust: Real. With a pool or exchange, you're trusting someone else's program or company to look after your ETH.
eth-staking-risks-fb-guaranteed: Rewards aren't guaranteed. They depend on the validator doing its job, and penalties can eat into them.
eth-staking-risks-explain: Staking pays because it carries responsibility. Solo stakers take on the validator risks themselves; pools and exchanges add the risk of trusting someone else.
eth-staking-exchange-prompt: An exchange offers staking with one tap. Compared with solo staking, what are you giving up?
eth-staking-exchange-fb-nothing: Convenience comes at a cost. Think about who stands between you and your ETH.
eth-staking-exchange-opt-control: Control. The exchange holds your ETH, so you depend on it to give it back
eth-staking-exchange-fb-control: Right. Exchange staking is custodial: someone else holds the keys. It's the simplest option, but you're trusting a company instead of holding your own keys.
eth-staking-exchange-opt-forever: Your ETH, forever. Staking can't be undone
eth-staking-exchange-fb-forever: Staked ETH can be withdrawn again. Staking isn't a one-way door.
eth-staking-takeaway-p1: Staking puts ETH to work securing Ethereum in return for rewards. The more of it you do yourself, the more control you keep, and the more responsibility you take on.
eth-exam-own-prompt: Someone tells you they own 2 Ethereum. What do they actually own?
eth-exam-own-opt-eth: 2 ETH, the currency built into Ethereum
eth-exam-own-opt-shares: Two shares in the company behind Ethereum
eth-exam-own-opt-network: A slice of the Ethereum network itself
eth-exam-own-explain: Ethereum is the network and ether (ETH) is the money that lives on it. Ethereum isn't a company with shares, and nobody can buy a slice of the network.
eth-exam-native-prompt: How is your ETH balance recorded differently from a token balance?
eth-exam-native-opt-network: Every node records it directly in your account, while a token's balances are kept by its smart contract
eth-exam-native-opt-same: No difference: both are kept by smart contracts
eth-exam-native-opt-app: Your wallet app records ETH, and the network records tokens
eth-exam-native-explain: ETH is Ethereum's native currency, built in from the start, so the network tracks each account's ETH balance itself. Token balances live in each token's smart contract, which is why ETH has to be wrapped to act like a token.
eth-exam-smallest-prompt: Put side by side, which of these amounts is worth the least?
eth-exam-smallest-explain: A wei is the smallest unit and a billion of them make one gwei, so 1,000 wei is far less than 1 gwei. 0.000001 ETH is bigger still: a thousand gwei.
eth-exam-gwei-prompt: A fee comes to 0.00042 ETH. How much is that in gwei?
eth-exam-gwei-opt-fraction: Less than 1 gwei, since gwei is a smaller unit
eth-exam-gwei-explain: 1 ETH is a billion gwei, so 0.00042 ETH is 420,000 gwei. Switching to a smaller unit makes the number bigger, while the amount stays the same.
eth-exam-shrink-prompt: When can the total supply of ETH shrink?
eth-exam-shrink-opt-busy: When the network is very busy
eth-exam-shrink-opt-quiet: When the network is quiet and fewer transactions are sent
eth-exam-shrink-opt-fixed: Never. The supply of ETH is fixed
eth-exam-shrink-explain: Every base fee is burned, and busy times burn more. Once burning outpaces the new ETH issued to validators, the total supply shrinks.
eth-exam-rules-prompt: A friend worries that someone could create extra ETH whenever they like. What actually decides how much new ETH is created?
eth-exam-rules-opt-founders: Ethereum's founders, who can add more at any time
eth-exam-rules-opt-bank: A central bank, the same way dollars are printed
eth-exam-rules-opt-rules: Public rules that every node checks
eth-exam-rules-explain: Issuance follows the network's public rules, and every node checks them, so anyone can verify how much ETH exists. How much is issued depends mostly on how much ETH is staked. Nobody can create ETH at will, and changing the rules would take an upgrade to the network.
eth-exam-discount-prompt: A stranger offers to sell you 1 WETH for only 0.8 ETH. Should the discount worry you?
eth-exam-discount-opt-normal: No. WETH is usually worth a bit less than ETH
eth-exam-discount-opt-backed: Yes. Real WETH always swaps back 1 for 1, so a cheap one is likely fake
eth-exam-discount-opt-name: No. A token called WETH is always the real thing
eth-exam-discount-explain: Every real WETH is backed by 1 ETH held in the WETH contract, so it's worth the same as ETH. Anyone can create a token called WETH, so check its address before trusting it.
eth-exam-keep-prompt: You want to use an app that only handles tokens, so you plan to wrap your ETH. What's the sensible way to do it?
eth-exam-keep-opt-keep: Wrap most of it and keep some plain ETH for gas fees
eth-exam-keep-opt-all: Wrap all of it, since gas fees can be paid in WETH
eth-exam-keep-opt-little: Wrap only a little, since WETH is worth less than ETH
eth-exam-keep-explain: Gas fees are paid in ETH, never in WETH, and each WETH is worth exactly 1 ETH. Keep some plain ETH back when you wrap so you can still pay for your next transaction.
eth-exam-risks-prompt: A friend calls staking free money with no downside. Which of these are real risks of staking?
eth-exam-risks-opt-slashing: Having part of the deposit destroyed for breaking the rules
eth-exam-risks-opt-forever: Never being able to withdraw the staked ETH
eth-exam-risks-opt-offline: Small penalties while the validator's computer is down
eth-exam-risks-opt-trust: A staking service losing or misusing the ETH
eth-exam-risks-explain: A validator that cheats has part of its stake destroyed, and one that goes offline loses small amounts. With a pool or exchange you also trust someone else with your ETH, but staked ETH can be withdrawn again.
eth-exam-solo-prompt: You have 32 ETH and want to stake it while keeping as much control over it as possible. Which option fits best?
eth-exam-solo-opt-exchange: Staking through an exchange, which holds it for you
eth-exam-solo-opt-solo: Running your own validator on your own computer
eth-exam-solo-opt-pool: Joining a staking pool, combined with other people's ETH
eth-exam-solo-explain: Solo staking needs at least 32 ETH today and keeps every key in your own hands. Pools and exchanges trade some control for convenience, and an exchange holds your ETH for you.
smart-contracts-description: Programs that live on Ethereum: what they do, how you use them and what can go wrong.
smart-contracts-what-title: A program with its own address
smart-contracts-what-summary: What a smart contract is, where it lives, and who controls what it holds.
smart-contracts-what-intro-p1: "Smart contract" sounds like a legal document, but it's really a program. A smart contract is a program that lives on Ethereum at its own address, just like yours. People can send ETH to it, and it can hold that ETH.
smart-contracts-what-intro-p2: But nobody has a private key for a contract's address. Only its code decides what happens to the ETH it holds. And once a contract is deployed, meaning published to Ethereum, its rules can't simply be changed.
smart-contracts-what-holds-prompt: Lots of people have sent ETH to a contract, and it's holding all of it. Who decides what happens to that ETH?
smart-contracts-what-holds-opt-creator: The person who made the contract, using their private key
smart-contracts-what-holds-fb-creator: A contract's address has no private key, not even for the person who made it. Try it in the next step.
smart-contracts-what-holds-opt-code: The contract's own code, following its rules
smart-contracts-what-holds-fb-code: Right. Only the code can move what the contract holds, and it does so exactly as written. Try it in the next step.
smart-contracts-what-holds-fb-validators: Validators, who stake ETH to run the network, run a contract's code exactly as written. They don't decide who gets its ETH. Try it in the next step.
smart-contracts-what-jar-prompt: This class trip jar is a smart contract. Fill it up, then try taking ETH out as its creator, and try changing its rules.
smart-contracts-what-jar-explain: The jar's code moved the ETH by its own rule, and nobody could take it out another way, not even its creator. Its rules stayed exactly as written. In real life each of these actions is a transaction, so each one also pays a fee, even the ones that are turned down.
smart-contracts-what-change-prompt: A contract collects ETH for a community garden. Its creator deployed it last month, and now wants to add a rule that sends some of the ETH to them. Can they just edit the code?
smart-contracts-what-change-opt-edit: Yes, creators can edit their code any time
smart-contracts-what-change-fb-edit: Deployed code stays exactly as it was published. That's what lets everyone rely on the rules.
smart-contracts-what-change-opt-vote: Only if validators vote to allow it
smart-contracts-what-change-fb-vote: Validators run contracts as written. They don't vote on changing anyone's code.
smart-contracts-what-change-opt-no: No. Deployed code can't simply be changed
smart-contracts-what-change-fb-no: Right. The code at that address stays the same. A contract's rules can only change if its original code includes a way to change them, which is worth checking before you use one.
smart-contracts-what-takeaway-p1: A smart contract is a program at its own address on Ethereum. It can hold ETH, only its code decides what happens to that ETH, and once it's deployed, its rules can't simply be changed.
smart-contracts-calling-title: Reading is free, writing costs gas
smart-contracts-calling-summary: The two ways to use a contract, and which one you pay for.
smart-contracts-calling-intro-p1: Using a smart contract is called calling it, and every call is one of two kinds. Reading asks the contract for information, like a balance or a price. Your app asks a node, one of the computers that keep a copy of the blockchain, instead of sending a transaction, so it's free: no transaction and no gas.
smart-contracts-calling-intro-p2: Writing asks the contract to change something, like adding ETH to a jar contract or sending someone a token (a balance that a contract keeps track of). That takes a transaction signed with your private key and a gas fee for the work, and it only counts once a validator includes it in a block.
smart-contracts-calling-predict-prompt: You open an app and it shows your token balance. Did checking it cost you any gas?
smart-contracts-calling-predict-opt-yes: Yes, every time an app talks to a contract
smart-contracts-calling-predict-fb-yes: Only calls that change something cost gas. Showing a balance just looks.
smart-contracts-calling-predict-opt-no: No. Reading a balance changes nothing, so it's free
smart-contracts-calling-predict-fb-no: Right. Apps read from contracts all the time, at no cost to you.
smart-contracts-calling-predict-opt-firs: Only the first time you check
smart-contracts-calling-predict-fb-first: There's no one-off charge. Looking is free every time, because nothing on Ethereum changes.
smart-contracts-calling-sort-prompt: Sort each action: is it a free read, or a write that needs a transaction and gas?
smart-contracts-calling-sort-explain: Ask one question: does this change anything on Ethereum? If it does, it's a write, so it needs a signed transaction and gas. If it only looks, it's a free read.
smart-contracts-calling-fee-prompt: A website says you must sign a transaction and pay a small gas fee just to view your token balance. What's going on?
smart-contracts-calling-fee-opt-normal: That's normal. Every contract call costs gas
smart-contracts-calling-fee-fb-normal: Reading a balance is free. Nothing needs to change, so no transaction is needed.
smart-contracts-calling-fee-opt-suspicio: Something's off. Viewing a balance shouldn't need a transaction
smart-contracts-calling-fee-fb-suspiciou: Right. A site asking you to sign a transaction just to look may be trying to get you to approve something else. Don't sign it.
smart-contracts-calling-fee-opt-premium: It's a paid premium feature for faster results
smart-contracts-calling-fee-fb-premium: Reads are already quick and free. Paying gas wouldn't make looking any faster.
smart-contracts-calling-recap-prompt: Complete the sentences about reading and writing.
smart-contracts-calling-recap-text: Reading a contract changes {b1}, so it's free. Writing needs a signed {b2} and gas, and it only counts once a {b3} includes it in a block.
smart-contracts-calling-recap-explain: Reading only looks, so there's no transaction and no gas. Writing changes something on Ethereum, so it takes a signed transaction that a validator includes in a block.
smart-contracts-calling-takeaway-p1: Reading a contract is free and changes nothing. Writing changes something, so it needs a signed transaction and gas.
smart-contracts-tokens-summary: Why tokens never leave their contract.
smart-contracts-tokens-intro-p1: Your wallet doesn't hold tokens any more than it holds ETH. A token is a smart contract that keeps a list of balances: addresses on one side, amounts on the other. Your tokens are your entry on that list.
smart-contracts-tokens-intro-p2: So sending a token is a write: you ask the token's contract to lower your balance and raise someone else's.
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-prompt: You send some tokens to a friend. Where do those tokens go?
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-opt-apps: From your wallet app into your friend's wallet app
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-fb-apps: Wallet apps only hold keys, so tokens can't be inside them. Test your idea in the next step.
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-opt-list: Nowhere. The token's contract updates its list
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-fb-list: Right. Your balance on the list goes down, and your friend's goes up by the same amount. Try it in the next step.
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-opt-leave: Out of the token's contract and over to your friend's address
smart-contracts-tokens-predict-fb-leaves: An address isn't a container that tokens travel into. Test your idea in the next step.
smart-contracts-tokens-ledger-prompt: Alice sends Bob some tokens. Update the token contract's list to match.
smart-contracts-tokens-ledger-explain: The contract subtracts from the sender and adds to the receiver. The total stays the same, because a transfer moves tokens between entries on the list without creating or destroying any.
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-prompt: Wrapped ETH, or WETH, is a token that stands for ETH: you send ETH to the WETH contract, and it adds the same amount to your balance on its list. After you wrap some ETH, where is your WETH recorded?
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-fb-wallet: Your wallet app only shows what the WETH contract's list says. Delete the app and your WETH is still on that list.
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-opt-list: On the WETH contract's list, under your address
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-fb-list: Right. WETH is a balance kept by the WETH contract, which is why getting your ETH back means asking that same contract to unwrap it.
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-opt-eth: Added to your ordinary ETH balance
smart-contracts-tokens-wrapped-fb-eth: Your ETH balance is kept by Ethereum itself. WETH is a separate balance, kept by the WETH contract.
smart-contracts-tokens-takeaway-p1: A token is a smart contract that keeps a list of balances. Sending one asks the contract to update the list: the tokens never leave it.
smart-contracts-public-summary: Reading a contract's code, and contracts that build on each other.
smart-contracts-public-intro-p1: Every smart contract's code is public, stored on the blockchain where anyone can see it. But it's stored as machine code, which is very hard for people to read.
smart-contracts-public-intro-p2: So developers can publish the source code, the human-readable version, on a block explorer (a website that shows what's on the blockchain). The explorer checks that it matches the code on Ethereum and marks the contract as verified. Then anyone can read what it really does.
smart-contracts-public-trust-prompt: An app says its contract only ever takes a tiny fee on trades. The contract isn't verified on any block explorer. What do you know for sure?
smart-contracts-public-trust-opt-true: The claim is true, since apps can't misdescribe their contracts
smart-contracts-public-trust-fb-true: Anyone can write anything on a website. Only the code decides what the contract actually does.
smart-contracts-public-trust-opt-unknown: Nothing yet. Without verified source code, you can't easily check the claim
smart-contracts-public-trust-fb-unknown: Right. Verification lets you, or experts you trust, read what the contract really does. Until then, it's just a claim.
smart-contracts-public-trust-fb-scam: Unverified doesn't mean malicious. It means you can't easily check, so be extra careful.
smart-contracts-public-blocks-p1: Because contract code is public and anyone can call it, contracts can call other contracts too. Developers snap existing contracts together like building blocks instead of rebuilding everything from scratch.
smart-contracts-public-blocks-p2: Say a trading app only trades tokens, so it needs your ETH as WETH, the wrapped ETH token. It doesn't build its own: its contract simply calls the existing WETH contract, then the contract of the token you want, all inside your one transaction.
smart-contracts-public-swap-prompt: You trade ETH for a token in this trading app. Put what happens in order.
smart-contracts-public-swap-item-send: You sign one transaction sending ETH to the trading app's contract
smart-contracts-public-swap-item-wrap: The trading contract calls the WETH contract to wrap your ETH
smart-contracts-public-swap-item-pay: The trading contract asks the token's contract to move tokens to you
smart-contracts-public-swap-item-read: Your wallet reads your new balance from the token's contract
smart-contracts-public-swap-explain: One transaction ran through three contracts: the trading contract called the WETH contract and the token's contract like building blocks. Showing the result afterwards was a free read.
smart-contracts-public-takeaway-p1: Smart contracts are open: verified source code lets anyone check what a contract does, and contracts build on each other like blocks.
smart-contracts-risks-summary: What can go wrong with a contract, and how to limit what it can touch.
smart-contracts-risks-intro-p1: When a phone app has a bug, the next update fixes it. A smart contract's code can't simply be patched once it's deployed, and because the code is public, attackers can study it too, hunting for mistakes.
smart-contracts-risks-intro-p2: That's why many teams pay for an audit: independent experts review the code before launch. An audit lowers the risk, but it can't promise there are no bugs.
smart-contracts-risks-audit-prompt: A brand-new app says its contracts are "audited, so totally safe". How should you read that?
smart-contracts-risks-audit-opt-safe: It's safe to deposit everything you have
smart-contracts-risks-audit-fb-safe: Audits don't catch every bug, and a bug in a deployed contract can't be patched quickly.
smart-contracts-risks-audit-opt-sign: A good sign, but not a guarantee
smart-contracts-risks-audit-fb-sign: Right. An audit is an extra review that reduces risk. Only put in what you could afford to lose, especially with new contracts.
smart-contracts-risks-audit-opt-pointles: Audits are meaningless, so ignore it
smart-contracts-risks-audit-fb-pointless: Audits do catch many problems. They just can't promise there are none.
smart-contracts-risks-approvals-p1: Some apps need to move your tokens for you, for example to complete a trade. So the first time, your wallet asks you to sign a token approval: a write to the token's contract that lets one specific contract move your tokens, up to an amount you set. Some apps ask for this permission as a message to sign instead, so read every request before you sign it.
smart-contracts-risks-approvals-p2: Some apps ask for an unlimited approval so you never have to approve again. It's convenient, but if that contract has a bug or turns out to be malicious, your whole balance of that token is exposed. Approvals don't expire.
smart-contracts-risks-approvals-p3: You can revoke an approval at any time: a small transaction that cancels it.
smart-contracts-risks-scope-prompt: A trading app needs to move a few of your tokens for a trade. Choose the approval that gets the trade done without exposing more than it needs.
smart-contracts-risks-scope-explain: Approve what the app needs right now. Anything extra stays approved after the trade, where a buggy or malicious contract could use it.
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-prompt: Months ago you gave an app an unlimited approval. You don't use the app anymore. What should you do?
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-opt-disconn: Disconnect your wallet from the app's website
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-fb-disconne: Disconnecting only stops the website seeing your address. The approval lives on the token's contract, so the app's contract can still use it.
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-fb-revoke: Right. Revoking is a write to the token's contract, so it costs a little gas. Tools such as block explorers can list every approval you've given.
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-opt-wait: Nothing. Approvals expire after a while
smart-contracts-risks-revoke-fb-wait: Approvals have no expiry date. One you gave years ago can still be used today.
smart-contracts-risks-takeaway-p1: Contracts can have bugs that nobody can quickly fix, so approve only the tokens an app needs and revoke approvals you no longer use.
smart-contracts-exam-creator-prompt: Someone says they can take ETH out of a contract whenever they like, because they wrote it. When is that true?
smart-contracts-exam-creator-opt-anytime: Always, because whoever writes a contract holds its private key
smart-contracts-exam-creator-opt-rule: Only if the contract's code has a rule that lets them
smart-contracts-exam-creator-explain: A contract's address has no private key. Only its code decides what happens to the ETH it holds, so its creator can take ETH out only if the code includes a rule for that.
smart-contracts-exam-deployed-prompt: You're about to use a contract that was deployed a year ago. Could its creator have simply edited its code since then?
smart-contracts-exam-deployed-opt-anytim: Yes. Creators can edit deployed code whenever they like
smart-contracts-exam-deployed-opt-valida: Yes, as long as validators voted to approve the edit
smart-contracts-exam-deployed-opt-publis: Not simply. Deployed code stays as it was published
smart-contracts-exam-deployed-explain: Once a contract is deployed, its code can't simply be changed, which is what lets everyone rely on its rules. Some contracts are built to switch to new code later, but only when their original code allows it.
smart-contracts-exam-gas-prompt: Which of these need a signed transaction and a gas fee?
smart-contracts-exam-gas-opt-stock: Checking how much ETH a jar contract holds
smart-contracts-exam-gas-opt-add: Adding ETH to that jar contract
smart-contracts-exam-gas-opt-balance: Checking your token balance in your wallet app
smart-contracts-exam-gas-opt-send: Sending some tokens to a friend
smart-contracts-exam-gas-explain: Adding ETH and sending tokens change something on Ethereum, so they're writes that need a signed transaction and gas. Checking what a contract holds or what your balance is only looks, so it's a free read.
smart-contracts-exam-price-check-prompt: Before a website will show you a token's current price, it asks you to sign a transaction and pay a gas fee. What should you do?
smart-contracts-exam-price-check-opt-dec: Decline. Looking up a price is a free read, so the request is a warning sign
smart-contracts-exam-price-check-opt-alw: Sign it. Every contract call needs a transaction
smart-contracts-exam-price-check-opt-onc: Sign it this once. After the first time, looking is free
smart-contracts-exam-price-check-explain: Reading a contract changes nothing, so it never needs a transaction or gas. A site asking you to sign just to look may be trying to get you to approve something else.
smart-contracts-exam-transfer-prompt: A token contract's list has an entry for you and one for a friend. You send your friend some tokens. What does the list show afterwards?
smart-contracts-exam-transfer-opt-create: Your entry is unchanged, and the contract creates new tokens for your friend
smart-contracts-exam-transfer-opt-travel: Your entry goes down, and the tokens travel out to your friend's wallet app
smart-contracts-exam-transfer-opt-update: Your entry goes down and your friend's goes up by the same amount, so the total stays the same
smart-contracts-exam-transfer-explain: Sending a token asks its contract to lower your balance and raise your friend's by the same amount. The tokens never leave the contract, so the total doesn't change.
smart-contracts-exam-restore-prompt: You wrap some ETH into WETH, then delete your wallet app. Later you restore your wallet from its recovery phrase. Where is your WETH?
smart-contracts-exam-restore-opt-list: Still on the WETH contract's list, under your address
smart-contracts-exam-restore-opt-gone: Gone, because it was stored in the app you deleted
smart-contracts-exam-restore-opt-eth: Turned back into ordinary ETH when the app was deleted
smart-contracts-exam-restore-explain: WETH is a balance the WETH contract keeps for your address, and your wallet app only displays it. Restoring your keys gives you back the same address, and its balance is still on the list.
smart-contracts-exam-source-prompt: Every contract's code is already stored on Ethereum. Why do developers also publish its source code on a block explorer?
smart-contracts-exam-source-opt-hidden: Block explorers can only show contracts whose source code is published
smart-contracts-exam-source-opt-machine: The code on Ethereum is machine code, which is very hard for people to read
smart-contracts-exam-source-opt-change: Publishing the source code lets them change the contract's rules later
smart-contracts-exam-source-explain: Contract code is public, but only as machine code. Verified source code is a human-readable version the explorer has checked against the code on Ethereum, so anyone can read what the contract really does.
smart-contracts-exam-swap-prompt: You trade ETH for a token in a trading app. Its contract wraps your ETH through the WETH contract, then gets your tokens from the token's contract. How many transactions do you sign?
smart-contracts-exam-swap-opt-three: Three, one for each contract involved
smart-contracts-exam-swap-opt-two: Two: one to wrap the ETH and one to get the tokens
smart-contracts-exam-swap-opt-one: One. The trading contract calls the other contracts for you
smart-contracts-exam-swap-explain: Contracts can call other contracts like building blocks, so your one transaction runs through all three. Seeing your new balance afterwards is a free read.
smart-contracts-exam-audit-prompt: An app's contracts were audited before launch. What does that tell you?
smart-contracts-exam-audit-opt-lowers: Independent experts reviewed the code, which lowers the risk without ruling out bugs
smart-contracts-exam-audit-opt-bug-free: The contracts have no bugs, so it's safe to deposit everything
smart-contracts-exam-audit-opt-useless: Nothing useful, because audits don't catch real problems
smart-contracts-exam-audit-explain: An audit catches many problems but can't promise there are none, and a deployed contract can't simply be patched. Only put in what you could afford to lose.
smart-contracts-exam-approval-prompt: A year ago you gave a trading app an unlimited approval for one of your tokens. You've stopped using the app. Which of these are true?
smart-contracts-exam-approval-opt-still: The app's contract can still move those tokens today
smart-contracts-exam-approval-opt-discon: Disconnecting your wallet from the app's website cancelled the approval
smart-contracts-exam-approval-opt-revoke: Revoking the approval takes a small transaction with a gas fee
smart-contracts-exam-approval-opt-held: The approval only covers the tokens you held when you gave it
smart-contracts-exam-approval-explain: Approvals live on the token's contract and never expire, and an unlimited one covers your whole balance of that token, including any you receive later. Revoking cancels it with a small transaction, which costs a little gas.

nodes-description: See what a node does all day, why there are different kinds of node software, and what it takes to run one at home.
evm-description: Every node runs the same small computer, called the EVM. Learn how it runs a contract step by step and why each step costs gas.
mev-description: The order of transactions in a block can be worth money. Find out who profits from it and how to protect your trades.
roadmap-description: Learn the plans for lower fees and lighter nodes, and the problem each upgrade is meant to solve.
privacy-description: Everything on Ethereum is public by default. Learn what that reveals about you and how tools like zero-knowledge proofs can help.
build-description: Ready to write your own smart contract? Tutorials, developer docs and hands-on challenges are waiting for you.
